question: Refer to the 2025 IRP Main documents, pp. 35-36, stating that “The size of many of these [new large load] projects far exceed historical annual norms.” Please provide data demonstrating that the new large loads exceed historical norms in spreadsheet format with all formulas and references intact. Provide sourcing for any external data, where applicable.
response: The statement that “The size of many of these [new large load] projects far exceed historical annual norms” was based on qualitative rather than quantitative analysis. From 2015 to 2020, the Company made only one external adjustment to the forecast due to the expected addition of a large load customer. The adjustment made was less than 200 MW. Beginning in 2022 and continuing through 2024, numerous large load customers began looking at the state of Georgia and Georgia Power to build new projects. Many of the new loads exceeded 500 MW, and some have even exceeded 1 GW. These loads are much larger than anything that the Company has ever seen before. As a result, there is no spreadsheet with data and formulas to provide that demonstrates the new large loads exceed historical norms.

question: Refer to the document titled “B2025 Load and Energy Forecast PUBLIC DISCLOSURE,” in Technical Appendix Volume 1, p. 16, Attachment 2.0-1. Please explain how the Company calculates its “Territorial Supply (GWh)”.
response: Retail energy is energy at the customer level, which is referred to as Level D. Territorial Supply is measured at the generator level, which the Company refers to as Level A. The difference between Level A and Level D is line losses that occur between the generator and the delivery to the customer’s meter. To calculate Territorial Supply, Retail sales are multiplied by the estimates of loss factors.

question: Refer to the document titled “B2025 Load and Energy Forecast PUBLIC DISCLOSURE,” in Technical Appendix Volume 1, p. 32. Please describe the “IPGA” variable and justify the inclusion of this Industrial Production Index.
response:
An Industrial Production Index (“IPI”) measures the real output of the manufacturing, mining, and utilities sectors in an economy. It is a key economic indicator used to gauge the level of industrial activity and production over time. The index is typically expressed relative to a base year, which is set to 100. For example, an index value of 103 indicates that industrial production in an economy has increased by 3% compared to the base year.
The IPI for the United States is published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. There is no official IPI at the state level. However, S&P Global, the Company’s provider of historical economic data and forecasts, produces one for each state based on the U.S. index. “IPGA” is the IPI provided by S&P Global for the State of Georgia. The Georgia IPI is preferred because it is calculated based on the state’s industrial mix, rather than the national average. The expectation is that the IPGA should thus be a better indicator of industrial activity in the state, which is why it is included in the forecast model for Industrial sales.

question: Refer to the document titled “B2025 Load and Energy Forecast PUBLIC DISCLOSURE,” in Technical Appendix Volume 1, p. 38. Please describe the term “unbilled sales,” and why these occur.
response:
Unbilled sales refer to the electricity that has been delivered to customers but has not yet been billed in a month. The Company bills its customers across the month in 21 different Bill Groups. Calendar energy sales are the basis of the Company’s actual financial record. Both billed and unbilled sales are utilized to calculate calendar sales, where unbilled represents sales in the portion of the month that has not yet been billed but must be estimated.
The forecast is estimated on a billing basis, and unbilled energy is estimated as to mimic how actual sales data are ultimately reported on the calendar month basis. Calendar sales = Billed sales + current month Unbilled sales – previous month Unbilled sales.

response:
Residential customers are forecasted at an aggregate level using the model presented in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Section 4.2.1. This forecast is then disaggregated into single family, multi-family, and manufactured homes using housing type trends from the S&P Global housing stock forecast and calibrated to historic Georgia Power billing data splits.

question:
Please refer to p. 163 of the “2024 GA ITS Ten-Year Plan,” within the “2025 IRP Volume 3 TRADE SECRET,” regarding the Plant Yates Breaker and Half Station and respond to the following questions:
a. 	What operational and reliability benefits will the reconfiguration of the Yates 6 & 7 substation to a Breaker and Half configuration provide.
b. 	How will the project improve grid flexibility?
c. 	How will the new breaker and a half configuration impact fault isolation and system protection?
response:
In a breaker and a half configuration, each circuit is connected to two breakers, which allows a breaker to be taken out of service for maintenance without interrupting power to the surrounding circuits, allowing more flexibility in switching operations. In the current ring bus configuration, the substation has a continuous loop of breakers connecting all circuits. If a breaker needs maintenance, it often requires opening adjacent breakers, which can disrupt service to multiple circuits. The rebuild of the Yates substation to a breaker and a half configuration provides additional bays to accommodate the generator tie lines for Yates #8, #9, and #10 combustion turbines (“CTs”), enhancing reliability and operational flexibility.
See the Company’s response to subpart (a).
In a breaker and a half configuration, each circuit is connected to two breakers therefore, under breaker failure or fault conditions, the circuit can still be cleared using the remaining breaker. This allows the rest of the substation to continue operating even if a breaker fails or requires maintenance. In the current ring bus configuration, the substation has a continuous loop of breakers connecting all circuits. While this provides some redundancy, a breaker failure can impact multiple circuits, potentially requiring the opening of more breakers to clear the fault.

question:
Please refer to p. 97 of the “2024 GA ITS Ten-Year Plan,” within the “2025 IRP Volume 3 TRADE SECRET,” regarding the GTC: LaGrange - North Opelika 230kV (New Line) and respond to the following questions:
How does this new 230kV line improve regional power reliability and support growing industrial loads?
What are the expected load flow impacts on the adjacent transmission infrastructure?
Will this project require additional substation investments, and what are the associated costs?
How does this project fit into Southern Company’s overall transmission expansion strategy?
response:
The Georgia Transmission Corporation (“GTC”): Lagrange-North Opelika 230kV line provides an additional network connection from Alabama Power Company (“APC”) into Georgia and a high-capacity corridor to alleviate the West to East flows. This new transmission line addresses thermal constraints as defined in the Steady State Transmission Planning Criteria of the NERC Reliability Standard (TPL-001-5) under P1-Single Contingency event. Please refer to Section III.A, Table 6 (p 29) of the 2024 GA ITS Ten-Year Plan and Section B2, R3 (p 18) of the ITS Planning Procedure #9, in Technical Appendix Volume 3. -This project also supports future Georgia Power unit retirements as noted in Appendix D of the 2024 Georgia ITS Ten-Year Plan in Technical Appendix Volume 3.
The GTC: Lagrange-North Opelika 230kV line provides load reduction mainly to the Fortson – Lagrange 230kV transmission line. Historically, the Fortson - Lagrange 230kV has been a heavily loaded line, supporting steadily the West to East flows. Additionally, accommodating and coordinating necessary outages to facilitate maintenance on the Fortson - Lagrange 230kV is difficult; therefore, the Lagrange - North Opelika 230kV New line project is essential to support the area.
The construction of the Lagrange - North Opelika 230kV line requires modifications at the Lagrange and North Opelika substation in addition to the construction of Oseligee Creek as a metering station. Refer to Section E (p 97) of the 2024 GA ITS Ten-Year Plan for the cost associated to the work needed at Lagrange substation owned by Georgia Power. Oseligee Creek will be constructed and owned by GTC. North Opelika is owned by APC; therefore, cost for these facilities will be incurred by GTC and APC.
Please refer to the Company’s response to subpart (a).

Refer to the document titled “B2025 Load and Energy Forecast PUBLIC DISCLOSURE,” in Technical Appendix Volume 1, pp. 124-125 and p. 111. Please respond to the following questions related to the DSM forecast:
On p. 111 the Company stated that “one of the DSM sensitivities assumes that there is no DSM included over the forecast horizon”. Please confirm that this statement refers to the “load growth with no DSM growth” sensitivity. If so, please clarify if the sensitivity assumes no DSM at all (i.e., removes all DSM related to the development of more efficient technologies, more stringent efficiency standards, and Company-sponsored DSM programs) or if the sensitivity assumes a baseline level of future DSM without any forecasted growth of that baseline level.
The Company stated that “DSM programs are assumed to continue through the forecast horizon.” Please describe how the DSM programs that Georgia Power offers to its residential and commercial customers were extended through the forecast. Were historical values from a given year used and held flat throughout the forecast horizon or was an escalation factor applied? Please identify the year(s) of historical data that were used to extend the forecast.
Please describe how the Company prevents double counting of energy efficiency adjustments in its forecast. For example, the Company stated that “other conservation measures undertaken by customers, whether explicitly induced by a marketing program or proactively undertaken by a customer for some other reason, will become embedded in the historical energy data and will be implicitly propagated throughout the forecast.”
Does the Company have separate and independent forecast values for energy efficiency adjustments that are driven by the Company’s DSM programs and related incentives versus adjustments that are driven by natural customer behavior that adopts more efficient technologies over time? If so, please demonstrate how the Company adjusts its load forecast for each of these adjustments, with each adjustment as a line item. Provide your response in spreadsheet format with all formulas intact.
If not, how does the company avoid double counting energy efficiency adjustments? Since DSM program incentives accelerate customer adoption of energy efficient technologies, how does the Company account for this acceleration given that end-use efficiency standards and natural customer behavior already would capture these energy efficiency adjustments over time?
Does the Company produce a forecast that removes future projected Company DSM program adjustments for use in IRP modeling so that the model can select DSM resources as part of an optimized portfolio? If so, please provide the results of this forecast in spreadsheet format. If not, please explain why not.
response:
Yes, the Demand Side Management (“DSM”) sensitivity that “assumes that there is no DSM included over the forecast horizon” refers to the “load growth with no DSM growth” sensitivity.
When the Company created the No DSM sensitivity, it removed the future impacts related to Company-sponsored DSM programs from the Budget 2025 forecast. The impacts of these programs on the energy and peak forecasts removed from the Budget 2025 forecast to create the No DSM sensitivity can be found in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment C TRADE SECRET.
DSM program adjustments included in the Budget 2025 forecast were based upon the programs in the DSM Program Planner filed with the 2022 IRP, updated to reflect savings and budgets from the Commission’s Final Order. Savings from DSM measures with installation dates of 2023 were excluded from external adjustments as these measures were assumed to be embedded in the historical energy data and implicitly propagated throughout the forecast. Savings from DSM measures with installation dates from 2024 through 2043 were subtracted from the energy and peak forecasts as an external adjustment. For forecasted years beyond 2043, the 2043 DSM savings levels were assumed to remain constant and subtracted from the energy and peak forecasts as an external adjustment.
The Company prevents double counting by only including incremental DSM impacts from Company-sponsored DSM programs in the forecast. The impacts of any conservation measures undertaken by customers, whether explicitly induced by a Company sponsored program or proactively undertaken by a customer for some other reason, are already included in the historical data. Since the Company’s short-term models are estimated using the historical data, reductions in energy use resulting from conservation measures are implicitly propagated throughout the forecast.
Yes. The Company has a separate and independent forecast for energy efficiency adjustments driven by the Company’s DSM programs and related incentives. Please refer to STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment C TRADE SECRET.
The Company does not have a separate and independent forecast for energy efficiency adjustments driven by natural customer behavior that adopts more efficient technologies over time.
As discussed in subpart (c) above, the Company avoids double counting by only including the incremental DSM impacts from Company-sponsored DSM programs. Any impacts from Company-sponsored programs or from changes in natural customer behavior would show up in the historical data and be part of the baseline forecast. The estimated impacts from Company-sponsored DSM programs are treated as an external adjustment in Budget 2025, reducing both energy sales and peaks.
Yes, the Company produced a forecast that removes future projected Company DSM program adjustments for use in Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) modeling so that the model can select DSM resources as part of an optimized portfolio. Please see STF-DEA-3-1 Attachment TRADE SECRET for the hourly loads in the No DSM load Scenario.

Refer to the document titled “B2025 Load and Energy Forecast TRADE SECRET,” in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Section 7.0 Forecast Adjustments for Large Customers:
a. 	Please describe the process for evaluating the Company’s available transmission capacity to host large load customers. Did the Company perform analysis to understand if there is sufficient available transmission capacity to host large load customers in the near-term (i.e., 5 years or less)? If so, please provide the analysis with all source workbooks and formulas intact. If not, why not?
b. 	In conversations with potential large load customers, have in-service dates been delayed, ramp up schedules changed, total announced load changed, or projects canceled due (in whole or in part) to insufficient available transmission capacity? If so, please provide the projects and the associated impacts to schedule, total load, etc.
c. 	Referring to Figure 7.1.2-1: Sequencing of Large Load and Sources of Uncertainty on p. 104, at what point(s) in the sequence during discussions with large load customers does the Company perform a transmission analysis to evaluate if there is sufficient available transmission capacity to serve the customer? After identifying the point(s), please describe how the transmission analysis is performed including if more detailed analysis and iterations occur after certain milestones are reached (i.e., after a letter of agreement is signed, interconnection study is performed, etc.).
d. 	Please describe the process for determining the cost of transmission, distribution, network, or other infrastructure upgrades triggered by a large customer’s interconnection request and how it is determined how much the large customer must pay for those upgrades. Have any large load customer projects been delayed, downsized, or cancelled after learning that the customer must pay for such upgrades? If so, please provide a list of each project.
response:
Yes. The Company conducts transmission planning analyses to identify necessary transmission improvements to facilitate the integration of the large load customers as part of a broader study and offer process outlined in the six steps below. Refer to the STF-DEA-3-6(a) folder in the CEII account on the FTP site for reports on the unsigned large loads in the forecast. The signed loads included in the forecast are incorporated in the 2024 GA ITS Ten Year Plan along with the 2024 load flow files. Refer to Trade STF-PIA-5-16 Attachment TRADE SECRET.
The following outlines the study and offer process for large load facilities:
Initial customer intake form is received by Business Development department.
Request moves to Generation Capacity Review committee to ensure that generation capacity is available to serve the load.
Once request clears Generation Capacity Review, the request moves to Transmission Planning to determine what transmission improvements are required to facilitate the integration of the load into the transmission system and coordinates with Area Planning in determining the customer substation layout. This initial process only covers steady state analyses. Dynamic modeling/analyses typically occur after a Request for Service (“RFS”) or Contract for Electric Service (“CES”) is received by the Company.
After Transmission Planning studies (steady state) are completed, the request along with the Transmission Planning report is forwarded to the Project Management Organization (“PMO”) to develop implementation timelines along with any outage coordination concerns.
After the PMO review is completed, the request along with all key analysis information is used in the evaluation of an initial offer.
Before any initial or binding offer is made, the request along with the proposed method of service, all required improvements and additions, including associated estimated costs, are routed for approval to the appropriate authorization groups as noted in Section G2, Exhibit 1 of Technical Appendix Volume 3.
No, projects have not been delayed or cancelled due to insufficient available transmission capacity.
See Company’s response to subpart (a). Once the Company receives either an RFS or CES from the customer, the load along with associated projects are modeled in the official transmission planning base cases and included in the expansion planning processes. This process is also used for similar loads signed by other load serving entities in the Integrated Transmission System. Additionally, dynamic modeling and analyses are initiated to identify any additional required transmission improvements or customer required improvements.
See Company’s response to part subpart (a). Refer also to Section G1 of Technical Appendix Volume 3 for a description of how system costs are incorporated into the financial evaluation of new customer projects. A customer offer is developed to meet the Company’s minimum financial requirements, and projects must also meet the applicable standards outlined in Georgia Power Company Rules, Regulations, and Rate Schedules for Electric Service. To date, no large load customer projects have been delayed, downsized, or cancelled based on the financial requirements reflected in the customer offer.

question:
Referring to the B2025 Load Realization Model, please respond to the following questions:
Please describe how the Company applies the results of the model to adjust the organic load forecast on an energy basis.
Please describe how the Company applies the results of the model to adjust the organic load forecast on a peak load basis.
response:
As stated in Section 7.0 in Technical Appendix Volume 1, p. 102, energy sales from the Load Realization Model (“LRM”) are treated as an external adjustment to the baseline organic sales forecast. This means that the risk-adjusted large load energy forecasts are added on to the baseline/organic energy forecasts.
Peaks are also treated as an external adjustment to the organic forecast. The large load data center energy forecast from the LRM gets a data center load shape applied to it to get hourly load values. These values are then added to the organic hourly load forecast values for the commercial class load and resulting class peak. Similarly, the energy forecast for new large load industrial customers gets an industrial load shape applied to it, and the hourly values are added to the baseline organic hourly load forecast to get the total industrial class peak.

question: Refer to the Company’s response to STF-DEA-1-10. response:
The Company utilizes Adjusted-R2 as part of the model selection process instead of R2.  Adjusted-R2 accounts for the number of independent variables in the model and penalizes the inclusion of unnecessary variables, which helps to avoid over-specification.
As previously discussed in STF-DEA-1-10, weather is the most significant driver for usage per customer (“UPC”) variability. To demonstrate, the Company ran models that included only weather variables, resulting in a slight decline in the Adjusted R2 (-0.4% for residential and -2.5% for commercial), as shown in the table below. Excluding weather variables, which are relevant for monthly usage variation, would result in a biased estimate of the coefficients and produce misleading forecasting results.
When economic variables are introduced in the models, the Company ensures their inclusion does not significantly change the values of the weather coefficients or their statistical significance, which would be a sign of multicollinearity. As for the inclusion of Autoregressive terms, please see STF-DEA-5-2 and STF-DEA-5-3.

question:
Refer to the Company’s response to STF-DEA-1-12. Please respond to the following questions.
Please provide a narrative explanation why it is appropriate to assume autocorrelation in the Residential Use per Customer model.
Please provide a narrative explanation of how Residential Use per Customer in billing day ‘n’ is correlated with Residential Use per Customer in billing day ‘n-1.’
Please provide a narrative explanation of how the autoregressive term accounts for variation in residential usage that is otherwise unaccounted for by other variables in the Residential Use per Customer model.
response:
The Company utilizes several statistical tests to identify autocorrelation in the residuals, including the Durbin Watson Statistic, the Breusch-Godfrey Serial Correlation LM Test, and the Autocorrelation and Partial Correlation functions.
The residential use per customer model is a time series model in which autocorrelation is a common occurrence. In the residential use per customer model, weather is a key driver, and it is highly autocorrelated. For example, today’s temperature is likely to be similar to the prior day’s temperature, creating a pattern that persists over time, which introduces positive autocorrelation into the regression model.
Autoregressive terms are employed to correct for autocorrelation in the model. If autocorrelation is unaddressed, the Least Square estimators are inefficient, and the standard errors of the regression coefficients are biased and inconsistent, potentially leading to incorrect inferences.

Please provide a narrative explanation why it is appropriate to assume autocorrelation in the MARTA sales model.
Please provide a narrative explanation of how MARTA sales in month ‘n’ are correlated with MARTA sales in month ‘n-1.’
Please provide a narrative explanation of how the autoregressive term accounts for variation in MARTA sales that are otherwise unaccounted for by other variables in the MARTA sales model.
Please explain why the Company selected lag terms of 3 and 6 for each autoregressive term.
response:
The Company utilizes several statistical tests to identify autocorrelation in the residuals, including the Durbin Watson Statistic, the Breusch-Godfrey Serial Correlation LM Test, and the Autocorrelation and Partial Correlation functions.
The MARTA model is a time series model in which autocorrelation is a common occurrence. In addition to weather, recent historical commuting patterns and train schedules are significant drivers of MARTA sales. As these patterns persist over time, autocorrelation is introduced into the regression model.
Autoregressive (“AR”) terms are employed to correct for autocorrelation in the model. While weather explains monthly variations and the COVID variable accounts for the drop in commuters and train schedules during the pandemic, there lacks a suitable economic variable that reflects MARTA usage.
If autocorrelation is unaddressed, the Least Square estimators are inefficient, and the standard errors of the regression coefficients are biased and inconsistent, potentially leading to incorrect inferences.
The Company selected lag terms 1 and 6 for the MARTA model. Their selection was based on the study of the correlogram of the MARTA model without the AR terms. The Company used the Partial Autocorrelation function to identify the orders of the AR terms to include.

question: Referring to the Company’s peak load forecast model, conducted in Metrix, please demonstrate how the Company adjusts its calibrated long-term energy forecast to a peak demand forecast. Provide this demonstration for a representative year (2030) on a monthly basis. Include in your response both a narrative description of this calibration process as well as a quantitative spreadsheet demonstration of how the monthly energy forecast is adjusted to produce the peak demand forecast. Ensure the quantitative demonstration retains all formulas and references.
response:
The requested calculations do not exist. The Company utilizes the MetrixLT software to perform the calibration of hourly load shapes to monthly energy sales.
In general, the uncalibrated hourly load is summed for the month then compared to the monthly sales for the month.
A simple example: The sum of the hourly load is 1,000 and the sales forecast for the month is 1,100. The factor to calibrate the hourly load would be 1.10. That factor would be applied to every hour in the month so the resulting calibrated hourly load equals the input sales forecast target. After the calibration, the maximum hour is found to identify the peak.

This allows the short-term outlook to grow/decline using the long-term end-use growth trends.

question: Referring to the Company’s B2025 TRADE SECRET Load Realization Model, please explain if a project’s likelihood to 1) select Georgia Power, 2) change its load ramp schedule, or 3) materialize its load as expected, would change over time. For example, does the Company expect that a project introduced in the 2023 IRP update should present the same assumptions for the three variables identified above if it is still in the large load pipeline as of Q2 2024?
response:
The likelihood of a project selecting Georgia Power may change as that project advances through the Company’s internal review process and shows increasing signs of selecting Georgia Power. The customer-provided load ramp input could also change. For example, as time progresses and the Company receives updated customer information, information such as load ramp may change and, as such, the Company would reflect the updated customer information in the Load Realization Model (“LRM”). It is important to note that an update to the customer ramp does not imply a change in the likelihood. Instead, it represents a modification to the input load ramp, which would then be evaluated within the framework of the LRM.
A project’s load realization percentage remains unchanged over time, as the Company assesses load realization based on the customer’s specific class and segment. As long as the project's class and segment do not change, the project’s load realization ranges will also remain consistent.

question: Referring to the Company’s B2025 TRADE SECRET Load Realization Model, please explain why the Company chose to maintain a rolling large pipeline (whereby projects are added to and subtracted from the pipeline) as opposed to simulating different tranches of projects based on when they enter the pipeline.
response:
The decision to maintain a rolling large load pipeline, where projects are continuously added and subtracted, is based on established principles in probability and statistics. Specifically, there is no definitive relationship between the percentile of the sum of two random variables and the percentiles of the individual random variables. This means that simulating different tranches or subsets of the large load pipeline based on their entry time does not provide meaningful insight into the overall distribution of the full large load pipeline.
To accurately determine the distribution, including the P50, of the large load pipeline, it is necessary to simulate all projects jointly. This approach ensures that the full scope of the pipeline is considered, providing a comprehensive and accurate representation.
Additionally, creating separate tranches of projects based on their entry time does not eliminate the need to account for projects that are no longer in the pipeline. Given the dynamic and frequently changing nature of the pipeline, it is more practical and efficient to maintain a consolidated and centralized pipeline. This approach allows for updates and accurate reflection of all changes, avoiding the complexity and inefficiency of managing multiple tranches or subsets.

question:
Of the 107 projects in the 2022 plan, only 39 still appear as the same TEAMS numbered project in the 2025 plan.
Please confirm whether TEAMS numbers are ever reused or reassigned to a different project scope, and if so, provide the protocol for how that is tracked and disclosed.

response:
TEAMS identifier numbers are not reused or reassigned to different projects. Each TEAMS identifier is a unique project identifier. Project scope may evolve as planning studies progress and system needs change. Depending on the nature and extent of a scope change, the existing TEAMS identifier may remain associated with the project, or a new TEAMS identifier may be created to reflect a materially different project scope. TEAMS identifiers are tracked within the Company’s project management processes.
The TEAMS identifier numbers associated with projects included in the 2022 Ten-Year Plan have not been reused or reassigned to other projects.

Projects included in the GA ITS 10-Year Plan are developed based on the severity of planning criteria violations identified for a given study year, NERC compliance requirements, and associated system risks. As the transmission system evolves, power flow patterns change, which can alter the location, severity, and timing of thermal and voltage violations. Consequently, projects may be reevaluated, modified, deferred, or moved outside the 10-year planning horizon as system conditions and planning assumptions change.
Increases in project cost estimates between January 1, 2022, and December 31, 2025, may reflect changes in project scope, engineering assumptions, equipment requirements, right-of-way needs, and construction sequencing or outage requirements. Estimates may also be affected by unforeseen conditions and external factors beyond the Company's control, including supply chain constraints, equipment availability and delivery delays, increased demand for skilled labor and associated labor costs, material cost increases, inflation, and tariffs or other trade-related costs. question:
Georgia Power's TYP project listings reference zone numbers in addition to TEAMS numbers (e.g., in project location or planning area designations.
Please describe the zone numbering methodology, including how zone boundaries are determined, how zone numbers are assigned to projects, and whether zone numbers or boundaries have changed between the 2022 TYP and 2025 TYP.
Please provide a supporting map showing all current transmission planning zones, their boundaries, and zone numbers.
response:
The transmission planning zone numbers referenced in the Georgia Ten-Year Transmission Plans (“TYPs”) have remained unchanged for more than a decade. question:
In Tables I-1 and I-2 in the Reserve Margin Study, please explain
How average transfer capability and other inputs were used to calculate the availability of imports during Southern Company’s periods of peak need.
Were the higher thermal ratings of transmission lines during peak winter conditions accounted for, and if so how?

response:
The average transfer capabilities, obtained from the December 2023 Open Access Same-time Information System (“OASIS”), were used to define the maximum hourly energy transfer that could be made between the regions. If excess generation was available, the economics in the buying and selling regions supported a purchase, and transmission capacity was available, the model made the transaction. During periods of emergency need in the Southern Company System, the additional capacity benefit margin (“CBM”) was also made available. However, the model could only utilize this additional transmission capacity if the neighboring region had excess generation to sell.
The determination of the average transfer capabilities is not based directly on thermal ratings of transmission lines during peak winter conditions.
The cold weather outage assumptions were implemented in the study as additional load that appeared at each temperature per the trend lines on Reserve Margin Study page 22. This was calculated as the nominal dispatchable capacity subject to cold weather outages times the incremental cold weather equivalent forced outage rate (“EFOR”) for each degree of temperature below 25°F. This additional load is additive to the actual expected temperature-based demand. If the neighboring region could meet its hourly load including the additional load that represents resource outages, any remaining available capacity could be marketed to any connected region.

question:

Southern Company’s Commercial Operations organization has advised that under extremely high summer load conditions, the availability of purchases in the marketplace is unlikely to exceed 2,000 MW. Likewise, under extremely high winter load conditions, the availability of purchases in the marketplace is unlikely to exceed 1,500 MW. These limitations exist for two reasons. First, during such extreme conditions, other market participants may also be experiencing conditions that approach the limits of their own systems. Therefore, even though the model may show some available diversity between the regions, those entities may be unwilling to sell that capacity due to the risks and uncertainty within their own systems. Second, during such extreme conditions, there is often a high likelihood of transmission curtailments, in which case some capacity that may be available may not be deliverable to the System – even if there is transmission interface capability available. These limitations cannot be precisely modeled within SERVM, but a combination of both limits on sales price and hurdle rates between regions has been implemented as a means of addressing these issues.”

What sales price limit and hurdle rates were used?

There were no hourly limits imposed on market purchases except for the average transfer capabilities defined on pages 7-8 of the 2024 Reserve Margin Study.
The max sales price limit used in the 2024 Reserve Margin Study, which represents the highest price resource that a region will sell to another, was $50/MWh for all Southern Company purchases. This price was only applied during non-scarcity conditions and did not impact emergency purchases. The sales price limit was $250/MWh for all Southern Company sales. question:

Based on these efforts, it is expected that these incremental outages will not begin to materialize until the local temperatures reach approximately 10°F for retail, owned or operated resources and approximately 18°F for contracted resources.”

On January 8, 2015, the system-weighted temperature dropped to 12.9°F resulting in an incremental cold weather outage rate of 7.63%. A forced outage analysis was performed at the peak load hour for Winter Storm Elliott for Power Purchase Agreement (“PPA”) resources contracted by Georgia Power at the time.
 | Total Capacity | Capacity on Reserve | Capacity on Planned | Capacity on Forced | Available Capacity | Forced Outage Rate
PPA | 2,336.12 | 310.18 | 317.69 | 611.20 | 1,097.05 | 36%
Biomass PPA | 303 | - | - | 267 | 36 | 88%
Per results of this analysis, the forced outage rate for PPA resources was much higher than normal. In contrast, Georgia Power resources had a total outage rate of 12% during the same hour. question: Please see the statement at page 34 of the Reserve Margin Study that “For the type of analysis performed in this study, where the objective is to balance the cost of the incremental capacity with the reliability benefits achieved by that capacity addition, it is necessary that the capacity considered represents a true reliability addition, as opposed to an addition for both reliability and energy economics. question: Please see the following statement in the Renewable Integration Study at page 13: “The base case database provided by Southern Company Services contained a total of 71 active solar resources in the study year, which together represented approximately 4,488 MW of solar capacity. Several of these modeled resources included an aggregation of a geographically diverse set of aggregated distributed generator (“DG”) solar resources. Together, these resources are reasonably representative of the future geographic diversity that could be expected on the Southern Company system. Therefore, each of the solar scenarios were created by scaling the capacity of these resources until the total capacity of the portfolio reached the desired tranche size.” Please provide justification, and all analysis relied on the by the Company, for the claim that “these resources are reasonably representative of the future geographic diversity that could be expected on the Southern Company system,” and explain why higher penetrations of solar resources will not see lower fleet-wide output variability due to the geographic diversity inherent in deploying solar at new locations.
response: The primary purpose of the Renewable Integration Study is to identify the operating costs necessary to maintain a base level of intra-hour reliability across multiple solar scenarios. The hourly solar load shapes that were scaled for each scenario are not critical to this intra-hour analysis since flexibility violations as measured in this study occur inside each modeled hour. Instead, the intra-hour volatility parameters are the critical component. The intra-hour volatility parameters included the existing solar sites, but only for the first 4,488 MW. Additional solar sites added to meet the scenario targets (10 GW, 15 GW, 20 GW, etc.) were chosen based on planned solar sites and the transmission interconnection queue as a proxy for where future solar sites might be located. Thus, the study accurately captures intra-hour geographic diversity based on current information. Figure 4 on page 14 of the study further supports this statement, demonstrating that as solar penetrations increase, the extreme tails of the divergence profiles exhibit less deviation from a smooth profile.

question:
Regarding the Company’s “strategic transmission planning process,” whereby the Company “complet[es] transmission evaluations separate from and incremental to the standard ten-year transmission planning processes” (Main Panel Test. 37:21-23):
a. 	Please describe how this strategic transmission planning process differs from that described in Technical Appendix Vol. 3 Sections A, Transmission Planning Description and Process, and D.1, 10 Year Expansion Plan.
b. 	Please describe how the Company mitigated unnecessary duplication of efforts in running two, separate transmission evaluations contemporaneously.
c. 	If the Company accounted for changes in the generation mix as part of its standard ten-year transmission planning process, would separate strategic transmission planning processes be necessary? If yes, why?
d. 	Does the Company expect Order 1920-A compliance will reduce or eliminate the need for strategic transmission planning because its standard transmission planning process will account for changes in the generation mix? If not, why not?
response:
The Company defines its strategic transmission planning process as identifying long lead time projects that solve multiple constraints on the transmission system. These strategic projects can be developed as part of the standard ten-year transmission planning process, or they can be developed in separate and incremental transmission evaluations as the need for those types of evaluations arise, such as the Solar Sensitivity analyses and Unit Retirement analyses due to environmental rules.
There are no duplicate efforts when running studies that are separate and incremental to the ten-year transmission planning process. These studies involve distinct scenarios that are not evaluated as part of the standard ten-year planning process.
For the development of the base ten-year plan, the Company takes into consideration firm and future firm generation and load.
FERC Orders 1920, 1920-A, and 1920-B mandate a Long-Term Regional Transmission Planning (“LTRTP”) process with a 20-year planning horizon and various changes to the current, 10-year horizon regional planning process. Compliance with these orders will not eliminate or reduce the need for strategic transmission planning given that the LTRTP is limited in terms of scenarios and is solely for the purposes of the selection of Long-Term Regional Transmission Facilities by the Southeastern Regional Transmission Planning (“SERTP”) sponsors for cost allocation based on the identified benefits. To continue to meet the future needs of its customers, the Company will need to continue strategic transmission planning to identify necessary transmission system expansion. The resultant Company transmission plan will be included in the SERTP processes to determine if there are “regional” transmission facilities that are more efficient or cost effective.

question:
Several projects in the Ten-Year Plan include building or rebuilding 115kV or 230kV lines. In the following instances the Ten-Year Plan proposes to build two lower-voltage lines next to or in close proximity to one another:
Union City – Yates 230kV White Line Rebuild and Union City – Yates 230kV (Black) Line Rebuild
CC – QTS Fayetteville Transmission Needs
CC – Tomochichi 500/230kV Solution (CC Network Improvements)
For each, please explain whether the Company considered building, instead, a single, 500kV line. If not, please explain why.
response:
The Company and Integrated Transmission System (“ITS”) practices do not permit load to be served directly from the 500kV network. Consequently, the decision to build or rebuild lower-voltage lines, as outlined in the Ten-Year Plan, was made to align with these practices.
A single 500kV line from Union City to Yates was not considered in this scenario because there is no existing 500kV infrastructure at Yates substation. In addition to acquiring new right of way (“ROW”) and building a new 500kV line, a 500/230kV autotransformer and a 500kV substation switchyard would have to be added at Yates. The timeline to complete this work to meet compliance need dates was not feasible when compared to rebuilding both 230kV lines. Refer to Section B.1 and B.2 in Technical Appendix Volume 3 of the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”).
The two 230kV lines are being constructed from Ashley Park 500/230kV substation to Charles 230kV and Creola 230kV. The two lines serve a customer load and are needed to provide reliability and redundant service. This allows for one line to be out of service for maintenance or an unexpected outage while the customer maintains connectivity through the second line. A single 500kV line to the customer would not provide this flexibility, and it creates excess segmentation, which can degrade the system integrity and reliability.
Two 230kV lines are being constructed from Tomochichi 500/230kV substation to Towaliga River customer substation. Two lines are needed for reliability purposes of redundancy of service to the customer. This allows for one line to be out of service for maintenance or an unexpected outage while the customer maintains connectivity through the second line. A single 500kV line to the customer would not provide this flexibility.

a. 	Does the Company’s practice only planning transmission for large loads that are confirmed with signed contracts risk underbuilding network transmission that would be used by multiple potential large loads? If not, why not?

response:
No. Each customer load interconnection is studied in detail either by itself, if it is the only large load in the local area, or in a cluster study to ensure that the transmission solution provides increased reliability and adequate capacity headroom for future growth. If new large loads materialize in an area that a transmission solution has been planned for a different large load, that solution can either be adjusted or expanded to accommodate the newly signed large loads if the original solution did not have enough headroom.
No. Projects are designed to provide solutions that create enough capacity to address the immediate constraint while allowing for future load growth.  The Transmission Planning models are regularly updated to reflect the latest contracted large loads, and the transmission system is assessed in a cycle basis as described in Section A of Technical Appendix Volume 3 to the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan.
Yes. The Company performs area cluster studies adding multiple potential customers’ loads and assesses the transmission system needs to serve those loads.

response:
The B2025 Load and Energy Forecast TRADE SECRET included with the 2025 IRP filing is the documentation describing the development of the Georgia Power official baseline load forecast (peak demand and energy). Excel versions of all the data tables presented in the Technical Appendix were also provided to Commission Staff as workpapers on January 31, 2025.
There is no documentation specific to the development of an overall Southern Retail Operating Company forecast. Rather, forecasts are developed for each of the operating companies (Alabama Power, Georgia Power, and Mississippi Power). Georgia Power’s peak and energy forecasts have already been provided in Section 2 of the B2025 Load and Energy Forecast TRADE SECRET. The aggregated Southern Company load forecast (peak demand and energy) is included in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment A.
The initial IRP filing on January 31, 2025, included working models for the Georgia Power short-term energy forecast; long-term energy forecast; peak forecast; and large load realization forecast. Five Georgia Power workpapers were also included, which were used in the development of the Budget 2025 baseline forecast. Workpapers, models, and adjustments of other operating companies are not provided as they contain the proprietary and confidential information of other companies.
Workpapers for Georgia Power’s forecast adjustments, including cogeneration, demand-side management (“DSM”), behind-the-meter solar, and electric vehicles (“EVs”) are provided in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment B TRADE SECRET; STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment C TRADE SECRET; STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment D TRADE SECRET; and STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment E TRADE SECRET, respectively.
Georgia Power load sensitivities are described and summarized in Section 8.1 of the B2025 Load and Energy Forecast TRADE SECRET. These sensitivities are created by changing one concept at a time while keeping all other variables at their baseline levels and then reporting the forecasts of energy and summer and winter peak loads. As described in Section 8.1, the Company developed seven sensitivities: (1) high economic growth; (2) low economic growth; (3) no load growth; (4) high growth in large load customers; (5) load growth with no DSM growth; (6) load growth with aggressive DSM growth; and (7) load growth using a 20-year normal definition of weather. The results for each sensitivity, including energy, summer peak demand, and winter peak demand are summarized in Attachments 8.1-1, 8.1-2 and 8.1-3, respectively in B2025 Load and Energy Forecast TRADE SECRET. The inputs from S&P Global for both the High and Low Economic Growth sensitivities are provided in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment F TRADE SECRET (for short-term models) and STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment G TRADE SECRET (for long-term models).

The High Growth (P95) in Large Customers is treated as an external adjustment. In this case, the baseline forecast of large loads is replaced with the high growth (P95) forecast of large loads. Similar to the High Growth (P95) in Large Customers sensitivity, DSM is treated as an external adjustment. Workpapers, models, and adjustments used to develop Georgia Power’s sensitivities and/or scenarios are presented within this data request. The Company cannot provide the Southern Company workpapers used to calculate the load forecast in Aurora, as this information contains other retail operating company proprietary information.
The Company considers two different views of load growth across its planning scenarios—a Standard view, i.e. the Budget 2025 forecast, and a Standard+HG0 delta view. The Standard+HG0 delta view considers a different load forecast projection consistent with a higher view of future natural gas prices than is behind the Standard load forecast view. For the analyses supporting this IRP, the Company did not consider load forecasts that were based on different assumptions regarding CO2 or environmental regulation.
Relative to the Standard view, the Standard+HG0 delta load forecast view is adjusted based on load forecast differences between two cases from EIA’s Annual Energy Outlook (“AEO”). The AEO includes projections of electricity consumption in the southeastern U.S. for both its Reference case and its Low Oil & Gas Supply case. The Low Oil & Gas Supply case is less optimistic about future improvements in gas production and availability than the Reference case and thus has higher prices for natural gas. The percent difference between electricity load growth in the southeast in these two cases is calculated in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment AS. This percent difference is applied to the Company’s Standard forecast of load growth to yield the Standard+HG0 delta forecast, as provided in STF-JKA-1-1 Attachment AT TRADE SECRET.
As compared to the Georgia Power and Southern Company load forecasts presented in the 2025 IRP, the Resource Mix Study identifies the capacity resources needed to meet the aggregate retail operating companies’ needs. The system peak demand forecasts are derived by summing each retail operating companies’ non-coincident peaks (“NCPs”) and then applying a load diversity factor. This process is carried out by applying the diversified peak load change set used within the Aurora model. When this change set file is applied within Aurora, hourly loads that correspond to the System (SOCOnoSPC) peak hour will be adjusted so that the sum of the retail operating companies will equal the winter diversified system peak demand. For example, in year 2030 the System winter peak occurs on January 24 at hour 8. Regarding economic development projects, provide the following electronically, with all formulae intact:
Describe the process that Georgia Power uses to determine load materialization risk and inclusion/exclusion of prospective loads into the various base and sensitivity forecasts.
Provide an analysis/workpapers describing the economic development pipeline assumed in the load forecast in the 2025 IRP and compare that to the pipeline assumed in the 2023 IRP Update.
Explain what level of commitment is required from a customer to be included in the load forecasts. Describe the various stages of contract negotiation (Request for Service, Electric Service Agreement, etc.) in your response.

If so, please provide a list of such contracts and when they were signed and copy of contract. Also, provide the load ramp and expected load of these customers.
response:
The Company continues to utilize the Load Realization Model (“LRM”) developed for the 2023 IRP Update. The LRM uses a probabilistic approach to evaluate the range and likelihood of future potential outcomes of load growth from new committed and prospective large load customers. The LRM accounts for the size and various progress stages of individual projects in Georgia Power’s large load economic development pipeline. The LRM assesses the risk associated with announced loads being realized by assigning lower likelihoods than to committed customers. As such, all projects are included in the load forecast, but at different levels of materialization.
For a detailed list of the economic development pipeline assumed in the load forecast in the 2025 IRP, please refer to Georgia Power’s Q2 2024 Large Load Economic Development Report filed on August 16, 2024. For a comparison with the 2023 IRP Update, please see Table 2 of the provided report.
The LRM is a probabilistic model that includes all customers in Georgia Power’s economic development pipeline, capturing the size and various progress stages of projects. The LRM assesses load materialization based on individual project milestones and characteristics. As such, all projects in the Q2 2024 Large Load Economic Development Report are included in the company’s load forecast, but at different stages and levels of likelihood.
For example, customers who have signed an Electric Service Agreement (“ESA”) are treated as having a higher likelihood in the Company’s LRM. Conversely, customers earlier in the process are generally treated as having a lower likelihood.
The contract negotiation process involves several stages:
Proposal Development/Contracting Phase: This phase involves developing a rate proposal which includes the method of service, target timelines for construction completion, and rate offerings.
Request for Service (“RFS”): The Company sends the RFS along with the rate proposal to the customer.
ESA: Once the RFS is signed, the Company drafts an ESA for the customer to execute.
Fully Executed Phase: Once the ESA is executed by the customer and returned, the project moves to the fully executed phase.
This structured approach ensures that projects are appropriately included in the load forecast based on their progress and commitment level.

question: Provide source documents for any capital cost escalation rates that were modeled.
response:
All technologies except for wind, solar, and battery storage are escalated at the rate of the Gross Domestic Product Implicit Price Deflator (“GPDIPD”). Please refer to attachment JKA-1-8 Attachment A TRADE SECRET for development of the Implicit Price Deflator used to model generic units in the Resource Mix Study.
Escalators for solar and battery storage, as represented in Figure 12 of the Resource Mix Study in Technical Appendix Volume 2, were developed using capex forecast data from the “1Q 2024 Global PV Market Outlook” from Bloomberg New Energy Finance (“BNEF”). The escalator for wind is based on similar data from the “2024 v1 Annual Technology Baseline” (“ATB”) from the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (“NREL”). The calculation of these escalation rates begins with the overnight capital cost forecasts for each technology from the most recent BNEF Levelized Cost of Energy (“LCOE”) spreadsheet that can be accessed by BNEF clients. When these escalation trajectories were established, the most recent BNEF LCOE publication was the “Energy Storage System Cost Survey 2023.” Solar PV was informed by BNEF while wind was informed by the ATB. The forecasted values published by BNEF were originally in 2023 dollars. To be consistent with other costs included in the Resource Mix Study, nominal values were calculated for this forecast by escalating each year’s projection in real terms using the Company’s forecast of the GDPIPD. The final step normalizes the forecasted trajectories so that the capital cost changes can be applied to the Company’s most recent overnight cost estimate in the first year of the forecast. The normalization calculation divides the nominal capital cost projection for all future years by the overnight cost estimate in year one. The normalized capital escalation trajectories for onshore wind, solar PV and battery energy storage are included in the “Mix Study - Figure 12 Normalized Wind Solar BESS Projections TRADE SECRET.xlsx” workpaper provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025, in the Technical Appendix Vol 2 – Resource Mix Study workpapers folder. Development of the chart provided in the workpaper is detailed in STF-JKA-1-8 Attachment B TRADE SECRET.

question: For a number of years, the Company has taken steps to mitigate risks of cold weather reliability. Please describe all efforts undertaken since the 2022 IRP including capital investment and O&M expense, and explain how those steps have paid off, and how the Company’s Aurora and SERVM modeling assumptions have been revised since the 2022 IRP as a result of the mitigation efforts undertaken.
response:
Since the 2022 IRP, cold weather outage assumptions in the model have been adjusted to account for the ongoing winterization improvements performed across the System. In the 2021 Reserve Margin Study, incremental cold weather-related outages for all modeled resources were anticipated to start when system-weighted temperatures fell below 13°F. In the 2024 Reserve Margin Study, this threshold was adjusted downward to 10°F but only for retail resources owned and operated by Southern Company. For contracted resources, the threshold was increased to 18°F due to fewer winterization improvements being performed on these units. In addition to the threshold, a geographic adjustment was also made at each generation site to account for differences between local temperature and the system-weighted temperature. Part I, Section I of the 2024 Reserve Margin Study provided in Technical Appendix Volume 1 details the cold weather outage modeling methodology and assumptions applied. The Aurora modeling for the Resource Mix Study applies the target reserve margin determined in the Reserve Margin Study to help identify an optimized resource expansion plan. Loads modeled in the Resource Mix Study are based on normal weather, so no incremental extreme weather outages are applied.
Southern Company is currently implementing a fleetwide winterization program with the goal of not only improving the reliability of freeze protection systems at each plant but also lowering the minimum operating temperature and freeze related parameters. This includes adding/replacing various components such as heat tracing, insulation, instrument enclosures, heated tube bundles, equipment enclosures, and other auxiliaries related to protecting components during cold weather events. Procedures have also been updated to assure compliance with NERC EOP-012-2 Extreme Cold Weather Preparedness. To date, Georgia Power has invested over $100M capital and over $7M O&M in this effort. As a result, the Georgia Power fleet winter reliability continues to improve. No unplanned generation weather related events were experienced for Company owned resources during Winter Storms Enzo and Cora.

For all the modeled portfolios, provide any annual and cumulative build limits that were modeled by resource. Also, provide all workpapers used to derive the limits as used in Aurora modeling in the IRP.

response:
See 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Vol 2 Resource Mix Study for all modeled annual and cumulative build limits. Additionally, see STF-JKA-1-11 Attachment A TRADE SECRET for derivation of the natural gas firm transportation (“FT”) availability limit used for expansion CC resources.
Table 1 below summarizes the build limits assumed in 2025 IRP capacity expansion modeling and provides a comparison with assumptions in the 2023 IRP Update.
Table 1. Summary of Limits on Expansion Units.
Technology | 2023 IRP Update | 2025 IRP
CT w/SCR | No limit | No limit
CC | Cumulative build limit based on annual FT availability | Cumulative build limit based on annual FT availability
CC w/CCS | Cumulative build limit based on annual FT availability | Cumulative limit based on annual FT availability Distinguishes between Local and Distant CCS Local CCS limited to REDACTED total (REDACTED limit for GPC)
Solar | Annual Max – 1,500 MW/yr | Annual Max – 1,500 MW/yr
Wind | Annual Max – 600 MW/yr Cumulative Max – 8,100 MW | Annual Max – 300 MW/yr Cumulative Max – 4,500 MW
BESS | Annual Max – 3,000 MW/yr Cumulative Max – 18,000 MW | Annual Max – 3,000 MW/yr Cumulative Max – 18,000 MW
MDESS | No limit | No Limit
Nuclear | Annual Max – 300 MW/yr | Annual Max – 600 MW/yr
Annual Limit on CT and CC Builds
The Company used an annual maximum build limit in the 2023 IRP Update for CTs and CCs that was calculated based on the system’s annual incremental capacity need.  The purpose of this limit was to reduce the number of new resource options Aurora evaluates and improve runtime.  Because the limit was set at or above the system’s annual incremental capacity need, it did not actually limit the number of CTs or CCs that were selected by the model.  For the 2025 IRP, the Company determined that having a static value that is large enough to allow Aurora to meet an entire year’s capacity need with a single new resource type (if optimal), but not calculated based on annual need, simplifies the calculations required for each scenario and does not significantly increase run time.
For CTs and CC w/CCS, this limit is set to 30 blocks per year, which is equivalent to 9,000 MW (300 MW/block).  For CCs, the build is limited to 3 blocks in 2029, the first year CC is allowed, and 15 blocks in 2030 to represent the estimated amount that could be constructed in that timeframe.  For 2031 and beyond, the CC build limit is set to 30 blocks per year.
FT Availability Limit on CC Builds
In both the 2023 IRP Update and the 2025 IRP, the Company assumed FT used for existing units would become available to new CCs as the existing units either retired or power purchase agreement (“PPA”) expired.   In addition, for planning purposes, the Company assumed some additional pipeline expansion and associated FT would become available during the planning horizon. STF-JKA-1-11 Attachment B TRADE SECRET shows the resulting cumulative MW build limits that were included in the capacity expansion modeling for the 2023 IRP Update and the 2025 IRP.
Assumptions on Gas Availability for CTs
Given the current operational realities and the challenges facing the pipeline infrastructure industry, the Company assumes the most reliable operational plan for new generic expansion CTs is for them to be dual-fueled, capable of combusting either fuel oil or natural gas.  For the 2023 IRP Update, the Company assumed year-round fuel oil operation for new generic CTs because the pipelines serving the Company region have become increasingly constrained and less flexible in recent years. For the 2025 IRP, this assumption was revised to only require CTs to operate on oil during the winter months (Dec-Jan-Feb) and to operate as needed on gas throughout the remainder of the year.
Local Versus Distant CC w/CCS
Areas of favorable geology for carbon storage within the Southern Company footprint are limited.  For CCs that are distant from carbon storage regions, application of CCS requires that the captured CO2 be transported by pipeline to a storage site (i.e., Distant CC w/CCS), which results in significant additional cost to construct and operate the unit.   For the 2025 IRP, the Company has determined that it is reasonable to assume that only REDACTED of CC w/CCS could be constructed near favorable carbon storage sites (i.e., Local CC w/CCS), with significantly less cost for CO2 transport than Distant CC w/CCS.  The Company assumes REDACTED miles of pipeline for Local CC w/ CCS and REDACTED miles of pipeline for Distant CC w/ CCS.  In addition, the Company assumes that only REDACTED of Local CC w/CCS could be constructed in the GPC service territory. Local CC w/CCS builds in the capacity expansion modeling are limited based on operating company need (e.g., if GPC is the only Operating Company with a capacity need, the build cannot exceed GPCs need for that year and cannot exceed REDACTED) and is limited to a system total of REDACTED.  This limit was not included in the 2023 IRP Update modeling.
The Company aims to develop any generic resource limits tailored to technology deployment within its regulated service territory, rather than relying on public sources, which often cover a broader geographic scope. It is common utility practice to apply limits on generic resources in expansion plan modeling.
Given the challenges facing the pipeline infrastructure industry, the Company has applied a limit on the amount of new CC (including CC w/CCS) builds allowed in capacity expansion modeling. The limit is a cumulative build constraint that is based on the amount of natural gas firm transportation (“FT”) that is estimated to be available from retirement of existing resources, PPA expiration, and/or pipeline expansion.  See JKA-1-11 Attachment A TRADE SECRET for derivation of the FT limits used for CC expansion resources.

The Company uses four carbon pressure views that use a price. The Lower view uses a price of $0 for the entire modeling period. The Moderate view uses a price of $20 (2023$) per metric ton starting in 2030 and rising at 5% above inflation. The Higher view uses a price of $50 (2023$) per metric ton of CO2 starting in 2030 and rising at 7% above inflation. The 111-Higher view uses a price of $50 (2023$) starting in 2035 and rising at 7% above inflation. Real values are converted to nominal values using the Company’s forecast of inflation.

question:
Regarding the Company’s retirement analysis:
Please compare and contrast the coal retirement methodology used in the 2025 IRP versus the 2022 IRP.
Did the Company evaluate the most optimal year to retire coal units in the coal retirement study? Provide all workpapers, notes, documentation regarding the assumptions required to evaluate optimal timing.
response:
The methodology used in the 2022 IRP and the 2025 IRP both compare the incremental costs and benefits of the unit being evaluated to the costs and benefits of replacement unit(s). The costs for the replacement unit in the 2022 IRP were assumed to be results from the 2,356 MW of low-cost replacement capacity identified in the 2022-2028 Capacity RFP, which was intended for the replacement of coal unit retirements. The replacement capacity cost assumption used in the 2025 IRP was assumed to be a generic natural gas combined cycle “NGCC.” The methodology used in the 2022 IRP assigned a capacity value to the unit being evaluated and to the replacement unit in order to make a direct comparison. Due to various environmental compliance pathways, the 2025 IRP methodology shifted to a total cost view so that more than one compliance pathway could be evaluated for each resource. When evaluating total costs, a capacity benefit is not assigned. Instead, capacity costs are assigned when the unit is assumed to retire.
No, the Company did not evaluate the most optimal retirement year. The Company evaluated costs and benefits of continuing to operate coal units beyond 2028, including assessing the potential impact of various environmental compliance pathways, and is not requesting a retirement date in this IRP.

question:

Explain if the Market Differential Adjustment (“MDA”) used in the economic analysis for the wholesale to retail analysis are reflective of the market price of capacity or a generic resource price (economic carrying charge of a CT). response:
The Company has historically used a defined resource type as replacement technology. The 2022 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) Unit Retirement Study used a replacement portfolio due to the availability of results from the 2022-2028 Capacity Request for Proposals (“RFP”), which were specifically procured for coal retirement replacement. Yes. The natural gas combined cycle (“NGCC”) generic replacement was assumed for all units under all fuel cases. While combustion turbine (“CT”) and battery energy storage system (“BESS”) were contemplated as replacement options, the Company determined that the NGCC was the lowest cost replacement in most scenarios and best reflected the near-term replacement option if a retirement decision were made. No. The Company did not consider using results from the All-Source RFP to determine the replacement resources in the Unit Retirement Study. The Company is not expected to make a certification filing with the Commission based on the All-Source RFP until July 2025; therefore, the timing was not compatible with completion of the Unit Retirement Study, which was completed several months in advance of filing the 2025 IRP. Additionally, the capacity sought in the All-Source RFP is intended to meet capacity needs associated with load growth. Additional resources would be needed to replace existing units if a retirement decision were made.
The Company conducted the Unit Retirement Studies at the plant level because the capital expenses associated with ELG compliance were applicable to the full plant and not individual units. Furthermore, the Company’s current capacity needs support consideration of the full plant as any partial retirement would necessitate immediate replacement. As such, there is no reasonable need to differentiate between each unit.

“Study” Tab – The “Study” tab allows you to define the studies, which align with the environmental compliance pathways. These study names flow through to other tabs, which allow for cost input, capacity input, energy input, results, etc. This is also where the following items are defined: the study period, the replacement unit, capacity equalization MW, firm transportation (“FT”) rate for the generic replacement unit, and scaling of replacement unit.
“CapacityNeeds” Tab – The “CapacityNeeds” tab allows you to define the capacity need for that specific study or environmental compliance pathway. These values are used to calculate Term Equalization on the “Capacity” tab.
“Capacity” Tab – This tab allows the user to define capacity associated with each study or environmental compliance pathway. It then assigns a Term Equalization cost for each Scenario. If there is a capacity need, which is pulled from the “CapacityNeeds” tab, and the capacity is not provided by the units in that study, then a Term Equalization is calculated. The Term Equalization is calculated using the net marginal cost of a combined cycle (“CC”), which is pulled from the “GenericFixedCost” tab and the “GenericProdCost” tab.
“Cost Inputs” Tab – The “Cost Inputs” tab allows the user to input all costs associated with that study or environmental compliance pathway. Column E tells the spreadsheet how to sum the costs in summary tables on the “Annual Economics” tab. Column F tells the spreadsheet if the costs need to be converted to a Declining Revenue Requirement (“DRR”) or if they should be treated as expenses.
“Cost DRR Calculator” Tab – This tab looks at cost inputs on the “Cost Input” tab and converts them to DRR as applicable. This tab pulls the useful life assumption from the “Study” tab and pulls the modified accelerated cost recovery system (“MACRS”) assumption from the “Assumptions” tab using lookups.
“Energy” Tab – This tab allows the user to input energy values. These values are outputs from AURORA files.
“Transmission” Tab – This tab allows the user to input transmission projects, costs, and assumed in-service years to calculate transmission costs associated with each study.

This tab also looks up the FT rate input on the “Study” tab for the generic CC to calculate a net present value (“NPV”) for the FT stream associated with that rate. The “Capacity” tab pulls the economic carrying cost (“ECC”) stream in row 6 to be used as the marginal cost of a CC, and the “Cost Inputs” tab pulls the technology costs in rows 9-14 so that the CC modeled as the immediate replacement and the ECC used as the Term Equalization for the deferred replacement are utilizing the same cost assumptions.
“GenericProdCost” Tab – This tab allows the user to input energy values for generic replacement technologies from AURORA. The “Capacity” tab pulls the values to be used as the net marginal cost of a CC, and the “Energy” tab pulls the energy values so that the CC modeled as the immediate replacement and the ECC used as the Term Equalization for the deferred replacement are utilizing the same energy assumptions.
“Annual Economics” Tab – This tab summarizes all costs and benefits determined in the sheets mentioned above. This tab also calculates the NPV associated with each cost category or benefit category.
“EUS” and “GUS” Tabs – These tabs pull the NPVs from the “Annual Economics” tab to summarize all costs and benefits associated with each study or with each generic replacement option.
“Results_TotalCosts” - These tabs allow you to pull specific studies to compare. The ELG pathways are compared on one tab and the 111 pathways are compared on another tab.
“Results_Matrix” Tabs – These tabs pulls the total cost from the “EUS” tab and nets the total cost from the “GUS” tab of the studies the user specifies to create a matrix of benefits among all scenarios.

response: The “capacity equalizer” assumption defined on the “Study” tab is meant to account for capacity differences among environmental compliance pathways. The Effluent Limitations Guidelines (“ELG”) “No Cessation” Pathway would require the plant to install a zero liquid discharge (“ZLD”) system to treat scrubber wastewater. It is assumed that this would add a station service load of approximately 10 MW for the entirety of Plant Bowen. The co-fire pathway would require the same ZLD system and therefore the same approximately10 MW of incremental station service load. The 100% gas conversion pathways assume a net capacity increase of approximately 20 MW for Plant Bowen Units 1-2 and a net capacity increase approximately 30 MW for Plant Bowen Units 3-4. This assumption accounts for the reduction in station service load related to the removal of fuel handling equipment and environmental equipment such as the scrubber. The carbon capture and sequestration (“CCS”) pathway assumes a 25% derate due to a large station service load and process steam requirements associated with the carbon capture facility.

response:
The Company reviewed the Internal Revenue Code (“IRC”) Section 45Y, and the Section 45Y Clean Energy Production Credit regulations as posted in the federal register as the basis for ascertaining eligibility requirements and applicability.
Please reference STF-JKA-2-22 Attachment A TRADE SECRET and STF-JKA-2-22 Attachment B TRADE SECRET. The model within the attachments applies the guidance from IRC Section 45Y (“PTC”) to calculate the value of the selected tax credit. As its megawatt-hour (“MWH”) input, the model uses the annual difference in MWH resource outputs between the base case in Aurora and the change case in Aurora which illustrates the incremental MWH provided by the uprate.
The Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”) includes provisions for transfer or sale of tax credits. Market transactions for tax credits have been observed to trade below the full value of the tax credit due to, among other reasons, risks that are borne by the purchasers. For modeling purposes, the Company has assumed a 10 percent discount on Clean Electricity (48E and 45Y) tax credits.

The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (“NRC”) regulates the maximum power level at which a commercial nuclear power plant may operate. This power level is used, with other data, in many of the licensing analyses that demonstrate the safety of the plant. This power level is included in the license and technical specifications for the plant to operate within. NRC controls any change to a license or technical specification, and the licensee may only change these documents after NRC approves the licensee's application for change. The process of increasing the maximum power level at which a commercial nuclear power plant may operate is called a power uprate. The licensee submits a formal License Amendment Request (“LAR”) to obtain approval.
The traditional timeline for NRC review and approval for a power uprate is 18 months.  The licensee conducts the engineering analysis oversight of the appropriate Original Equipment Manufacturer (“OEM”) of the nuclear reactor technology to ensure the appropriate technical basis to support the power uprate. The engineering analysis is approximately a 2-year process to ensure the appropriate calculations and modification scope is certified to be correct prior to NRC submittal for review and approval.
