question:
Regarding the Nuclear Unit Upgrades,
Provide any additional documentation the Company has that explains the Extended Power Uprates, and the Maximum Extended Load Line Limit enhancements
What companies will be helping the Company perform these uprates?
What other nuclear units is the Company aware of that have either performed these upgrades or have decided to perform these upgrades similar to the Company?  When were the upgrades performed?
response:
Utilities have been using power uprates since the 1970s as a way to increase the power output of nuclear plants. To increase the power output of a reactor, typically more highly enriched uranium fuel and/or more fresh fuel is used. This enables the reactor to produce more thermal energy and more steam, thereby driving a turbine generator to produce more electricity. In order to accomplish this, components such as pipes, valves, pumps, heat exchangers, electrical transformers and generators, must be able to accommodate the conditions that would exist at the higher power level. For example, a higher power level usually involves higher steam and water flow through the systems used in converting the thermal power into electric power. These systems must be capable of accommodating the higher flows.
In some instances, licensees will modify and/or replace components in order to accommodate a higher power level. Depending on the desired increase in power level and original equipment design, this can involve major and costly modifications to the plant such as the replacement or retrofit of main turbines and/or main generators. All of these factors must be analyzed by the licensee as part of a request for a power uprate, which is accomplished by amending the plant's operating license. The analyses must demonstrate that the proposed new configuration remains safe and that measures continue to be in place to protect the health and safety of the public. These analyses, which span many technical disciplines and may be complex, are reviewed by the Nuclear Regulatory Commission’s (“NRC”) technical and legal staffs and NRC management before a request for a power uprate is approved.
Maximum Extended Load Line Limit Plus (“MELLLA+”) is an approved method used in a boiling water reactor (“BWR”) power plant to safely increase the allowed core flow range. A plant is licensed to operate within a specified power and flow domain. By giving operators a larger range of licensed core flow, MELLLA+ allows more operational flexibility and can improve plant capacity. MELLLA+ is increasingly important for BWRs with Extended Power Uprates (“EPU”) since EPU by itself reduces the allowed core flow range. MELLLA+ restores the allowed range of core flow, returning operational flexibility to the operators.
Westinghouse, General Electric Vernova, General Electric Steam, Sargent & Lundy, Enercon, Southern Company Services, Day and Zimmerman are the major suppliers, vendors, and engineering firms that will be assisting Southern Nuclear with the uprates.

response:
As part of the integrated resource plan (“IRP”) process, Georgia Power requests Public Service Commission (“Commission”) approval of the capital and operations and maintenance (“O&M”) costs to be incurred for the hydro modernization projects to be completed. Additionally, for any projects resulting in a capacity increase of more than 15%, Georgia Power is required by Commission Rules to submit a certification amendment application to be reviewed and approved by the Commission.
A Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”) license amendment is required for any changes to the features or operations of the hydro projects. All of the modernization work proposed by Georgia Power will require a license amendment. FERC reviews the amendment applications, concentrating on whether the proposed modifications impact dam safety, environmental, operational, and other effects. Items that are reviewed as part of the license amendments process at FERC can include, but are not limited to, the following:
New vendor-designed turbine and generator design power outputs and discharge flows to evaluate the impact of water flows to the receiving stream (quantity and quality) and annual charges.
Analysis of whether licensed recreation, lake levels, or flow releases will be affected during construction.
Required laydown areas and, if land disturbance is required, any cultural, historical, wetlands, endangered or listed species or habitats impacted.
Historic photography documentation of structures and Memorandum of Agreements to be executed between FERC, the State Historic Preservation Offices, and Indian Tribes if they choose to participate.
To complete the analysis of some of these items to the detail that FERC requires for a license amendment, agency consultation and FERC review and public comment, it requires detailed scopes, engineering design to be completed by the vendor for the turbine and generators and supporting systems designs be substantially complete so that we know specifics about the new turbines, generators, water flow quantities and temperature, plans for staging, and impacts to operations during construction. Vendors will not complete this level of turbine and generator design until commitments are made to purchases, and the supporting systems design cannot begin until the unit turbine and generator design is complete.
As discussed in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 1, Hydro Modernization, Section 2, completing the modernization of the full hydro group on a river chain not only provides efficiencies during the project process but also enables improved operations following completion. The Company will be able to realize the full benefits of enhanced fleet dispatch and operational efficiency of each river chain. Specifically, the turbine and generator upgrades are expected to increase the efficiency of each unit. Also, upgraded control systems will allow for optimized water flow between interconnected facilities along each river chain. Modernized facilities will be updated with digital instrumentation and control systems that will allow for optimized dispatch of each facility.
Approval of the remaining facilities by river chain will create efficiencies for any FERC license amendments that may be needed for the completion of these projects, which would be beneficial to the overall hydro modernization schedule.
Additionally, it was important for Georgia Power to evaluate the hydro modernization projects and dam removal alternatives by river chain in the required cost-benefit analysis due to the interconnected impacts of facilities in the hydro group. This operational relationship means that changes at one dam can significantly impact the others, such as adverse effects on turbine performance and operational range. The cost-benefit analysis provides alternatives with the addition of a weir upstream of the dam removed as part of the scenario, in order to mitigate the impacts to the rest of the river chain. See the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 1, Hydro Modernization, Section 4, for more information on the cost-benefit analysis approach by river chain.
In the 2019 IRP, Georgia Power requested approval of hydro modernization projects for the entire Georgia Power-operated hydro fleet due to the flexibility and efficiency benefits to be gained by receiving approval for all projects. These benefits also included the operational and logistical optimization to be gained by completing modernization on a full river chain. However, as part of the stipulation process in the 2019 IRP, five lower-cost sites with urgency for refurbishment/replacement work to ensure continued operation were agreed to in order to start the hydro modernization program. As described in the 2025 IRP and subpart (b) above, the Company maintains that there are significant benefits to modernizing all hydro facilities in a river chain, as well as receiving approvals for the full remaining hydro fleet.
Due to the limited approvals stipulated in the 2019 IRP, Georgia Power chose to prioritize the requests in the 2022 IRP to the next few sites with the greatest urgency for modernization, which included Plant Sinclair on the Central Georgia river chain, in addition to a facility on both the North Georgia (Plant Burton) and Chattahoochee (Plant North Highlands) river chains. Each of the six active demand side option (“DSO”) programs was independently simulated with the SERVM reliability model. The table below details the variables and restrictions applied to each program based on program parameters. The Georgia Power Demand Plus Energy Credit (“DPEC”) program is modeled with a unique load shape based on actual customer energy usage. The addition of this load shape in the modeling process more closely aligns available interruptible energy with modeled reliability events as opposed to assuming contracted capacity is available in all hours. The response magnitude applied to the DPEC program is based on the historical performance from the last three interruption events that occurred on January 7, 2014, October 10, 2017, and December 24, 2022.

There were two steps performed to determine the final DSO effective load carrying capability (“ELCC”) values. Step 1 consisted of evaluating each DSO program independently as the first-in program in a system that had no other DSO programs embedded. These “first-in” values tend to be the highest possible ELCC values but do not consider the synergistic or antagonistic interactions of multiple DSO programs, each with their own unique parameters. Step 2 consists of evaluating the entire DSO fleet in aggregate. This is performed by adding all DSO resources at the same time and evaluating them together to determine a single ELCC value, representing the entire DSO fleet. The final step consists of individually weighting each DSO program based upon their relative program size and first-in ELCC value while ensuring that the final ELCC capacity MW values of all programs sum up to the aggregate, fleet-wide ELCC value determined in step 2. This aggregate step ensures that the reliability contribution of the entire DSO fleet is not over or understated. See STF-JKA-2-35 Attachment A for the program ELCC calculations and the DPEC program load shapes that were applied.
The Demand Comparison Factor is not applicable to Georgia Power’s programs and is set to 100% for all programs. It is not a consideration in the calculation.
The Loss Expansion Factor provides an adjustment to the capacity value to account for the fact that load reduced at the customer meter results in greater avoided capacity at the generator level because of losses on the system in the delivery of energy. The values are calculated as part of a load flow study and are based on the level of service taken by the majority of customers enrolled in the respective program or rate. question: See the comparison of peak load and energy forecasts on pages 24 and 25 of the Main Document.  Please provide insight as to why the forecasts are nearly on top of each other.  Doesn’t that mean any results produced using the alternative load forecast would provide very little value since there is no real differentiation in the assumptions?
response:
In the Resource Mix Study supporting the 2025 IRP, the Company has used two different views of load growth—Standard and Standard + HG0 Delta. The latter is a load forecast that represents an adjustment to load associated with a higher forecast of natural gas price. These two load forecasts are not dramatically different from each other because a higher gas price has opposing effects on electricity consumption. Because natural gas is an input to electricity production, a higher price of natural gas will increase the cost of electricity, thereby decreasing load growth. Because natural gas is a substitute for electricity in some end-uses, a higher price of natural gas will increase electricity consumption in those uses, increasing load growth. The net of these opposing effects is a decrease in load growth relative to the Standard view.
While load growth is not dramatically different in the Standard + HG0 Delta view, the scenario that uses this view also uses a significantly higher view of the future price of natural gas, so the results produced when using the alternative load forecast are meaningfully different from results produced when using the Standard load forecast and the Moderate fuel price view, for example, because of the combination of these two drivers.

response: The Company’s long-term coal price projections are adopted from three cases provided by the U.S. Energy Information Administration (“EIA”) in its Annual Energy Outlook (“AEO”). Those three cases, Low Oil and Natural Gas Supply, Reference, and High Oil and Gas Supply, differ with respect to assumptions regarding the resource size and productivity of oil and natural gas, not coal. question: See p. 41 of the Main Document. Why was it considered reasonable not to round the short-term Reserve Margin Targets, but it was considered important to round the Long-term Reserve Margin Target.

The results of the long-term reserve margin analysis resulted in a winter target reserve margin (“TRM”) of 26.00% and a summer TRM of 20.00%. question:
Refer to page 9 of “2025 IRP Resource Mix Study TRADE SECRET.docx” the Company states, “For modeling purposes, the Company has assumed a 10 percent discount on Clean Electricity (48E and 45Y) tax credits. Because of the nascent state of CCS and associated concerns with commercial deployment of the technology, the Company assumed a 25 percent discount on 45Q tax credits.”
How did the Company determine 10% was a reasonable assumption for Clean Electricity? Please explain.
How did the Company determine 25% was a reasonable assumption for CCS? Please explain.
Does the Company expect to be able to use the tax credits itself or monetize them through subsequent transactions? Please describe how the Company intends to utilize and account for the tax credits.
response:
The 10% discount for Clean Electricity tax credits accounts for risks associated with the Company’s anticipated inability to directly utilize large amounts of tax credits generated under the Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”) and the tax market appetite for credits. Market transactions for tax credits have been observed to trade below the full value of the tax credit due to a number of reasons, including the following:
Transaction Costs: Transaction costs can include fees for advisers and syndicators and for conducting due diligence.
Recapture: If specified conditions of a project are not met, the federal government may determine that the project was not eligible for the investment tax credit (“ITC”) and that that a portion or all of the tax credits previously claimed must be paid back to the government. There is typically a five-year period for determining whether conditions were met.
Developer creditworthiness and control: Developers will be responsible for maintaining and operating the system throughout the recapture period in addition to supporting whatever indemnities they give to the buyer.
Novel or unproven technologies: Novel clean energy technologies, such as carbon capture and sequestration (“CCS”), would be expected to experience a significant discount on IRA tax credits primarily due to risks and uncertainties associated with their early-stage development and commercial deployment.
The 10% discount was informed by these risks and guided by professional judgment of the Company’s finance and tax experts. The Company will pursue the maximum value possible for customers when specific Company-owned projects are identified and approved.
The 25% discount for 45Q tax credits accounts for risks associated with the Company’s anticipated inability to directly utilize large amounts of tax credits generated under the IRA and the tax market appetite for credits associated with fossil fuel-fired technologies utilizing CCS. The 25% discount was guided by professional judgment of the Company’s finance and tax experts.
The Company assumes that the volume of the tax credits generated under the IRA is likely to be greater than the Company’s tax burden. Excess tax credits would be transferred to third parties in order to monetize the benefits of the credits for customers. Additionally, for ITCs, which can be more beneficial than production tax credits (“PTCs”) for capital intensive projects (e.g., nuclear) and/or projects that might be eligible for additional tax credit bonuses, transfer enables regulated utilities to avoid normalization, which can provide additional economic benefit to customers.

Please describe the “iterative process” and whether the prices changes considered were escalation changes and/or base price changes.

response:
The iterative process included escalation rate changes, base price changes, and changes to the price in individual years.
The Company applied a two-step approach to solve the Emissions Limit (“EL”) case. In the first step, the Company applied an annual carbon (“CO2”) emissions limit that declined over time through 2050 to achieve the 95% emissions reduction target (from 2007 levels). Upon completion of the first step, Aurora produced a CO2 price that was used to achieve the annual CO2 emissions reductions. In the second step, Aurora was run with the CO2 price from step one, similar to the other scenarios that include a price on carbon.
In addition to this two-step approach, the case required iterative solves to determine the combination of constraints necessary to relax to achieve the emissions limit target. Ultimately, the EL case applied relaxed combined cycle (“CC”) build limits, relaxed nuclear build limits, and a relaxed reserve margin limit to meet the 2050 target with minimal demand side curtailment. These changes are described in subpart (d).
See response to subpart (a).
As described in subpart (a), the EL case required a two-step approach and iterative solves to produce a reasonable solve that achieved the emissions limit target. Ultimately, the EL case used relaxed CC and nuclear build limits and increased the reserve margin limit to 40% to meet the 2050 target with minimal demand side curtailment. These changes are described in more detail in part (d).
The “Relaxed FT Nuclear” change set increased the number nuclear blocks allowed each year from the default of two blocks, which begins in 2037 in all cases, to three blocks starting in 2045. This change set also increased the cumulative amount of combined cycle megawatts (“MW”) allowed each year.
The “B2025 Final IRP-RM Window Fix-MG0-40P” change set increased the maximum reserve margin on the system from 30% to 40%. This allowed the model to select low carbon resources earlier to help reach the 2050 emission limit. 

The “Set Curtailment Price High” change set imposed a higher price on load curtailment (i.e., reduced demand) to incentivize the model to avoid “demand side curtailment”. 

The “Shadow Price” change set provides the CO2 price stream derived from the step one solve.

Aurora version 14.2.1104 is a version update that includes a fix for a problem discovered in how previous versions of Aurora, including 14.2.1084, handled the co-firing of gas at existing coal units. For Resource Mix Study analyses using the Company’s 111 view of future CO2 pressure, co-firing was identified as the preferred 111 GHG Rule compliance pathway for the impacted units at Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer. To have co-firing handled correctly in the cases that used the 111 view, the Company coordinated with the software vendor to issue a revised version of Aurora (14.2.1104) to use for those cases. The error was discovered and its fix implemented after the non-111 analysis supporting this 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) had been completed; it was not feasible to re-do all analyses using the revised version 14.2.1104.
The Company has made some comparisons between solutions using versions 14.2.1104 and 14.2.1084. The main difference between solutions produced by the different versions is that in the solves using the 111 view of future CO2 pressure, the co-firing and operational pattern for Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer is reasonable in solves using version 14.2.1104 and not reasonable in solves using version 14.2.1084. For example, some Bowen units co-fired at 40% in every operating hour rather than optimizing the use of coal and gas throughout the year. question:
Refer to page 2 of the Reserve Margin report. Please provide the following:

response:
The regression models used, including coefficients and t-statistics are found in STF-JKA-5-1 Attachment A TRADE SECRET. Actual and predicted values are provided in STF-JKA-5-1 Attachment B TRADE SECRET.
The database containing the variables used to estimate the models are provided in STF-JKA-5-1 Attachment C TRADE SECRET.
The Reserve Margin Study load/weather model was developed in Statistical Analysis System (“SAS”) with Southern Territorial Load as the dependent variable and various weather and calendar variables as the independent variables. Southern Territorial Load is defined as the sum of Alabama Power, Georgia Power, Mississippi Power, and Southern Power Company full requirements customers, whereas the weather variables were developed using the weighted average of five weather stations across the Southern Company territory. The training dataset is comprised of years 2018-2022, excluding year 2020 to minimize impacts related to the COVID-19 pandemic. The dataset is then divided into subsets based on specific temperature ranges: below 36°F, 34-45°F, 38-66°F, 61-75°F, 68-81°F, and above 80°F. For each of these temperature ranges, a separate linear regression model is built using independent variables such as temperature, lag temperatures, daily minimum and maximum temperatures, heating degree hours (“HDH”), cooling degree hours (“CDH”), and dummy variables representing hours, months, days, weekday, and holidays.

In this scenario, capital budgets also cannot be estimated because the timing of these individual repairs or replacements is not known due to the uncertainty of the heightened risk of when a component could fail causing a forced outage.
There are no annual budgets for bringing back the offline units at Plant Goat Rock and Plant Morgan Falls. These units have major component failures, and most of the other parts are obsolete and require full replacement with modern equipment. Engineering and designing a subset of units would substantially increase the cost per unit, while also increasing long-term maintenance costs, as compared to a planned whole plant approach as proposed. The individual unit model would require each unit to be designed in isolation as each unit fails. Therefore, instead of spreading engineering and construction costs across the plant once for a coordinated hydro modernization effort, these costs would be repeated each time on each unit. This method would also increase the long-term maintenance cost due to having different equipment across each unit in the plant.

question:
Refer to the Mix Study results presented in “Capacity Expansion Plans - 2025 IRP.xlsx” which reports results for 20 years, while the Aurora Mix Studies are configured to run longer periods, out through 2059 (35 years).
How was the Mix Study length in the Aurora Study determined? Please explain.
Explain if the Company has considered a certain study length required to appropriately account for CCS tax credit modeling. Please explain.
response:
There is no change to the length of the study period in the Resource Mix Study for this IRP. The length of the Resource Mix Study modeling has consistently been 35 years. This period was determined based on the need to capture long-term planning horizons and the impact of various resource additions and retirements over an extended period. The IRP rules and regulations require the Company’s plan to cover the twenty-year period from the year of the filing; therefore, the Resource Mix Study, documentation, and workpapers report results for the next 20 years.  The modeling for the Resource Mix Study is also used to develop marginal costs for a 30-year period. The Aurora documentation recommends adding five “extra” years (beyond the desired study period) to ensure the integrity of the results for the desired study period itself; therefore, 35 years are analyzed for capacity expansion to support the Company’s IRP filings and other analyses.
The Company has considered the study length required to appropriately account for carbone capture and sequestration (“CCS”) (45Q) tax credit modeling. The Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”) tax credit assumptions used in Aurora modeling are detailed in Sections 2.2.2 and 3.6.1 of the Resource Mix Study. The 45Q tax credits are assumed to be available for generic combined cycles (“CC”) with CCS resources with a commercial operation date (“COD”) prior to 2039. These credits are modeled as a reduction in the total fixed capital costs, which are annualized for input to Aurora. Since 45Q credits, like production tax credits (“PTCs”), are based on the output of the unit, resources offered in Aurora are assumed to run at availability during the twelve years for which the credits are available. This approach helps ensure that tax credits are accurately reflected in the long-term financial modeling and resource planning.

question:
Refer to Company response to STF-JKA 1-6 part f, and response STF-JKA-3-16. STF-JKA 1-6 part f states, “Under the NSPS regulation, new simple-cycle CTs must meet a capacity factor limitation that is equivalent to the unit’s design efficiency.”
Please describe what the unit design efficiency metric is.
What does it mean to “meet a capacity factor limitation that is equivalent to the unit’s design efficiency.” Also, what is the unit design efficiency for new generic CT modeling as an equivalent annual capacity factor limit?
What NSPS regulation conditions are being assumed? A specific fuel type or availability, size, etc.?
Please provide the calculations used to derive a 20% limitation on new CT capacity factor based on the NSPS regulation. Also, please provide specific unit design specifications of the assumed resource(s).
response:
In the New Source Performance Standards (“NSPS”) regulation for combustion turbines (“CTs”), the United States Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) defines “design efficiency” as (see 40 CFR part 60 subpart TTTT section 60.5580):
Design efficiency means the rated overall net efficiency (e.g., electric plus useful thermal output) on a higher heating value basis at the base load rating, at ISO conditions, and at the maximum useful thermal output […].

question: See the Direct Testimony of the McNelly panel, at p. 11, l 14, which states, new CC units without CCS must limit annual capacity factors to 40%, and new CTs must limit their capacity factors to no more than 40%, and potentially as low as 20%.  Explain when new CTs would be limited to no more than 40%, and when they would be limited potentially as low as 20%.  Explain the conditions requiring each of those limits.
response:
The capacity factor limitations for new combustion turbine (“CT”) and combined cycle (“CC”) units are based on requirements in the Environmental Protection Agency’s (“EPA”) 111 Greenhouse Gas (“GHG”) Rules. These federal rules, specifically 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart TTTTa, categorize new and reconstructed CTs or CCs by capacity factor and set standards for each of these categories.
New CTs and CCs are limited to capacity factors less than 40% beginning on January 1, 2032 when these units are not equipped with carbon capture and storage (“CCS”). Units that operate at a capacity factor above 40% are defined as “base load combustion turbines” in 40 CFR Part 60, Subpart TTTTa.
New CTs that operate below a 40% capacity factor are categorized as “intermediate load CTs” and “low load CTs.” Intermediate load CTs have a capacity factor between 20% and 40%, while low load CTs have a capacity factor of less than 20%. Intermediate load CTs must meet a numerical emissions limit based on gross energy output (i.e., pounds carbon dioxide [“CO2”] per Megawatt-hour gross generation). Low load CTs are generally only required to combust what are referred to as “lower emitting fuels” such as natural gas and distillate oil. A new CT could be limited to a capacity factor less than 20% if the unit cannot meet the numerical emissions limit for intermediate load CTs.

response:
The refereced comment concerns Plant Bartletts Ferry, not Plant Tugalo. The Plant Bartletts Ferry modernization project had significant early delays due to the COVID pandemic and related restrictions. These delays were largely around the FERC approval process and turbine manufacturing.
As stated in the direct testimony, other delays for the Plant Bartletts Ferry modernization project were caused by discovery work attributable to some turbine components being in significantly worse condition than anticipated. For example, the original project scope identified that the Plant Bartletts Ferry Unit 1 operating ring was to be inspected and refurbished; however, the inspection revealed over 800 flaws in the casting and, as a result, the component had to be replaced. The condition of parts such as this example require more time and labor to evaluate their continued use, which can contribute to schedule delays. As a result of this discovery, the Company used this experience as a lesson learned to proactively replace other major turbine parts to reduce risk and schedule delays.
The cost impacts associated with the supply chain issues and increased equipment wear and damage discovered have contributed to the adjustment of the total project cost estimate at completion to approximately $188 million from approximately $144 million in the project forecast finalized in Q4 2021. The final timeline impact is currently unknown as Georgia Power continues to implement proactive measures to mitigate project delays. Updated cost and schedule information is provided semiannually to the Commission as part of the Company’s hydro modernization reports.
While risks associated with supply chain exist for all projects, supply chain issues have been improving in the years since the COVID pandemic. Most major procurement activities for the Plant Burton modernization project are complete, which lowers the risk of supply chain related delays. Plant Sinclair turbines have been awarded, but other major plant equipment is still in the design process.
The Company will continue to leverage experience from completed and ongoing modernization projects to mitigate supply chain risks for the modernization projects requested in the 2025 IRP; however, some components still have longer procurement lead times. For example, lead times for generator step-up (“GSU”) transformers have extended from 18 months to 3 years or more. To mitigate this lead time, the Company has contracted with vendors to hold production slots, which could potentially be used for hydro modernization projects. However, it is difficult to contract these types of equipment on a short-term basis. For this reason, the certainty associated with Commission approval of all of the remaining hydro modernization projects, as proposed in this IRP, would allow the Company to further mitigate supply chain risks through awarding long-term procurement contracts.

question:
Refer to Table 1-5 (Approximate EFOR by Unit Class) in the 2022 IRP Reserve Margin Report and the similar table, Table 1-7, in the 2025 IRP Reserve Margin Report.
Provide an explanation, as well as any analysis the Company has that explains why the EFOR for Coal and Gas Steam units both increased by about 30% (rounded) between the 2022 IRP and the 2025 IRP (Coal 2.8 to 3.6, Gas Steam 2.0 to 2.6).
Provide an explanation, as well as any analysis the Company has that explains why the EFOR for Combined Cycle units decreased by about 30% (rounded) between the 2022 IRP and the 2025 IRP (Combined Cycle 2.1 to 1.4).
response:
There are two primary reasons for the difference in reported equivalent forced outage rates (“EFOR”) values. The first reason is related to the calibration process that is performed to benchmark actual outages to simulated outage probability as described on page 19 of the 2025 Reserve Margin Report (“2025 RMS”). The first step in developing the outage data used in the model is to import the outage history for each unit. A benchmarking process that involves making slight changes to the modeled EFOR is then performed to ensure that the total capacity on outage has a similar probability of occurrence as compared to actual data. The results of this benchmarking are presented in Figure I.8 in the 2025 RMS. Because the benchmarking process is independently performed prior to each reserve margin study, the reported EFOR between the studies will be different even though they are based on similar data sets. The modification in the historical data set between studies involves a three-year shift to include the most recent three years of data and exclude the oldest three years, thereby preserving a ten-year data set.
The second reason is due to how the benchmarking analysis was performed for the 2025 RMS. In the 2022 RMS, the unit EFOR modifications were made on an annual basis. That is, the time-to-fail (“TTF”) and time-to-repair (“TTR”) inputs as described on page 17 of the 2025 RMS were assigned on an annual basis. For the 2025 RMS, this analysis was expanded to a monthly analysis. This meant that some months might have had higher EFOR values assigned to make sure that there were good actual-to-simulated outage curve fits for every month and not just the peak month.
The EFOR values reported in tables I-5 and I-7 are based on annual EFOR as reported from the SERVM model once simulations were completed. Due to the benchmarking process and the change from annual to monthly outage data inputs described above, a difference in reported annual EFOR is expected. However, this does not mean that actual generator reliability dropped from 2022 to 2025 in the Southern System.
Please see the EFOR Weighted Averages table below, which includes the annual EFOR data for all Southern Company owned and operated resources that were included in the 2025 RMS based on the historical data set used to develop the TTR and TTF data as well as the post-benchmarked EFOR data from SERVM for January and August.
 | EFOR Weighted Averages
 | Hist 2013-2019 | Hist 2020-2022 | Hist 2013-2022 | SERVM January | SERVM August
Coal | 3.51% | 1.91% | 3.03% | 2.70% | 3.58%
Gas Steam | 3.13% | 2.82% | 3.11% | 1.35% | 1.80%
Combined Cycle | 0.95% | 1.50% | 1.12% | 1.11% | 1.43%
Per this data, coal EFOR has actually improved from the 2013-2019 time period. In addition, the modeled EFOR is slightly below in January, but above in August. Gas Steam shows similar EFOR improvement in 2020-2022 but is also modeled at a much lower rate, again due to the calibration that was performed. Combined cycle was modeled at almost the same rate in January but was slightly higher in August due to the calibration.
The by-unit details used to derive the values in the above table are provided in STF-JKA-6-2 Attachment.
See the response provided above.

question:
Refer to Figure 1.9 of the January 2025 Reserve Margin Report. Please provide the following information:
Provide a detailed narrative explaining how the EFOR values used to estimate the regression model were developed. Specifically include a full and complete explanation of the following statement included in the workpaper supporting Figure 1.9: “This is the total EFOR during the hour with the greatest EFOR during ALL events that are deemed cold weather related. (Cold and Correlated EFOR)” Include an explanation of “events that are deemed cold weather related.
Provide the workpapers, in Excel, used to calculate the EFOR values used in the Figure 1.9 regression model.
Please explain why the data set used to estimate the regression model supporting Figure 1.9 only included 4 observations for the most recent 25 year period March 1996 through December 2022.
response:
The development of the cold weather outage curve was the result of a thorough analysis that involved several steps detailed below. Please see the specific data tabs in the worksheet, STF-JKA-6-3 Attachment A, referenced in the steps described below.
Identify historical cold weather events within the Southern System and the total unplanned (forced and derate) outage rate that the system experienced during those events. This outage information was obtained from the Company’s Generating Availability Data System (“GADS”) data repository. Data was examined back to 1982 (data prior to this was not readily available) and only included years that had a minimum system-weighted temperature of less than 15°F. The 15°F threshold was chosen based on anecdotal evidence suggesting weather-related equipment problems begin to appear at/below this threshold. All forced outage or derate equipment failures that occurred around the hour in which the lowest system temperature occurred were deemed as being “cold weather-related” regardless of the event description. This was done in order to capture any correlated cold weather-related outages that may not have been described completely by the unit operator due to secondary equipment failures. Note that a base level of outages will be removed in later steps. See tabs “Hourly FO 1H Data” and “Hourly 4W Data” for this historical outage information.
Cold weather equivalent forced outage rate (“EFOR”) was then determined for +/- four hours around the hour during which the coldest temperature occurred (nine hours evaluated per cold weather event). The hour in which the highest EFOR occurred during each cold weather event was chosen as the representative EFOR corresponding to the lowest system-weighted temperature that occurred during the event. This +/- four-hour range was chosen because the peak cold weather EFOR doesn’t always line up with the hour in which the lowest temperature occurred during each cold weather event. This could be due to the timing of the event relative to the sunrise and sunset as well as differences in time zones. For example, if the temperature started falling at sunset, peak cold weather outages might have occurred during the night although the temperature continued to fall right before sunrise which would have created a mismatch in total outage and low temperature timing. Additionally, if a cold weather event was prolonged, outages may become more frequent near the end of the event even though temperatures may have warmed slightly from the lowest temperature recorded during the event. See tab “Hour Max EFOR Review” for the summary calculations for each hour considered. See tab “Hour Max EFOR Review” for the analysis used to determine the maximum system EFOR for each cold weather event. The final data from this step supports the assertion that maximum EFOR occurs one to four hours after the lowest recorded temperature of an event for most data points. A summary of each event is shown on tab “Eval – Hrly FO EFOR” in cells A1:F22, which denotes the historical EFOR versus Temperature data.
Using the combined EFOR versus Temperature data, a linear fit to the historical data was generated as shown on tab “Eval – Hrly FO EFOR.” Note that the R2 fit for a linear trend is 36% versus 25% for an exponential fit. In reference to the statement mentioned in subpart (a) of this data request, it indicates that all outage events occurring during the specified cold weather event were included. Each unique unit outage was not individually evaluated to determine if it was cold weather-related as long as it fell within the evaluation timeframes as described in step 2.
The curve developed in step 3 is based solely on historical events, which includes units that are no longer in service. It was necessary to include all units in the analysis because cold weather events are relatively rare and excluding older events would result in a curve that is not informed by extreme cold weather events below ~7.5°F.
After the cold weather event in 2014, Southern Company began implementing procedures and enhanced winterization to minimize the impacts of extreme cold weather events. To account for these updates, the cold weather curve analysis was adjusted to account for winterization improvements as well as geographic differences to account for unit location relative to the average system temperatures. All owned, retail resources were assigned a cold weather outage threshold of 10°F and all contracted resources, including Southern Power, were given a cold weather outage threshold of 18°F. These unit-by-unit temperature assignments including the geographic adjustments by unit are shown on tab “Unit Master” along with the geographic adjustment.
A base level of outages was then determined without the impacts of cold weather outages. This was determined via SERVM simulations without the effects of incremental cold weather outages. The results of this winter-only analysis are shown in tab “BASE SERVM Outages.”
The historical EFOR as described in step 3 was then converted from a % of EFOR versus Temperature to forced offline megawatts (“MW”) versus Temperature as shown in tab “Curve Calculation.” This was done using a total available capacity subject to cold weather outages summation as calculated in tab “Load Resource Report.” Some resources were not included in this analysis because their historical outages are being captured elsewhere as is the case for hydro resources or the resources have not been notably impacted by cold weather in the past such as nuclear resources.
The MW versus Temperature trend was then adjusted for the base level of outages as determined in step 5 and reconverted back to an EFOR versus Temperature curve using the same total capacity subject to cold weather. The last calculation in this step was to build a EFOR versus temperature threshold table using the new base-outage-adjusted curve. The purpose of this table is to determine the incremental EFOR that a unit would experience if the temperature dropped below its geographically adjusted threshold for all temperatures down to -10°F. For example, if a unit was rated at an adjusted threshold of 0ׄ°F (column L of the “Curve Calculation” tab), it should not contribute any cold weather EFOR above -1°F but would contribute cold weather EFOR below 0°F. To determine the incremental EFOR of this unit at -5°F, for example, the EFOR delta from 0° to -5°F would need to be calculated, which in this case is 3.45% as shown in cell L12 (18.18% at -5°F minus 14.73% at 0°F).
The unit-specific cold weather outage thresholds are then combined with the incremental outage curve described in step 6 to determine system-wide cold weather MW for all temperatures from -10°F to 32°F. Note that this range was chosen to capture all possible temperatures, but the cold weather outage MW summation had dropped to 0 MW by 22°F. See tab “CWO by Curve” for this analysis.
The final step from this worksheet is to convert the MW versus Temperature outage values determined from step 7 back into an EFOR versus Temperature curve. See tab “FINAL Eval – CWO EFOR,” column C for the final step in this workbook.
This curve is the initial, improved incremental cold weather outage curve, but this curve does not account for equipment time-to-repair (“TTR”) information. It is simply an EFOR versus Temperature curve using the unit temperature thresholds and historical curve which was formed using a single EFOR point for each cold weather event. It does not account for the elevated, above-base-level EFOR that can occur in the hours leading up to and after the peak hours of cold weather events. When cold weather outages occur, they do not immediately end when the ambient temperature climbs back above a unit’s temperature threshold. It can take several hours to make necessary repairs (TTR), reducing total available capacity during that time.
In order to capture the TTR impacts, SERVM simulations were needed with TTR values applied to individual units based on historical data. The result of this analysis is provided in STF-JKA-6-3 Attachment B. The final analysis for this step is detailed on tab “Temperature vs Outage Summary.” On this tab, hourly data from several simulations with cold weather outages on and off are summarized. question:
Refer to page 64 of the January 2025 Reserve Margin Report (Cold Weather Outages sensitivity analyses).
Please explain why the impact of excluding incremental outages for Winter EORM had a small reserve margin change (22.75% to 22.2%), while the reserve margin change based on LOLE was significant (25.75% to 22.50%).
Please provide a narrative explaining how the Company performed the historical incremental outage analysis.
Please provide the workpaper showing the development of the historic incremental outage curve, in Excel. Include all of the data used to estimate the curve.
response:
The EORM/LOLE worksheet for the base winter case (“Base Case”) was provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025, in Technical Appendix Volume I, Reserve Margin Study, III. Base Case Results, workpaper: Figure 1 III.1 III.10 III.11 III.12 - Winter EORM U-Curve (TS).xlsx. The EORM/LOLE worksheet for the no cold weather outage curve (“No CWO Case”) case was provided in Technical Appendix Volume I, Reserve Margin Study, IV. Sensitivity Analysis, workpaper: 2024 RMS - Winter - No CWO (TS).xlsx. These worksheets provide all of the data necessary to determine the Economic Optimum Reserve Margin (“EORM”) and Loss of Load Expectation (“LOLE”) differences between the two simulations.
Changes in reliability-impacting inputs, like the cold weather outage curve, can have different effects on EORM and LOLE analyses. The EORM analysis seeks to determine the lowest cost reserve margin. It does not target a specific reliability value, unlike the LOLE analysis. The two analyses also consider two different reliability metrics that can yield different insights. Expected unserved energy (“EUE”) indicates the magnitude of annual load shed, while LOLE indicates the frequency of load shed events equal to or greater than 1 megawatt hour (“MWh”). Both metrics are important. For example, if weighted average EUE was 500 MWh, it might not be concerning. However, if the average weighted LOLE in the same study was 250 days, that would be concerning even if the load shed was only 2 MWh per day (250 days x 2 MWh per day = 500 MWh per year). Both EUE and LOLE metrics are considered in the reserve margin study precisely because they can impact the target reserve margin in different ways.
Revisiting the worksheets referenced above and focusing on EUE and LOLE impact, it is apparent that the EUE reliability component is much lower across every tested reserve margin level in the No CWO Case. The goal of the EORM study was not to determine a new reserve margin at the same level of reliability, unlike the LOLE study. In other words, an improvement in LOLE is more impactful to the LOLE analysis than the improvement in EUE in the EORM analysis due to other cost factors considered in that analysis.
The first steps in the development of the historical outage curve are very similar to the base cold weather outage curve as described in the Company’s response to STF-JKA-6-3. All worksheet tab references are for STF-JKA-6-6 Attachment A.
Step is identical to the step described in the Company’s response to STF-JKA-6-3(a).
Step is identical to the step described in the Company’s response to STF-JKA-6-3(a).
Using the combined equivalent forced outage rate (“EFOR”) versus Temperature data, an exponential fit to the historical data was generated as shown on tab “Eval – Hrly FO EFOR.” The choice of an exponential fit was made when the sensitivities were being developed and prior to the decision to use a linear fit for the base curve.
A base level of outages was then determined without the impacts of cold weather outages. This was determined via SERVM simulations without the effects of incremental cold weather outages. The results of this winter-only analysis are shown in tab “BASE SERVM Outages.”
The historical EFOR as described in step 3 was now converted from a % of EFOR versus Temperature to forced offline MW versus Temperature as shown in tab “Curve Calculation.” This was done using a total available capacity subject to cold weather outages summation as calculated in tab “Load Resource Report.” Some resources were not included in this analysis because their historical outages are being captured elsewhere as is the case for hydro resources or the resources have not been notably impacted by cold weather in the past such as nuclear resources.
The MW versus Temperature trend was then adjusted for the base level of outages as determined in step 5 and reconverted back to an EFOR versus Temperature curve using the same total capacity subject to cold weather.
This curve is the initial, historical incremental cold weather outage curve, but this curve does not account for equipment time-to-repair (“TTR”) information. It is simply an EFOR versus Temperature curve using the historical curve, which was formed using a single EFOR point for each cold weather event. It does not account for the elevated, above-base-level EFOR that can occur in the hours leading up to and after the peak hours of cold weather events. When cold weather outages occur, they do not immediately end when the ambient temperature climbs back above a unit’s temperature threshold. It can take several hours to make necessary repairs (TTR), reducing total available capacity during that time.
In order to capture the TTR impacts, SERVM simulations were needed with TTR values applied to individual units based on historical data. The result of this analysis is provided in STF-JKA-6-3 Attachment B. The final analysis for this step is detailed on tab “Temperature vs Outage Summary.” On this tab, hourly data from several simulations with cold weather outages on and off are summarized. Two smoothed curves were created at lower and higher temperatures and blended as shown in column G.
The TTR curve from step 6 and the initial, improved curve from step 5 were then blended to determine a final curve cold weather outage curve as shown in STF-JKA-6-6 Attachment B. The final analysis for this step is shown in the “CWO Calculation” tab. This step blended a little art and science to build a curve that did not prioritize one curve over the other. The result of this analysis resulted in an average shift upwards of 0.5% as compared to the initial, improved curve.
The final step was to import the curve into the SERVM model for the reserve margin study. The final curve was imported as a negative output resource using the final, improved cold weather outrage curve in column J of STF-JKA-6-6 Attachment B, tab “CWO Calculation.” This resulted in a set amount of load appearing at each temperature, beginning at 32°F down to -10°F based on the size of the fleet in the model that was subject to cold weather outages.
See the response in subpart (b) for all worksheets.

question:
Refer to the Technical Appendix Volume 2.  Referring to the Environmental Compliance Cost Recovery (ECCR) Table, did the Company (including SCS or any other organization on behalf of the Company) prepare more than one estimate for the environmental projects detailed in that Table?
If not, explain fully why not.
If so, provide the estimates.
How did the Company decide which estimate was most appropriate?
response:
The Company did not create separate estimates but rather considered compliance options as they were evaluated. The resulting estimates are included in the Environmental Compliance Strategy (“ECS”) and incorporated into the unit retirement study scenarios. Following this analysis, the Company determines the most cost-effective approach for each unit that meets regulatory requirements. The most appropriate approach for each unit may not be the least cost option, all things held equal, because of the unit-specific risks and requirements to comply and the need to incorporate reliability considerations. Where appropriate, the Company continues to look for alternative compliance options that are in the best interest of customers.
The development of the Company’s ECS first considers a regulatory review of current and possible future local, state, regional, and federal environmental requirements. Following the regulatory review, the Company evaluates the specific requirements for each generating plant and/or unit, as well as availability and the timeline to implement the control technology, to determine what control technology options are available to comply. The feasible control options are evaluated based on technical performance, reliability, operational flexibility, and capital and O&M cost impacts. question: Identify and explain how the Company is accounting for CCR costs at plants that are expected to continue to operate after their ash ponds are closed and remediated.  Identify the amount of CCR ARO as of 12/31/2024 and as estimated for 12/31/2025, 12/31/2026, 12/31/2027 and 12/31/2028 at each such steam generating plant.
response:
The Company accounts for coal combustion residuals (“CCR”) costs at all plant sites based on the Financial Accounting Standards Board’s Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) Topic 410, Asset Retirement and Environmental Obligations since its adoption in 2003. As such, the CCR asset retirement obligation (“ARO”) accounting entries for each plant site follow the accounting entries listed below which are in accordance with ASC 410-20 and ASC 980.
Recognize new ARO or Update existing ARO
	DR 101 Plant in Service 
		CR 230 Asset Retirement Obligation Liability
(To record initial fair value of the ARO Liability)
Depreciation of ARC Asset [FAS 143/ASC 410 (Over life)]
	DR 403 Depreciation Expense
		CR 108 Accumulated Reserve 
(To record straight-line depreciation on the asset retirement cost)
Accretion of ARO Liability [FAS 143/ASC 410 (Over life)]
	DR 411 Accretion Expense
		CR 230 Asset Retirement Obligation Liability
(To record accretion expense on the ARO liability)
Rate Recovery
DR 407 Regulatory Debit
		CR 254 Regulatory Liability
(To record a regulatory liability related to ARO costs recovered from customers in rates)
Defer Depreciation and Accretion
	DR 182 Regulatory Asset 
		CR 407 Regulatory Credit
(To defer depreciation and accretion expense to regulatory asset. GAAP and Ratemaking accounting entries must both be followed; however, the Company cannot book both. Therefore, the effects of FAS 143/ASC 410 are reversed and only the actions of the regulator are reflected in the Company’s financial statements)
Settlements
	DR 108 Cost of Removal				DR 230 Asset Retirement Obligation
		CR Cash 						CR 108 Cost of Removal
DR 254 Regulatory Liability
		CR 182 Regulatory Asset
(To record settlement of the ARO liability)

question: Going into 2025, have any of the research activities that were envisioned by the Company in its 2022 IRP been dropped or discontinued? If so, identify which ones and explain the reasons for dropping or discontinuing each.
response:
The research activities listed below have been discontinued since the filing of the 2022 IRP.
Planned Research Activity | Justification to Cancel
Assess the value of terminal tractor electrification | Southern Company Services Research & Development (“R&D”) will no longer pursue due to low priority and resource availability.
Develop and commercialize charging infrastructure solutions to serve fleets and MDHD vehicles | After stakeholder discussions, it was determined that there was not a viable path forward for DC as a service technology. There are no fleets in our territory that would currently be able to utilize MW+ charging infrastructure. Future investigations will focus on harvesting learnings from demonstrations in other markets. Decision was made based on data from a project conducted by the Electric Power Research Institute (“EPRI”) to examine DC as a Service.
Develop cost targets for all relevant utility-scale hydrogen production pathways to determine necessary costs for hydrogen production to be viable via electricity | Southern Company Technology & Planning group completed similar work through a project with EPRI evaluating electrolyzer demonstrations at Plant McDonough. Work canceled as it would be duplicative.
Complete DOE Funded Tall Tower Demonstration | This project was not selected by the Georgia Public Service Commission as a research demonstration project.
Demonstrate the CMBlu 3MW energy storage technology | Delay of CMBlu design maturity will delay any larger-scale demonstration.
Demonstrate the feasibility of the linear state estimator (“SE”) to become a backup to EMS's traditional SE at transmission level with an accuracy within 5% of traditional SE | R&D will no longer pursue due to low priority and resource availability.
Develop short & long-term R&D strategy for decarbonization of residential and commercial buildings that supports Southern Company and customer goals | EPRI is completing decarbonized buildings roadmap and R&D has determined that future work in this area has diminishing returns and will not be pursued.
Vehicle Grid Integration - demonstrate passenger vehicles as a grid-tied resources | Original plans to conduct customer-sided demonstration - reduced scope to lab testing only due to contracting delays.
Examine micro-nuclear reactor technologies in support of customer decarbonization needs | After exploration, it was determined that micro-nuclear as a specific technology interest is a lower priority area.
Successfully commercialize the Net Power technology | NetPower ownership has changed. Further investigation of the technology will continue only at a "monitoring" level.
Expand usage of fiber optic infrastructure to aide in DER integration. advanced monitoring, and data backhaul while creating the opportunity to provide grid and customer services | Submitted proposal with Fiberize to APC Connectivity team. It was determined that the speed limitations of the technology did not warrant the investment.
Demonstrate Asset Health functionality of transformer monitoring and visualization pilot | Inadequate data was available to execute the desired scope of work
Define potential technology roadmaps for utility-scale hydrogen production via nuclear integration | R&D will no longer pursue due to low priority and resource availability.
Assess Gulf of Mexico offshore wind lease opportunities for planning models | Canceled based on evaluations that wind resource is insufficient.
Develop proposal for offshore wind pilot project | Upon completion of offshore wind analysis, economics of offshore wind project prove not to be feasible without state mandates for development. Remaining work will focus on preliminary characterization of offshore development areas.
Review and assess technologies for production of hydrogen at $1/kg at relevant scale | Work to reduce the cost of hydrogen production is the specific focus of DOE programs. R&D not well positioned to influence outside of the DOE projects.
Assess ability of 3D printing to help address energy equity in new construction neighborhoods. | R&D will no longer pursue due to low priority and resource availability.
Demonstrate electric multi-family water heating that is cost competitive with NG | R&D will no longer pursue due to low priority and resource availability.
Identify Future Applications for AI Technologies in Load Forecasting/Planning | Due to closing of technology developer, this concept will not be pursued further.

question: What happens to the incremental revenue from the NU-1 tariff? Identify and explain the accounting treatment for all revenue and expenses associated with the tariff. Does this accounting treatment differ from what is required by accounting standards? Regarding the proposed accounting treatment, what specifically does Georgia Power have to receive approval from the Commission?
response:
The Company is proposing to collect revenues under the NU-1 tariff associated with the nuclear uprate project in two ways.
The Program Enrollment Contribution (“PEC”) will be collected from subscribers prior to the in-service date of the Plant Hatch uprate project and will be recognized as a prepaid liability under the accounting guidelines. The prepaid revenue will be amortized over the assumed remaining life of the asset to other operating revenues, which will reduce retail cost of service for retail customers. The Company does not require separate approval from the Commission for this accounting treatment. However, as discussed with Staff and per the Company's Application for Approval of the 2026 Plant Hatch Units 1-2 Nuclear Extended Power Uprates, the Company is requesting Commission approval for the following accounting treatment. For any PEC payments received from the tariff subscribers in 2028, the Company will apply the payments to CWIP base in 2028 solely for the purposes of calculating AFUDC on the project and the payment will be excluded from retail rate base. Beginning in 2029, any PEC payments will be applied as a reduction to retail rate base following GAAP accounting and will be reflected as such in the 2028 base rate case projections. In the event the current Alternate Rate Plan (“ARP”) is extended beyond 2028, any further application of the PEC payments to CWIP base shall be considered as part of the ARP extension.
The Zero Emission Credit (“ZEC”) revenue will be collected from subscribers once the nuclear uprate is in-service and recognized as collected under the accounting guidelines. This revenue will be recorded to other operating revenues and reduce retail cost of service for retail customers. The Company does not require separate approval from the Commission for this accounting treatment. However, as discussed with Staff and per the Company's Application for Approval of the 2026 Plant Hatch Units 1-2 Nuclear Extended Power Uprates, the Company is requesting Commission approval for the following accounting treatment. Any ZEC payments received from the tariff subscribers through December 31, 2028, will be recorded as a regulatory liability until the next base rate case. If the ARP is further extended, deferral of ZEC payments beyond 2028 will be considered as part of the terms of the extension. Beginning January 1, 2029, any ZEC payments received from the tariff subscribers will be trued-up on an actual basis to the projected amounts included in the next base rate case.
In order to mitigate revenue requirement impacts to non-subscribing customers before the full benefits of uprated capacity can be realized, the Company is requesting approval from the Commission to defer depreciation and interest expenses associated with the Plant Hatch project capital cost closed to plant in service. The deferred depreciation and interest expenses are proposed to be amortized over the life of the asset once the project is complete and uprate projects reach commercial operation date (“COD”). Amortization of the deferred depreciation and interest would begin in the month the incremental uprate capacity is placed in service and begins generating incremental electricity through the end of the life of the units, aligning cost recovery with the start of incremental generation and the associated project benefits.

question: Ratemaking treatment of $███████████ payment: Would the Company object to placing the        $███████████ in a regulatory liability and applying the regulatory liability against the Hatch 1&2 CWIP balance for the duration of the construction period?
response:
The $███████████ Program Enrollment Contribution (“PEC”), once received from the       subscriber, will be recorded to a contract liability as unearned revenue per revenue recognition GAAP guidance in ASC 606 and cannot be recorded to a regulatory liability. However, from a ratemaking perspective, a contract liability and a regulatory liability are both credited to retail rate base immediately and impact retail cost of service equally.
Based on the accounting guidance described above, the contract liability cannot be recorded as an offset to a Construction Work in Progress (“CWIP”) account. However, as discussed and agreed to with Staff and per the Application for Approval of the 2026 Plant Hatch Units 1-2 Nuclear Extended Power Uprates, the Company will apply any Program Enrollment Contribution (“PEC”) payments received from the tariff subscribers in 2028 to CWIP base in 2028 solely for the purposes of calculating AFUDC on the project and the payment will be excluded from retail rate base. Beginning in 2029, any PEC payments will be applied as a reduction to retail rate base following GAAP accounting and will be reflected as such in the 2028 base rate case projections. In the event the current Alternate Rate Plan (“ARP”) is extended beyond 2028, any further application of the PEC payments to CWIP base shall be considered as part of the ARP extension.

question: In B26_AV_Tool_HatchEPU - GPC Ownership TRADE SECRET.xlsx, explain the difference between Incremental Capital and Baseline Capital.
response: Baseline capital represents the ongoing capital required to keep Hatch Units 1–2 operating without the uprate (e.g. costs that would occur regardless of the EPU project). In contrast, incremental capital reflects the additional capital that results from the decision to implement the uprate, including new equipment and modifications needed to increase output. The tool separates these categories to isolate the economics of the decision: baseline capital exists in both the uprate and no-uprate cases (with timing differences driving value impacts), while incremental capital captures the portion of spending attributable specifically to the uprate and, therefore, represents the true incremental cost of the project.

question: Regarding proposed uprate ZEC program, please explain whether the Company is proposing a standalone, distinct program specific to nuclear uprates, or if this represents an expansion of the existing Flex-REC program.  Compare and Contrast the proposed program to the Flex-REC program and identify limitations with the Flex-REC program.
response:
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program is proposed to be a standalone program and not an expansion of the Flex-REC program, which is a program that offers access to attributes from renewable energy resources. There are several differences between the proposed Nuclear Uprate Subscription program and the Flex-REC program listed below.
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program allows for a 25-year term, which permits the customer and Georgia Power to lock in long-term fixed prices for the Zero Emissions Credits (ZECs). In contrast, the Flex-REC program only allows for a maximum 3-year term and is based on market prices, which can fluctuate over time.
The Nuclear Uprate Subscription program allows for hourly matching of ZEC production and customer energy consumption since the ZECs are created by baseload nuclear units. Whereas, the Flex-REC program only procures solar RECs produced during daylight hours, which do not necessarily align with the customer’s energy consumption.  The customer interested in participating in the ZEC program is seeking to support resources that produce clean energy that aligns with their energy use.
The revenue from the Nuclear Uprate Subscription program will reduce rates for customers while the Flex-REC program is simply a pass-through for the actual costs to procure the RECs. Additionally, a portion of the revenue from the Nuclear Uprate Subscription program will be realized during the construction period to offset some of the cost of the uprates, preceding the delivery of ZECs. The Flex REC program bills monthly as RECs are delivered.

question: Provide the current subscription status of the Flex-REC program. Additionally, please clarify how existing nuclear ZECs/RECs are currently accounted for or assigned to specific customers, and whether any are uncommitted.  If Company produced RECs are not being monetized to the benefits of customers, please explain why not.
response:
Flex-REC Subscription Status
Georgia Power currently has 10 customers under contract, with an additional 3 customers pending.
For May, Georgia Power retired 25,333 renewable energy credits (“RECs”) on behalf of the 10 contracted customers. June reporting is expected to be completed next week.
Year to date, Georgia Power has retired 177,412 RECs for participating customers.
Current REC inventory includes 124,912 solar RECs and 6,838 wind RECs.
As it relates to the Flex-REC Subscription program, Georgia Power purchases unbundled solar and wind RECs and maintains them within the North American Renewables (“NAR”) Registry, which provides the ability to inventory, track, and retire RECs on behalf of participating customers. The registry also produces retirement certificates identifying the REC serial numbers and associated renewable generating resources.
REC procurement is managed to support both existing customer obligations and expected future program participation. Accordingly, all RECs are acquired as needed for program purposes and retired as required to satisfy customer subscriptions. Georgia Power purchases RECs periodically to maintain adequate inventory and ensure fulfillment of current and anticipated program demand.
The solar RECs used for the program are not generated by Georgia Power-owned solar resources. Solar RECs that supply the program may be sourced from a variety of suppliers.
The Company is not currently tracking, inventorying, or assigning nuclear ZECs as part of the Flex-REC program. The program is supported by unbundled solar and wind RECs that are procured, held in inventory, and retired on behalf of participating customers as needed to meet their renewable energy requirements. Per Commission Policy, RECs produced by Company-owned renewable resources are reported as part of the system mix serving all customers.

question: Please provide the analytical justification for the changes in the State Tax Rate (decreased from ███████████████ and the Property Tax Rate (decreased from ███████████████ utilized in the current GPC evaluation versus prior filings.
response: The state tax rate is established by the State of Georgia, while the property tax rate is derived from an aggregation of applicable county-level property tax rates. question: The 2026 CBA model separates baseline capital from incremental capital, showing incremental costs extending through the end of the plant's life. This contrasts with the 2025 IRP, which showed a planned spending offset from 2031–2039 and zero incremental capital thereafter. Please reconcile this accounting change and provide a detailed itemization of the specific projects subject to accelerated capital tracking.
response:
There has been no accounting change made to the B26_AV_TOOL_HatchEPU workbook (“B26 AVTool”) relative to the 2025IRP_AV_Nuclear TRADE SECRET TN STAFF (“’25IRP AVTool”).  Rather, when inspecting the cost sheets in both of the tools, be aware that the data is being input differently.  In the 25IRP AVTool, a consolidated EPU budget spend curve was entered into the cost sheet and the tool calculated revenue requirements.  In the current iteration of the economics, the choice was made to utilize the Standard Analysis Model (“SAM”) to generate revenue requirements, not only to enhance the accuracy of the revenue requirements which are now calculated at the individual asset level, but also to help process other inputs like the customer prepayment and regulatory deferral.  SAM takes the individual asset spend curves and creates individual revenue requirements that are aggregated as an output of that tool and input directly into the cost sheet of the B26 AVTool.  Because the revenue requirements have already been generated the AVTool doesn’t need to calculate them which is why when trying to compare the cost sheet from the different tools, it will look different even though the project has not changed substantively from the budget perspective.  The B26 AVTool may look like it has incremental capital after the construction period but that isn’t the case, and those dollars are representative of the revenue requirements.
All assets including projects subject to advancement can be seen individually in SAM on the Input_Output sheet.

A plant is licensed to operate within a specified power and core flow domain. Maintaining proper core flow is essential as it ensures effective cooling of the reactor.
Maximum Extended Load Line Limit Plus (“MELLLA+”) is an approved method used in a boiling water reactor (“BWR”) power plant to safely increase the allowed range of water flow through the reactor core. By giving plant operators a larger range of licensed core flow, MELLLA+ allows more operational flexibility to manage core flow effectively and can improve plant capacity. MELLLA+ is increasingly important for BWRs with EPU. EPU reduces the allowed core flow range and MELLLA+ restores the allowed range of core flow.
MELLLA+ involves upgrading the Power Range Neutron Monitor system and updating the power-to-flow map. The Power Range Neutron Monitor is used to monitor the neutron flux – the measure of intensity of neutron radiation – in the reactor core, which is crucial for ensuring the safe and efficient operation of the reactor.

question: Please explain in detail the specific analytical steps used by the Company in its decision-making process to determine the amount of energy efficiency kWh and kW savings to include in the Company’s Proposed Case and the Capacity and Affordability Case.
response:
Proposed Case:
In accordance with the Commission’s Order Adopting Stipulation in the Vogtle Prudency Proceeding in Docket No. 29849 (“Vogtle Prudence Order”), the Company developed the Demand Side Management (“DSM”) Proposed Case with a savings target of at least 0.75% of annual retail sales. The amount of kW savings for the Proposed Case was a result of measures used to meet the Vogtle Prudence Order’s energy goal and the strategic growth of the Residential Demand Response (“DR”) program, informed by the results of the 2023 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) Update and the filed 2023 Technical Economic Achievable Potential (“TEAPot”) Study.
Capacity and Affordability Case:
The amount of kWh and kW savings included in the Capacity and Affordability Case was informed by historical program performance and the results of the 2023 IRP Update and TEAPot Study. The Company balanced the benefits achieved through energy efficiency programs, as measured by the Total Resource Cost (“TRC”) test, with the upward pressure on rates to all customers, as measured by the Rate Impact Measure (“RIM”) test. This is consistent with the Commission’s economic screening policy, outlined in the 2004 IRP Order in Docket No. 17687, which requires the Company to offer a DSM plan that minimizes upward pressure on rates and maximizes economic efficiency.

question: Please describe the methodology used by the Company to develop the program participation forecasts by measure type for each proposed DSM program in the Company’s Proposed Case. Please explain if the Company believes that historical participation in an energy efficiency program represents a cap on what is possible for participation in future years.
response:
The Company relied on a combination of the following factors to develop program participation forecasts by measure type for each proposed Demand Side Management (“DSM”) program in the Company’s Proposed Case: historical program participation, input from Company program managers and planning staff, the Company’s 2024 Technical Economic and Achievable Potential (“TEAPot”) report, and Company’s evaluation results. The Company also calibrated participation for certain programs to achieve specific program targets. The table below describes the methodology for developing program participation.
Program | Participation Methodology
Products | Participation is based primarily on Home Energy Improvement Program’s (“HEIP”) Individual Improvements historic program participation with input from program managers, the Company’s 2024 TEAPot report, and planning staff.
HEIP | Participation is based primarily on HEIP’s Individual Improvements and Whole House historic program participation with input from program managers, the Company’s 2024 TEAPot report, and planning staff.
Energy Assistance for Savings and Efficiency (“EASE”) | Participation is primarily based on EASE historic program participation with input from program managers, the Company’s 2024 TEAPot report, and planning staff with the inclusion of a moderate-income level participation.
Residential Demand Response (“DR”) | Participation is primarily based on historic program participation, including the final 2023 IRP Order, with input from program managers and planning staff with baseline participation based on the Company’s 2023 IRP Update.
Residential Behavioral | Participation is primarily based on historic program participation and reflects annual attrition.
HopeWorks | Participation is based on historic program participation with input from program managers, the Company’s 2024 TEAPot report, and planning staff.
Commercial Custom | Participation is primarily based on historic program participation with input from program managers and planning staff.
Commercial Prescriptive | Participation is primarily based on historic program participation with input from program managers, the Company’s 2024 TEAPot report, and planning staff.
Small Commercial Direct Install (“SCDI”) | Participation is primarily based on historic program participation adjusted to reflect program growth through new measure opportunities that could lead to new participants.
The Company believes many factors impact program participation and that historical participation alone does not represent a cap on possible participation or future years.
