question: Please explain if any energy efficiency or demand response measures in the Company’s Technical Resource Manual (“TRM”) used for the 2025 IRP filing that pass the TRC Test have been excluded from any of the energy efficiency/demand response scenarios examined and filed by the Company in its 2025 IRP. If any such measures have been excluded, please provide an explanation of why such cost-effective measures have been excluded.
response:
Yes, a number of energy efficiency or demand response measures in the Company’s Technical Reference Manual (“TRM”) used for the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) filing that pass the Total Resource Cost (“TRC”) Test have been excluded from energy efficiency/demand response scenarios examined and filed by the Company in its 2025 IRP for the following reasons:
Mitigate evaluation risk: Some measures, for example, Residential Interior and Exterior Lighting and consumer electronics, are highly matured in the market and are thus subject to low net-to-gross ratios and low evaluated savings.
Exclude Inviable Programs: Some cost-effective appliance recycling measures are excluded, as a full Appliance Recycling Program is not a cost-effective standalone program. Business Energy Reports are excluded as the Commercial Behavioral Program will no longer be implemented by the Company. The Evaluation Measurement & Verification (“EM&V”) results found no statistically significant energy savings and therefore the Company did not find the program to be cost-effective for the 2026-2028 cycle.
Reduce Implementation Complexity: Some unique measures, especially in the Commercial Sector, are combined with similar measures or are instead assumed to be eligible under the Commercial Custom Program in order to reduce implementation complexity.

question: Please list and describe all Company sponsored energy efficiency online tools that are currently available to Georgia Power customers.
response:
The following Company sponsored energy efficiency online tools are currently available to Georgia Power customers:
Online Customer Care (“OCC”) Portal
Georgia Power customers can sign in to the OCC portal for information regarding their energy usage including billing and payments, outage information, energy efficiency tips, links to energy efficiency program websites, and detailed usage information through My Power Usage.
Online Home Energy Checkup
Customers can complete a series of questions online and learn how to improve their individual home’s energy efficiency with the online home energy checkup.
Home Energy Checkup: georgiapower.com/homeenergycheckup
Home Energy Efficiency Tips
Customers can review low to no-cost tips to save on their electric energy bill. By following these tips, customers can decrease energy usage and make their home more energy efficient.
Energy Efficiency Tips:
georgiapower.com/residential/save-money-and-energy/home-energy-efficiency-and-savings/energy-efficiency-tips.html
Income Qualified Assistance Portal
The Income-Qualified Assistance Portal allows customers to find programs that can help them manage energy cost more effectively. Customers begin by answering a few questions to determine program eligibility, including: HopeWorks, Energy Assistance for Savings and Efficiency (“EASE”), Income Qualified Discount, and other resources.
Income Qualified Assistance Portal:
georgiapower-iqportal.customerapplication.com
Community and Customer Assistance
The Assistance Locator tool helps customers find local resources and provides information about qualification for Georgia Power’s assistance programs.
Energy Assistance:
georgiapower.com/residential/billing-and-rate-plans/billing-options/payment-assistance.html
Residential Energy Efficiency Online Tools include:
Specialty Lighting Program Find a Store:
Customers can find retail locations that offer instant rebates on the purchase price of efficiency products through Georgia Power’s incentives.
Georgia Power FAS: Residential Lighting Store - Find a Store: georgiapower.customerapplication.com/contractor-search
Home Energy Improvement Program (“HEIP”) Find a Contractor:
Customers who are interested in a home energy assessment and participate in the HEIP can find a qualified participating contractor.
Georgia Power: GPC HEIP Find a Contractor - Find a Contractor: heip.customerapplication.com/contractor-search
Online application for HEIP
Customers can learn more about the program, review testimonials, understand the process, and apply to participate in the program.
Home Energy Improvement Program:
georgiapower.com/residential/save-money-and-energy/products-programs/home-energy-efficiency-programs/home-energy-improvementprogram.html
Georgia Power Online Marketplace
Customers can buy energy efficient items with an instant rebate provided by Georgia Power’s efficiency programs. The Marketplace also provides energy efficiency education on specific product categories and information on how to optimize energy usage using product(s) available on the Marketplace.
Georgia Power Marketplace: georgiapowermarketplace.com/
Online application for EASE
Customers can learn more about the program, review testimonials, learn the participation process, and apply to participate in the program.
Energy Assistance for Savings & Efficiency (EASE): georgiapower.com/residential/save-money-and-energy/products-programs/home-energy-efficiency-programs/ease.html
Donation page for EASE
Customers can find a testimonial from a program participant to learn more about program benefits, frequently asked questions, and donate.
Home Energy Efficiency Programs:
georgiapower.com/residential/save-money-and-energy/products-programs/home-energy-efficiency-programs/ease/ease-donor.html
Refrigerator Recycling Appliance Savings Tool
Customers can schedule a free appliance pickup, learn the participation process, and calculate savings for recycling their extra refrigerator.
Recycle Your Refrigerator:
georgiapower.com/residential/save-money-and-energy/products-programs/home-energy-efficiency-programs/refrigerator-recycling.html
Commercial Energy Efficiency Online Tools include:
Online application for Commercial Energy Efficiency Program (“CEEP”) (Custom and Prescriptive) where customers can apply to participate in the program.
Georgia Power Commercial Rebates: https://georgiapowercommercialrebates.com/
CEEP Participating Contractor Directory
Customers who are interested participating in the CEEP can find a qualified participating contractor.
CEEP Find a Contractor Tool: https://www.georgiapowercommercialcontractor.com/
Small Commercial Direct Install (“SCDI”) Program Free Assessment Request Form
Customers complete this online form to schedule a free on-site energy assessment.
SCDI Signup:
https://www.georgiapower.com/business/products-programs/efficiency-maintenance/small-commercial/scdi-signup.html
Online tools for all business customers to help manage energy and reduce energy consumption include:
Business Energy Efficiency Tips
Customers can review low to no-cost tips to save on their energy bill.
Energy Efficiency Tips for Businesses: https://www.georgiapower.com/biztips
Georgia Power Automated Benchmarking Tool
The Automated Benchmarking Tool enables building owners and property managers to generate a benchmark score and aggregate building usage data into a single virtual meter.
Automated Benchmarking Site: https://abtgeorgiapower.sightline-icf.com/
Business Energy Advisor Tool
This tool provides actionable advice on proven energy management strategies and technologies for businesses. The tool is aimed at helping customers identify ways to streamline their operations and save money and energy.
Georgia Power | BEA | Home: https://georgiapower.bizenergyadvisor.com/
EnergyDirect
Online tool to help commercial customers find ways to reduce their energy consumption and lower their energy bills.
EnergyDirect: https://www.energydirect.com/
My Power Usage Monitoring Tool
Businesses can monitor daily and hourly energy consumption, updated within 24-48 hours, enabling real-time tracking and adjustments for optimal energy management.
My Power Usage: https://www.georgiapower.com/mypowerusage

question: Please provide a list of the suggestions that were proposed by the DSMWG in the Ideation meetings held in February 2024 that were incorporated into the Company’s Proposed DSM Case. Also, please provide a list of the proposed suggestions that were not incorporated into the Company’s Proposed Case.
response:
Residential
Proposed Suggestions Incorporated into the Proposed Case:
In-Unit Multifamily Direct Install Program
Partially adopted. This overlaps with the multi-family Energy Assistance for Savings and Affordability (“EASE”) Program segment.
Air-Source Heat Pump Upgrades for EASE
Fully adopted into the EASE Program. Air-Source Heat Pumps SEER 16 is in the list of measures for income-qualified customers.
Air-Source Heat Pump Upgrades for Home Energy Improvement Program (“HEIP”)
Fully adopted into the HEIP Program. Air-Source Heat Pumps SEER 16 is in the list of individual improvements and whole home path.
Historical Certified Manufactured Homes
Partially adopted. Manufactured homes are modeled as eligible segments within the EASE and HopeWorks program and therefore are not modeled as a standalone program.
High Efficiency New Manufactured Homes Program
Partially adopted. Most of these measures are already incentivized through HEIP, EASE, and HopeWorks, with both EASE and HopeWorks having a manufactured homes segment.
Enhancement to HEIP Manufactured Homes Retrofit
Partially adopted. Suggestions around participant and contractor outreach will be assessed for inclusion during program implementation.
Battery Demand Response Program
The Company may include this measure in the Residential DR Program where various technologies can participate for ease and flexibility of implementation and customer participation to reach a set and approved demand reduction goal. Batteries would be one such technology that the selected implementer would be able to use.
Proposed Suggestions Not Incorporated into the Proposed Case:
EarthCents New Home Program
This program was previously offered by Georgia Power but concluded in 2019 after evaluation results found this program was not cost-effective.
Shift to Utility Cost Test (“UCT”) for Energy Efficiency Programs
Replacing the requirement in the Georgia Public Service Commission (“Commission”) Rule 515-3-4-.04(4)2 (“Rule”) that programs pass the Total Resource Cost test with a requirement that programs pass the UCT would require a change to the Rule by the Commission.
Home Energy Loan Program (“HELP”)
The idea is not applicable to program design.
Aligning HEIP with Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”) Home Efficiency Rebates
The idea is not applicable to program design.
Co-design or modify energy efficiency programs to align with GEFA administered IRA-funded Home Energy Rebate program
The idea is not applicable to program design.
Neighborhood Energy Efficiency Deliver Program (“NEED”)
The idea is not applicable to program design.
Commercial
Proposed Suggestions Incorporated into the Proposed Case:
Custom Multifamily Program
Partially adopted into the Custom program. Multifamily properties are currently eligible to participate within the Custom program, therefore not modeled as a standalone program for cost efficiencies.
Electric School Bus Grid Resource Pilot Program
Filed a request for Vehicle-to-Everything (“V2X”) pilot in Section 10.3.6 of the 2025 IRP Main Document.
Proposed Suggestions Not Incorporated into the Proposed Case:
On-Bill Financing for Tax-Exempt Entities
The information is not applicable to program design.
Residential and Commercial
Proposed Suggestions Incorporated into the Proposed Case:
Energy Star Certified Heating and Cooling Distributor-Focused Midstream Program
Partially adopted. Heat pump measures are included in the Residential HEIP and Commercial Prescriptive programs. Additionally, the Prescriptive program is designed with a midstream channel, and the Company may explore midstream as a delivery option for HEIP.
Energy Star Certified Heat Pump Water Heater Midstream Program
Partially adopted. Heat pump water heaters are included in the Residential HEIP and Commercial Prescriptive programs. Additionally, the Prescriptive program is designed with a midstream channel, and the Company may explore options of a midstream delivery channel for HEIP during implementation.

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 79 regarding Georgia Power’s proposed changes to the current Utility Scale RFP Procurement Strategy:
a. 	Describe how the 1,000 MW target amount and the ability to procure up to 3,000 MW to meet customer subscription demand amounts were determined. Describe if any alternative procurement amounts were considered. Provide workpapers to support these amounts if applicable.
b. 	Why was the average of the Total Net Benefits selected as the threshold to which bidders have the ability to buy down to?
c. 	Provide an estimated timeline for the extended RFP Period.
d. 	Is Georgia Power proposing to allow Company-Owned Proposals and Affiliate projects to be submitted during the Extended RFP Period?
e. 	Please describe how flexible Commercial Operation dates will improve the current Utility Scale RFP process.
f. 	Are the Company’s proposed procurement strategy enhancements modeled from another jurisdiction? If so, provide examples of other relevant jurisdictions that the Company is aware of that use a similar RFP process.
g. 	Provide all presentations, surveys, and/or summaries of market feedback received by the Company from interested parties that were reviewed and considered as part of the Company’s proposed Utility Scale RFP Enhancements.
response:
The Company’s intent in proposing an initial 1,000 MW target amount with the ability to procure up to an additional 3,000 MW was selected based on procurement expectations from ongoing Georgia Power requests for proposals (“RFPs”), recent Utility Scale Renewable RFP experience, expected customer demand for new renewable energy, and generic renewable allocations to Georgia Power across all scenarios in the Company’s 2025 IRP Resource Mix Study. STF-PIA-3-2 Attachment A provides the average generic renewable allocations that helped to inform the plan to add up to 4,000 MW of new renewable resources by 2035. Note, the years 2025 through 2031 are excluded from this calculation due to either (i) selection of zero renewable resources in the generic expansion plan for a given year or (ii) overlap with procurement years for active Georgia Power Utility Scale Renewable RFPs.
The intent of allowing RFP participants to buy down their submissions to a price that corresponds to the average of the Total Net Benefits of the selected portfolio is to ensure benefits are captured for all customers, as any incremental projects selected will deliver value equal to the entire portfolio, not the last selected submission. This proposed submission price refresh process supports the objective of the RFP process and ensures that the competitive procurement determines the best cost to customers.. Using average Total Net Benefit to evaluate submissions allows for a more accurate comparison of incremental projects to the initial Short List, as it includes factors such as resource type, configuration, inclusion of an energy storage system, and contract term length.
The Company has not finalized a timeline for the extended RFP period; however, the Company plans for the extended RFP period to start between Competitive Tier and Short List announcements. The extended RFP would conclude prior to bidding in the next Utility Scale RFP.
Yes.. Submission of projects during the extended RFP period would be contingent on a participant’s interest or ability at that time to partner with a customer, regardless of whether the participant is the Company or a Georgia Power Affiliate.
Allowing for changes in the required Commercial Operations Dates (“COD”) provides more flexibility for the market. RFP participants will have an opportunity to submit projects and proposals with CODs over a range of years rather than a single date certain. Allowing flexibility both within and beyond the COD range allows for the market to bid the most competitive projects and for the Company to consider more projects for selection;  thereby providing more value for Georgia Power’s customers.
The proposed enhancements to the Company’s procurement process were developed by Georgia Power exclusively and are primarily informed by the Company’s experience in its market and feedback from market participants and customers.–Although the Company has studied procurements from other similar vertically integrated utilities and incorporated best practices/strategies in the Company’s proposed procurement strategy enhancements, as appropriate, the Company’s regular RFP cadence and offerings provide the best source for lessons learned and procurement enhancements.

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 81 regarding Georgia Power’s proposed DG RFP Procurement Strategy and Enhancements:
Describe how the Proposed 100 MW DG target amount was determined. Were any alternative procurement amounts considered? Provide workpapers to support the Company’s analysis, if applicable.
Why does the Company propose to split the 100 MW DG procurement into two 50 MW RFPs?
Describe why the average of the Total Net Benefits was selected as the threshold to which bidders have the ability to buy down to.
Provide an estimated timeline for the extended phase of the DG RFP. How will these activities fit into a 3-year IRP cycle?
Is Georgia Power proposing to allow Company-Owned Proposals and Affiliates projects to be submitted during the Extended RFP Period?
Is the Company’s proposed procurement strategy enhancements modeled from another jurisdiction? If so, provide examples of other relevant jurisdictions that the Company is aware of that use a similar RFP process.
Provide all presentations, surveys, and/or summaries of market feedback that were received by the Company from interested parties that were reviewed and considered prior to the Company’s Proposed DG RFP Procurement Strategy and Enhancements.
Please explain in detail what the Company’s proposal to require visibility and control of new renewable resources through integration with DERMS will entail. When would this requirement be effective?
Has the Company determined whether the proposed requirement of integration with DERMS for new renewable resources will have an impact on future DG RFP bids? If so, please provide any potential cost estimates or impacts to future DG RFPs.
response:
The 100 MW target for the  DG RFP was determined to be an achievable target based on the Company’s experience with prior Georgia Power DG RFPs, as well as to set a target that supports the Company’s renewable expansion strategy. During the past three DG RFPs, the Company has procured on average <90 MW per IRP cycle:
RFP | Procurement
REDI DG RFP | 86.10 MW
2020 DG RFP | 88.96 MW
2023 DG RFP | 41 MW
2024 DG RFP | TBD
The 100 MW target is achievable based on these results, while providing the option for additional procurements. It should also be noted that the Company has proposed a mechanism to seek additional resources beyond 100 MW, if needed, to meet customer subscription demand.
The Company proposes to split the 100 MW DG procurement into two 50 MW RFPs based on the success of this approach over the past three years. As part of the 2022 IRP Final Order, the Company received approval for consecutive RFPs, which was consequently implemented with the 2023 and 2024 DG RFPs, respectively. The Company has not only seen on average more success with bids progressing to the target list but also received positive feedback from DG RFP stakeholders and participants on this approach.
The intent of allowing RFP participants to buy down their submissions to a price that corresponds to the average of the Total Net Benefits of the selected portfolio is to ensure benefits are captured for all customers, as any incremental projects selected will deliver value equal to the entire portfolio, not the last selected submission. This proposed submission price refresh process supports the objective of the RFP process and ensures that the competitive procurement determines the best cost to customers. Using average Total Net Benefit to evaluate submissions allows for a more accurate comparison of incremental projects to the initial Target List, as it includes factors such as resource type, configuration, inclusion of an energy storage system, and contract term length.
Pending Commission approval of the Company’s request in this case, Georgia Power estimates issuing the proposed DG RFPs in Q1 2026 and Q1 2027, respectively. The Company would seek to initiate the submission price refresh or “buy down” period upon finalization of the Target List. The Company estimates finalizing the Target List in Q2 2026 and Q2 2027. The Company would seek to initiate the extended RFP period at the conclusion of the DG RFP submission price refresh process, following certification of all PPAs.
Yes. Submission of projects during the extended RFP period would be contingent on a participant’s interest or ability at that time to partner with a customer regardless of whether the participant is the Company or a Georgia Power Affiliate.
The Company’s proposed procurement strategy enhancements to (1) incorporate Locational Value and (2) offer Buydown Optionality and an extended RFP period were not based on procurement strategies used in other jurisdictions. The Company’s proposal to procure Flexible DG Resources was also not modeled after another jurisdiction; however, the Company has conducted industry research in an effort to determine options and best practices for incorporating storage into DG procurement. Procurement programs researched include Duke Energy Carolina’s 2024 Solar and Solar Paired With Storage Procurement Program and Dominion Energy Virginia’s 2024 Solicitation for New Renewable Generation and Energy Storage Power Purchase Agreements.
See STF-PIA-3-3 Attachments A and B.
The Company is in the process of determining requirements that would enable visibility and enhanced control of new renewable resources through integration with DERMS. The Company will require generators to install communications and controls equipment, such as a Power Plant Controller, that can communicate with a Company-owned gateway device and adhere to specific data telemetry requirements. These requirements would go into effect as part of the 2026 DG RFP.
As stated in the above response, the Company is in the process of determining requirements that would enable DERMS integration. The Company anticipates that DERMS integration would have a financial impact on future DG RFP bids, specifically an increase in interconnection costs for communications and controls materials/equipment. The Company does not yet have an estimate of these costs as the required materials/equipment have not been determined.

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 96 regarding Georgia Power’s proposed CARES Utility-Scale Subscription Program Enhancements:
a. 	Provide all workpapers, including Excel spreadsheets with formulas intact, for the proposed price calculation methodology for the hourly energy credit.
b. 	Provide updated proposed tariffs and any other applicable program documentation including updated customer carveout amounts.
c. 	Please describe in detail how the customer carveout sizes and amounts were determined.
d. 	Please refer to the following language from p.97 “subscriptions will be offered through an enhanced NOI process and allocated to interested customers through a Commission-approved methodology.” When will this methodology be approved by the Commission?
e. 	As proposed, customers who submit a NOI in the extended subscription process phase must pay a participation fee and provide collateral, as appropriate. Please provide the Company’s proposed methodology to calculate such participation fees and levels of collateral for such customers.
f. 	Provide all feedback that was received by the Company from interested parties that were considered by the Company as part of the proposed CARES Utility-Scale Subscription Program Enhancements.
response:
Please see STF-PIA-3-6 Attachment TRADE SECRET for an example of the current calculation of the CARES variable program charge, which is based on the PPA price and provides participating customers a corresponding hourly energy credit. The Company proposes to continue to offer Clean and Renewable Energy Subscription  (“CARES”) Program subscriptions priced using one of two pricing mechanisms: (1) the CARES REC-based fixed program portfolio charge with no hourly energy credit (“Fixed Program Charge”); or (2) the CARES variable program charge based on the PPA price, with a corresponding hourly energy credit (“Variable Program Charge”). To minimize any additional costs borne by non-participating customers, the Company proposes to limit the amount of the hourly energy credit to subscribers participating in the Variable Program Charge option by introducing a maximum reimbursement credit threshold. The details of this methodology are still under development and will be informed by the results of the 2023 CARES Utility Scale (“US”) Request for Proposals (“RFP”) and presented to the Commission for approval in a separate tariff filing with the revised CARES Tariff once finalized.
Georgia Power plans to file updated tariffs corresponding with any approved changes to the CARES program following the Commission’s final order in this 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”). These revised CARES program details will be informed by the 2023 CARES US RFP results and the corresponding CARES customer subscriptions. Georgia Power proposes a base target for CARES of 1,000 MW of utility scale renewable resources, with the ability to procure up to an additional 3,000 MW of renewable resources procured through a phased procurement and subscription process if customer subscription need supports it.
Georgia Power has not proposed any carveouts for the CARES Utility Scale Subscription Program at this time. Future allocation of subscriptions cannot be accurately derived until the results of the 2023 CARES US RFP and the corresponding CARES subscription program results are known.
Following issuance of the Commission’s 2025 IRP Final Order, Georgia Power plans to file updated CARES program documents, including revised tariffs, for Commission approval. The Company anticipates that such filing will include proposed changes to the subscription pricing methodology and plan for allocating subscriptions to program participants.
Similar to the participation fees charged in the Company’s past subscription programs, a $5,000 application fee will be charged for each customer for their Notice of Intent (“NOI”) submission. As proposed, for the customer identified resource (“CIR”) process and prior to power purchase agreement (“PPA”) execution, a customer will be required to provide collateral in an amount calculated to prevent economic risk to all other retail customers. Costs considered in the calculation of the required collateral may include PPA costs above current RFP total net benefits, transmission costs, administrative fee, levelized additional sum, renewable integration costs, and other costs identified in the contracting process.
Georgia Power solicited feedback from a variety of Commercial and Industrial (C&I) customers through a series of meetings and informal listening sessions. These meetings and sessions included multiple customer stakeholder groups, such as the Clean Energy Buyer’s Association (“CEBA”) and the Drawdown Georgia Business Compact, as well as Q&A sessions with individual commercial customers and collaboration meetings with new large load customers. Georgia Power solicited feedback from both existing and new C&I customers, as well as from customers who are participants in Georgia Power’s existing renewable and/or subscription programs and customers who have not but would like to participate in CARES. Much of the feedback was informal, conversational and not provided in written format. Summarized, the feedback Georgia Power received reflects:
The need for certainty around renewable procurement timelines and quicker access to renewable resources
Access to additional renewable energy resources
Greater flexibility in the type and size of resources that the Company will consider procuring and the ability for customers to self-identify renewable resources

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 103 regarding Georgia Power’s Residential and Commercial Solar Plus Storage Pilot Program options:
Please describe how the proposed 50 MW Pilot cap was determined. Did the Company examine other Pilot amounts? With the proposed DERMS, why should there be a limit for participation in this pilot?
Describe how the maximum system sizes of 20 kW and 250 kW for residential and commercial applications respectively were determined.
Describe what the “appropriate application and interconnection requirements” are referring to.
Why is the Company proposing to require Pilot participants to take service on a rate other than R or GS?
Provide internal Georgia Power Company, memos, or other related documents addressing this Pilot.
Please explain why the Customer-Directed option is for new and existing assets while the Company-Directed option is for new assets only.
Describe why the Company-Directed option, as proposed, does not allow standalone storage.
Has the Company developed a proposed customer agreement or any other applicable program documentation? If so, please provide.
Did the Company model the Proposed Pilot after any other current Pilot or program? If so, please describe the pilots or programs considered in the development of the Company’s Pilot.
Provide all workpapers, including Excel spreadsheets with formulas intact, that were used by the Company or its consultant in the determination of the participant incentives for both pilot options.
response:
The Company based the proposed target amount for the Residential and Commercial Solar Plus Storage Pilot Program on its prior experience implementing customer-sited renewable programs. The 50 megawatt (“MW”) target was established in consideration of the expected volume of customer applications. To clarify, Georgia Power does not consider the 50 MW target to be a limit on program capacity and did not use the term cap or limit in its filing or testimony. If the 50 MW target is reached, the Company will assess the impacts of the pilot program and propose options to the Commission for moving forward with the program. Finally, the existence of a DERMS system doesn’t alleviate the need for a reasonable target for the pilot program to manage participation during the next three-year regulatory cycle. See page 40, lines 19-26 of the Direct Testimony of Dr. Ross Beppler, Carley Goff, A. Wilson Mallard, and Andy Phillips in Docket Nos. 56002 and 56003 for additional information.
For residential applications, the 20 kW limit was set with a goal to mitigate costs associated with distribution and service upgrades thereby simplifying the implementation process and minimizing additional costs to customers. This limit will also encourage right-sizing the ratio of solar and storage consistent with the Company’s existing behind-the-meter solar programs.
For commercial applications, the 250 kW limit is designed to align with the RNR-11 tariff, which caps commercial and industrial (“C&I”) customers at 125% of peak load or 250 kW. This size limitation also aligns with existing interconnection processes, as projects greater than 250 kW are subject to more in depth study, interconnection, testing, and equipment requirements.
All systems will be interconnected, tested, and operated consistent with the prevailing Southern Company Distributed Energy Resources (“DER”) Policy in compliance with Georgia Power’s specific Rules and Regulations for interconnection of a behind-the-meter generator.
Energy-only rates including R and GS do not provide an appropriate time-of-use (“TOU”) or demand signal to incentivize operation of the solar and battery resources to realize System benefit. Additionally, energy-only rates are not appropriate for the recovery of grid costs for customer generators installed behind-the-meter. See page 40, lines 9-18 of the Direct Testimony of Dr. Ross Beppler, Carley Goff, A. Wilson Mallard, and Andy Phillips in Docket Nos. 56002 and 56003.
As Georgia Power worked to design the pilot program, the Company developed a series of slide decks, which were subsequently shared as part of the required collaboration sessions. The program development presentations are attached as STF-PIA-3-8 Attachment A.
The Customer-Directed option is available for both new and existing assets because it operates on a pay-for-performance basis. Under this model, incentives are provided based on the system’s actual ability to deliver the expected performance. This approach allows for flexibility in including existing assets, as the incentives are directly tied to the measurable outcomes of those systems.
The Company-Directed option is limited to new assets because it involves providing a larger upfront customer incentive. For this option, it is crucial to have certainty and control over the capabilities of the assets being integrated into the program. By focusing on new assets, the Company can ensure that the systems meet specific standards and requirements, thereby justifying the substantial initial investment and ensuring predictable and reliable capacity contributions to the system.
The Company-Directed option, as proposed, does not allow standalone storage because the option requires that the storage systems be charged exclusively by solar resources. Allowing standalone storage systems to charge from the grid would necessitate the Company dictating when participating customers purchase additional electricity from the grid. By ensuring that storage is charged only from solar resources, the Company avoids causing customers to purchase additional energy and the associated program design impacts.
No, the Company has not yet developed a proposed customer agreement or other applicable program documentation. The customer agreement will be drafted in coordination with a third-party implementation facilitator to ensure that it meets all necessary requirements and effectively supports the pilot program’s objectives.
Yes, the Company gained insights from several other current pilots and programs from various peer utilities. In developing the Company’s pilot program, Georgia Power reviewed and considered programs from the following utilities: Duke Energy, Rocky Mountain Power, Green Mountain Power, Arizona Public Service, National Grid, and Xcel Energy.

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 105 regarding Georgia Powers’ Customer Connected Solar Program Enhancements:
a. 	Please describe in detail why the Company is proposing to change the minimum and maximum system size for this program.
b. 	Has the Company updated the customer agreements and/or program documentation for the proposed CCSP? If so, please provide.

response:
The Company seeks to update the eligible project size range in the Customer Connected Solar Program (“CCSP”) Program Guidelines for consistency with the DG RFP, the program after which CCSP was modeled. This range of system size provides customers with more options for facility design. Additionally, expanding the project size range to allow projects as small as 250 kW, provides seamless access to solar plus storage program options for customer projects of all sizes.
The Company has not yet updated the power purchase agreement (“PPA”) or Program Guidelines for CCSP. The Company will work with Staff to file and seek approval for the modified CCSP PPA and Program Guidelines from the Commission after the conclusion of the 2025 IRP.
The Company is still evaluating options for incorporating battery energy storage system (“BESS”) technology into CCSP and has not established any limitations for BESS technology that would be incorporated into CCSP. The solar and storage assets must comply with the Company’s Distributed Energy Resource (“DER”) Interconnection Policy. Further technical requirements may be proposed. Regarding BESS usage, the storage component of an eligible facility would be subject to control by the Company through integration with DERMS; such control provides the capacity value that can then be translated into the customer’s compensation for the facility’s output.
The Company’s proposed program enhancements to CCSP are based on feedback realized throughout administration of CCSP as well as through dedicated market feedback sessions held in 2024. See below for the feedback received in the 2024 market feedback sessions.
On 9/11/2024, GPC met with multiple customers and received feedback summarized below:
The limitation on facility size due to peak demand doesn’t account for customer’s other accounts.
Customer would like ability to build larger sites.
Higher CCSP pricing will likely increase the feasibility of customer sited solar projects.
On 9/25/2024, GPC met with a solar developer and received the following recommendation:
Allow the pricing to be updated on a regular basis
Additional feedback received from interested customers, new customers constructing facilities in Georgia, and installers includes comments on the following topics:
Current program limits the facility location to parcels directly adjacent and contiguous to their premises; interested customers are not able install facilities on other land they own.
The current CCSP precludes new customers from participating in the program because a participant must have “one or more existing Georgia Power meter(s) on its Premises at least six months prior to applying for the program.”
Current program is designed such that the Georgia Power account holder is required to be the solar contract counterparty. Therefore, landlords are unable to participate in CCSP and lack flexibility to transfer RECs, hindering customers participation.

question:
Please refer to the 2025 GPC IRP Technical Conference presentation regarding the proposed Customer-Owned Resiliency Program:
How did the Company determine that a credit of 75% of the system value is appropriate?

response:
The 75% shared savings model was selected to be consistent with Georgia Power’s other Distributed Energy Resource (“DER”) program offerings. The intent is to provide an adequate incentive to encourage customer participation and offset the additional expenses related to non-emergency generators and interconnection. The shared savings model helps to ensure the program provides value to non-participating customers by securing capacity at a cost lower than the system modeled avoided cost of capacity.
The Large Customer Owned Resiliency Program will be dispatched as a demand-side program, similar to the DER Customer Pilot. Load reductions will be called based on System need up to the hours defined in the customer contract. This approach ensures that the program supports grid reliability during critical periods.
No. The Company is not proposing a program cap.
The Company is seeking approval of the Large Customer Owned Resiliency Program in this IRP. Resources for this program will be owned and operated by customers as demand-side assets. Unlike the supply-side resources in the DER Colocation Program and Customer-Owned Program approved in the 2023 IRP Update, the Large Customer-Owned Resiliency Program seeks to leverage behind-the-meter resources to offset the load of participating customers. These resources are not intended to transmit electricity to the electric grid. Like with the DER Customer Program Pilot approved in the 2022 IRP, the Company intends to file a tariff for the Large Customer-Owned Resiliency Program, which will establish the terms and condition of participation, for Commission approval.

question:
Refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 7, stating: “An additional 6th scenario was run at 5 GW, but a mitigation cost could not be directly determined due to several factors.”
a. 	Please provide a detailed narrative description of why the mitigation cost could not be determined.
b. 	Provide all analysis and documentation calculating the mitigation cost for the 5 GW scenario that was omitted from the study results.
response:
Page 25 of the 2024 Renewable Integration Study provides further information regarding the 5 GW solar tranche. The base case model required 500 MW of quick start reserves be maintained as well as a load following target equal to 1% of hourly load in order to manage normal System volatility and contingencies. The combined flexibility of these existing resources was able to absorb the solar volatility present in the 5 GW penetration. However, the model does not report how much of the inherent flexibility of the System was eroded by the solar volatility. However, the flexibility or ramping capability provided by the existing generation in the System is needed to address intra-hour load volatility and other operational uncertainties. This existing System flexibility was not intended to manage solar volatility. Permitting solar volatility to diminish current system flexibility jeopardizes the System’s ability to effectively manage load and operational variability.
No documentation or analysis was provided from the consultant that performed the Study since the unmitigated 5 GW solar scenario had a flex violation metric equal to the base case.

question:
Refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 12-13, including Table 9, regarding the Southern Company operating reserve requirements.
a. 	Please provide a comparison of Southern Company’s current, actual operating reserve requirements with the operating reserve requirements modeled in the Base Case (Table 9).
b. 	Please provide a narrative description of how the assumptions listed in Table 9 were developed. Provide any supporting analysis or documentation, as applicable.
response:
The Company currently manages three operating reserves categories: regulation, contingency reserves, and total operating reserves. The actual reserve requirements are adjusted daily by the Southern Balancing Authority (“SBA”) based on current load forecasts and operating conditions. However, there are general guidelines the SBA follows when setting reserves.
Regulation Up and Down Reserves: Regulation Reserves requirements are not fixed but are adjusted monthly. Regulation targets are established using a monthly evaluation of the REDACTED percentile of Actual Net Load demand (Net Load Demand = Load Ramp – Variable Energy Resource (“VER”) Generation Ramp) over a 10-minute period. The Company will calculate the increased amount of VER penetration each month and utilize historical VER actuals in the computation of Regulation Reserve requirements.
Contingency Reserves: The current total contingency target is REDACTED although the minimum requirement is REDACTED, or the Most Severe Single Contingency. This contingency comprises Spinning (on-line), which includes Regulation Reserves, and Supplemental (off-line) resources.
Total Operating Reserves: The total operating reserves target is REDACTED and includes all Contingency Reserves plus other spinning reserves above REDACTED regulation but capped at REDACTED ramp capability as well as CT units on reserve shutdown that can be committed within REDACTED.
The SERVM model does not model reserves in exactly the same manner as the SBA. However, an effort is made to align them as closely as possible ensuring that the sum of the three reserves requirements shown in Table 9 (1,750 MW) fall into the range of the total “Contingency Reserves” targeted by the SBA. The 1% of load following as defined in Table 9 is meant to provide an additional margin of reserves above the 1,250 MW load shed point to prevent the model from experiencing excessive hourly capacity shortfalls but remain close to the contingency reserves target.
The reserve assumptions defined in Table 9 were guided by the “Commitment and Operating Reserves” assumptions described in Section I, part K of the 2024 Reserve Margin Study provided in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Section 2. One key difference is the regulating reserves requirement being defined as 500 MW + 8% of nominal solar capacity. The solar penetration defined in the Reserve Margin Study remained constant, whereas solar penetration was adjusted for each scenario in the Renewable Integration Study. In order to prevent a change to base case production costs with each scenario, the decision was made to keep regulating reserves at a constant 500 MW for the duration of the Renewable Integration Study.

question: Refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 14, describing the “divergence profile” as “the frequency at which a given level of divergence from the smooth profile would occur.” Please provide a narrative description of what a “smooth profile” is and how the Company calculates divergence from this smooth profile.
response:
The smooth profile in the model consists of the hourly solar output provided for each weather year, weather station, and technology (fixed or tracking). A single-year, five-minute aggregate profile was developed as described on p.14 of the 2024 Renewable Integration Study. This single-year volatility profile is then stochastically applied to the smooth profiles. This is done by SERVM randomly selecting a volatility value from an hour in the single-year divergence data that is like the hour being simulated. For example, the volatility for modeled hours where solar generation is ~90% of the nameplate will draw from hours where the solar generation was ~90% of the nameplate in the divergence data.
The divergence profiles are modeled on an aggregate portfolio basis, and a pro-rata share of the divergence is applied to every individual solar resource to determine its final output in each five-minute span. While some resources would have positive divergence and other resources negative divergence at a given point in time, the modeling is only concerned with the aggregate divergence.

question:
Refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 30, stating: “Below 1,250 MW, BESS effectiveness is significantly hindered because of regulation and spin requirements.”
a. 	Please elaborate on this conclusion and explain how the regulation and spin requirements hinder BESS effectiveness.
b. 	Provide all analysis supporting this conclusion.
response:
The SERVM model is set up to maintain at least 1,250 MW of regulation plus spinning reserves in all hours pursuant to the operating reserve requirements discussed in the responses to STF-PIA-3-28 and STF-PIA-3-29. If operating reserves drop below 1,250 MW during intra-hour, a flex violation is recorded. If there is not sufficient hourly capacity to maintain 1,250 MW of reserves, the SERVM model will shed load in order to recover reserves back to 1,250 MW. To maintain this 1,250 MW threshold, the SERVM model will allocate resource capacity to fulfill this obligation during each hour. Due to the flexibility of BESS resources, the SERVM model prioritizes these resources to meet these operating reserves. If BESS capacity is assigned to provide these capacity reserves, that same capacity is then unavailable to provide intra-hour volatility support.
This model configuration is intentional. Accordingly, additional analysis is not available.

question: Refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 22, stating: “The costs associated with increases in curtailment are implicitly included in these calculations since the production costs associated with the additional energy that was generated but did not serve load are included in TPCpost.” Please reconcile this statement with the discussion of solar curtailment on p. 31, stating that the cost of curtailment “is not captured in the solar integration cost analysis.”
response: The Renewable Integration Study differentiates between two forms of solar curtailment, that which is present in the the pre-mitigated case and the increase in curtailment present in the mitigated case. Solar curtailment that is present in the pre-mitigated case is a function of commitment constraints that result in total generation exceeding total demand. Under this condition, the model will curtail solar in order to balance generation and demand. The cost impact of this curtailment is not included in the solar integration cost. Solar curtailment may increase between the pre-mitigated case and the mitigated case. This increase in curtailment is a function of the mitigation creating additional commitment constraints in order to provide the needed load following reserves. The cost impacts of this curtailment are included in the solar integration cost analysis.

question:
In its 2022 IRP, the Company proposed to permanently retire Bowen Units 1 - 2 no later than December 31, 2028. In the October 31, 2021 letter entitled “Plant Bowen – NPDES Permit No. GA0001449 Notice of Planned Participation Bowen Units 1 and 2,” the 2020 ELG compliance path was a complete cessation of combustion of coal via plant retirement for Units 1 and 2.  In a December 20, 2024 letter entitled “NPDES Permit No. GA0001449 – Plant Bowen ELG Progress Report,” the Company stated the following:
“The PSC decision in the 2022 IRP to reassess the timing of decertification of Plant Bowen Units 1-2 in the 2025 IRP does not impact the FGDW compliance strategy for Plant Bowen, as the FGDW system is a common environmental control for all four generating units.”
While the compliance strategy for the Bowen units might involve a common environmental control, there could be additional costs to extend the 2020 ELG compliance to Units 1 - 2. Please provide 2020 ELG capital cost estimates for the additional plant and equipment required to extend the Bowen Units 3 - 4 compliance strategy to cover Units 1 - 2.
Please provide estimates of operating and maintenance costs for the ELG compliance strategy divided between Units 1 - 2 and Units 3 - 4.
In the 2025 IRP Unit Retirement Study, study results tables such as those appearing in Appendix A and Appendix B show Plant Bowen Units 1 – 4, as opposed to only Plant Bowen Units 1- 2. Did the Company separate Bowen Units 1 - 2 from Units 3 - 4 for any of the analyses? If so, please provide summary tables like those shown in Appendix A and Appendix B for the Bowen separated units 1-2 and 3-4.
response:
The 2020 Effluent Limitations Guidelines (“ELG”) Rule compliance costs for a physical-chemical-biological Flue Gas Desulfurization Wastewater (“FGDW”) treatment system at Plant Bowen remain unchanged whether the plant operates as a two-unit or four-unit site. The controls required for 2020 ELG Rule compliance are additional to the existing common systems at Plant Bowen. Eliminating two units at Plant Bowen does not significantly alter the overall water treatment needs due to the reduced evaporative water loss associated with the scrubbers. Treatment costs (sizing) are based on a worst-case treatment condition, which for Plant Bowen FGDW is Units 3-4 operating at low load. Due to the plant specific equipment and operations, this condition creates a higher flow rate than if Units 3-4 are running at higher load or dispatching Units 1-4 at high load. Units 1-2 were routed to the common scrubber wastewater system as part of the 2018 water management project to cease sending wastewater to the ash pond, so those piping runs are already complete.
Since the low load of Units 3-4 is the governing “worst case,” adding Units 1-2 is not expected to significantly increase O&M costs. There is a potential for the treatment system to require slightly higher chemical usage, as it will support four units. These costs have not been determined and will be assessed following equipment operation.
No. The Company did not separate Bowen Units 1-2 and 3-4 in any of the Budget 2025 (“B2025”) analyses.

question: Regarding ash handling costs, please explain how ash costs are included in the analysis of plant closure dates for Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer and in the resource portfolio analyses that include these two plants. Do the plant closure date and resource portfolio analyses include estimates of (1) ongoing capital expenditures, (2) ongoing O&M expenses for handling and storing coal combustion residuals, and (3) the costs of future closure of ash handling facilities?
response:
Ongoing capital expenditures for existing ash handling equipment are included in the analysis. The costs are embedded in the “Maintenance Capital” category in the detailed cost tables in Appendix A and Appendix B in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Unit Retirement Study. Ash handling costs for incremental environmental capital are included for Plant Bowen under all environmental compliance pathways except the full gas conversion. This cost is represented in Table 3 of Technical Appendix Volume 1, Unit Retirement Study and is embedded in the “Environmental Capital” category in the detailed cost tables in Appendix A and Appendix B in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Unit Retirement Study.
Ongoing ash handling operation and maintenance (“O&M”) expenses for Plant Bowen and Plant Scherer are included in the analysis. These costs are embedded in the “Energy Benefit” category in the detailed costs tables in Appendix A and Appendix B in Technical Appendix Volume 1, Unit Retirement Study. The input for this is modeled in AURORA and represented as Variable O&M for each resource. Fixed O&M for ash handling is also included, and it is assumed that there will be a fixed O&M reduction in the full gas conversion compliance pathway.
The costs of future closure of ash handling facilities are not included in resource portfolio analyses. The analysis assumes future closure costs are either accounted for as part of Coal Combustion Residual (“CCR”) Asset Retirement Obligation (“ARO”) or as part of the plant dismantlement ARO.

question:
In the IRP, Appendix H, the Company lists possible Research Activities.
Strategic Aspiration #1 is developing a sustainable future. The following are questions related to this aspiration.
The Company’s numbers in the Technology Screening appendix show that nuclear power has significantly higher capital cost than other technologies. Has the company considered how inverter-based technology could serve the functions that nuclear provides at the same or lower cost? Is the company performing the research and development needed to bring inverter-based resources to a state where they might be as effective as rotating generators in regulating a power system?
Given the currently existing EPA GHG regulations, investigating hydrogen and oxy-combustion technologies also seems potentially cost-effective compared to nuclear. Drawing on the results presented in the 2025 IRP Appendix Technology Screening and Application Standards and based on the representative load factors included in that Appendix, please provide a representative rolled-in levelized cost per MWh for use in comparing the technologies listed in the Aspiration #1 including oxy-combustion technologies, CCS technologies in conjunction with CC and/or coal generation, nuclear, and inverter-based renewable resources. Include in the list, the same rolled-in levelized cost for the fuel cells included in technology screening and identified as potentially useful in increasing resiliency, but from all outward appearances, not selected for application in the IRP process.
Aspiration #1 indicates that work will continue to study CO2 storage. In the Resource Mix Study of the 2025 IRP, the Company placed a limit on carbon storage in Georgia and for the total system (presumedly the Southern Power Company system). Please explain how the Company determined the appropriate limit for the carbon storage capacity available in Georgia. To the extent this limit was based on preliminary drilling test results, please summarize the drilling work and how the drilling test results were extrapolated from a small set of drilling sites to the entire state of Georgia.
Aspiration #2 highlights the need to improve resiliency among other goals. Regarding the second bullet under Aspiration #2, the paragraph dedicates entire sentences to EMP/geomagnetic disturbances and to cyber-attacks. There is a sentence split regarding “major threats and extreme events” between “both man-made and natural domains.” The presumption is that “natural domains” refers to the risks posed by extreme weather events such as the extreme flood events seen in western North Carolina in 2024. Please explain the Company’s current efforts to identify and mitigate the risks posed by extreme natural events to the generating facilities, coal ash ponds, and to other assets such as transmission that were studied in the 2025 IRP.
response:
i. It is important to differentiate technologies discussed in the Southern Company research aspirations from those having been considered as part of the Georgia Power Technology Screening Process. Southern Company’s research aspirations focus on continued development of technologies that may be beneficial to the future resource mix. Southern Company Research and Development (“R&D”) works closely with Georgia Power system planning to document projected price and performance metrics for such technologies. The Technology Screening Process may select technologies from the research portfolio to include as “pre-commercial” technologies. However, some technology focus areas within the research portfolio may not yet be of sufficient maturity to be considered as pre-commercial options for inclusion in the Technology Screening Process.
As noted in the Technology Screening and Applications Standards document:
“These options are generic representations of technologies in various stages of evaluation, testing or deployment. These differ from its commercial technology portfolio in that there are generally few if any operating examples of these technologies outside of development scale demonstrations. Technologies included in the precommercial portfolio have projected cost and performance assumptions representing an “nth-of-a-kind” deployment, or the point where the technology is understood well enough and deployed at scale.”
Because of this, it is not practical to make direct comparisons of pre-commercial technologies to commercial technologies. For example, the GEN IV Advanced Nuclear technology reflected in the Technology Screening appendix represents average values across the suite of GEN IV Advanced Nuclear options, which include multiple technologies such as Sodium-Cooled Fast Reactors (“SFR”), Very-High-Temperature Reactors (“VHRT”), Molten Salt Reactors (“MSR”) and Fluoride salt-cooled High-temperature Reactors (“FHR”).  Currently, there is insufficient data to provide exact price and performance data for any of the individual reactor technologies, but some of the individual technologies have potential to reach prices of $5,000/kW at a much greater capacity factor than inverter-based power technologies. These technologies continue to be studied and developed by Southern Company R&D under the scope of Strategic Aspiration #1.
The Southern Company R&D strategy is also focused on further development of inverter-based resources. The ongoing work seeks to improve the price, capacity, reliability, and flexibility of inverter-based resources. The following research objectives support this effort:
Reduce the impact of renewable variability by improving forecasts and improving the way those forecasts are used and linked with other information such as load forecasts
Investigate improved photovoltaic (“PV”) materials such as Perovskite and Advanced thin-film technologies
Improve options and tools for flexible renewable generation, where solar and wind generators can operate on automatic generation control (“AGC”) and optimally hold back “headroom” allowing them to ramp up (upward regulation reserves) or down when needed to increase grid reliability, decrease cost, and result in less overall renewable curtailment than more conventional control strategies
Identify and correct sources of flicker and harmonics impacting customers in a power-electronics-heavy environment
Enable the safe deployment of lithium-ion batteries
Evaluate and demonstrate non-lithium battery storage concepts to advance commercialization of long-duration energy storage
ii. As discussed in subpart (i) above, technologies in the research portfolio may not fully align with those included in the technology screening process due to their relative maturity. For example, R&D functions may continue to monitor technologies such as oxy-combustion, but it is not yet appropriate to include in the IRP process based on the current technology readiness.
Technologies selected for inclusion in the IRP process are also screened based on technology-specific characteristics that affect total system costs. While levelized cost of energy (“LCOE”) is one metric for comparison of technologies at a high level, it treats all MWh equally, regardless of other important factors that affect cost and system stability such as:
Grid stability requirements (some low-LCOE technologies may increase system costs if they require additional grid stability)
Flexibility Characteristics: Ramp rates, minimum loads, startup times, and load-following capabilities
Siting requirements: footprint, required transmission upgrades/investments
Water usage
Heat recovery potential
Maintenance patterns
Portfolio diversification needs: A collection of non-lowest-LCOE resources may reduce system risk and provide lower overall costs
Cost estimates for LCOE are highly variable based on each technology and can be overly reliant on assumptions. The Company's planning and system modeling framework incorporates LCOE as one consideration alongside portfolio analysis and other strategic considerations as outlined above. The overnight costs of many of the technologies mentioned above are included in Table 5, Page 25 of the 2025 Resource Mix Study provided in Technical Appendix Volume 2.
iii. In the Resource Mix Study, natural gas combined cycle with carbon capture and sequestration was separated into two categories, one with a cost for a local carbon sink and one with a cost for a distant carbon sink. The local category represents expansion capabilities at existing generating sites in the Southern Company System that are located on Coastal Plain geology, which is generally regarded as favorable for carbon sequestration. It was assumed that any further capacity would require greenfield siting, introducing uncertainty in location and potentially requiring the greater carbon transportation costs associated with the distant sink category, which was not subject to a limit.
The research aspirations reflect areas of R&D to be conducted for current and future needs of the system and do not necessarily reflect current efforts by the Company to mitigate extreme natural events. In Research Aspiration #2, the “natural domains” discussed are specifically focused on natural events capable of causing electric magnetic pulse (“EMP”)/geomagnetic disturbances such as solar flares or geomagnetic storms. To address more commonly occurring natural events, the Company utilizes engineering best practices and appropriate design safety factors according to the appropriate design codes and standards.
The Company has made efforts to increase the reliability of generating facilities during cold weather events. Please see the Company’s response to data request STF-JKA-1-9 for a discussion on modeling assumptions and ongoing weatherization efforts. The Company is also a participant in the Electric Power Research Institute’s Climate READi research effort aimed at establishing a comprehensive and consistent approach to physical climate risk assessments.

question:
In reviewing the 2025 IRP Unit Retirement Study, Appendix B shows that the most cost-effective option with Scherer Unit 3 for meeting the ELG and GHG requirements is CCS. Please comment on whether the Company is considering implementing a CCS installation to keep the Scherer units operating beyond 2032, in compliance with the GHG regulation.
In reading the Unit Retirement Study, it appears the estimated 45Q benefit that makes CCS cost competitive has been reduced by 25% to account for risk.
i. Please identify the risks that the Company accounted for with this 25% reduction.
ii. Please explain how the 25% risk adjustment was determined.
iii. There is a statement that the risk adjustment reflects “the potential need to transfer the credits.” What would cause the credits to need to be transferred and to what would the Company transfer the 45Q tax credits?
If the 45Q credit remains available and if the Company succeeded in installing and operating the CCS, the actual level of the 45Q credit would presumedly be higher than what is shown on the table in Appendix B. Please provide the estimated 45Q tax credit before the Company makes the risk adjustment.
response:
As stated in the IRP Main Document, the implementation of carbon capture and sequestration (“CCS”) at Plant Scherer by 2032 is infeasible due to (1) the required compliance timeline specified and (2) infrastructure and other significant challenges that remain unsolved.
The 25% adjustment accounts for risks associated with the Company’s inability to directly utilize large amounts of tax credits generated under the Inflation Reduction Act (“IRA”) and the tax market appetite for credits associated with coal-fired technologies including CCS.
The 25% risk adjustment was guided by professional judgment of the Company’s finance and tax experts.
The Company assumes that the volume of the tax credits generated under the IRA is likely to be greater than the Company’s tax burden. Excess tax credits would be transferred to third parties in order to monetize the benefits of the credits.
Assuming all Carbon Oxide Sequestration Tax Credit (“45Q”) criteria are met and generating units are eligible to receive the credit, the estimated 45Q tax credit before the Company makes the risk adjustment is approximately $3.1B (2025 net present value) for Georgia Power’s Retail Ownership of Plant Scherer Units 1-3. This assumes the CCS technology is 95% efficient, and the units run at availability during the entire 12 years of eligibility.

question:
Please refer to Section 2.5 (DSM Program Cost Effectiveness) of the Company’s Application, please explain how the Company adjusts DSM measure per unit incremental annual kWh and kW savings at the customer meter for the following factors:
a. 	Transmission and distribution line losses between the customer meter and the generation level of the Georgia Power Company grid
b. 	Planning reserve margin
response:
The Company adjusts for transmission and distribution line losses in the Company’s marginal costing tool, Profitability Reliability Incremental Cost Evaluation Model (“PRICEM”), by scaling the associated cost component (generation capital, transmission capital, distribution capital, fuel) by a loss factor that corresponds with losses between the customer’s service level and the level of the system associated with that cost component.
The Company adjusts for the planning reserve margin in PRICEM by scaling up the seasonal capacity need by the respective summer and winter reserve margin percentages.

question:
Please refer to the cost effectiveness tests discussed in Section 2.5 and Appendix E of the Company’s Application, please describe the source for the following avoided costs:
a. 	Avoided capacity
b. 	Avoided energy
c. 	Avoided transmission and distribution infrastructure
d. 	Avoided generation reserves
e. 	The date that the above values were determined
response:
The costs referenced in subparts (a) through (d) are all inputs into the Company’s marginal costing tool, Profitability Reliability Incremental Cost Evaluation Model (“PRICEM”). The avoided costs are determined by calculating the difference in the costs to serve a base case and a change case.
Avoided capacity costs in PRICEM are developed as part of the Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) process and are based on the Economic Carrying Cost (“ECC”) of the generic Combustion Turbine (“CT”) with Selective Catalytic Reduction (“SCR”) System as included in the Resource Mix Study in Technical Appendix Volume 2.
Avoided energy costs in PRICEM are sourced from Aurora output for the MG0 and 111-MG0 scenarios. Please refer to Attachment E, Section 3.1 in the 2025 IRP Main Document about Marginal Energy Costs.
Avoided transmission infrastructure costs in PRICEM are sourced from an internal marginal transmission cost analysis. This analysis calculates the cost of the marginal capacity gained by the next transmission system upgrades across a number of substations around the state. Please refer to Technical Appendix Volume 3, Section G1. Avoided distribution infrastructure costs in PRICEM are sourced from internal common distribution substation and feeder cost studies. These studies calculate the cost of recently connected distribution capacity across a number of substations and lines around the state.
Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-PIA-6-4.
For the energy efficiency economic evaluations for the 2025 IRP Main Document and Demand Side Management (“DSM”) Application Filings, the PRICEM tool with the inputs described in subparts (a) through (d) was finalized on December 10, 2024, while the cost inputs were determined in October 2024 and November 2024.

question:
Please refer to the IRP Main Document, p. 104 regarding Georgia Power’s proposed Residential and Commercial Solar Plus Storage Pilot Program:
For the purposes of this program, how is small commercial being defined?
For the Company-directed program, how frequently does the Company anticipate discharging customer batteries?
To calculate capacity under the Company-directed program, the proposed calculation is "the lower of (1) the maximum continuous discharge rate of the battery or (2) 80% of the energy storage capacity (kWh) divided by two." Should this be interpreted to mean that the maximum expected event duration for the company-directed program is two hours?
For the customer-directed program, the maximum event duration is 4 hours. If a four-hour event were called, would aggregators be directed to discharge batteries at a consistent rate over a four hour period, or would the battery be discharged at the maximum rate until depleted?
Under the customer-directed program, will customers have the ability to reserve a portion of their battery for resiliency purposes, or is their only option to opt in or out of an event?
Under the Company-directed program, will customers be free to discharge their battery in response to price signals under a TOU rate when the battery is not being used by the company?
Under both programs, does the Company intend to give customers some advance warning of an anticipated call/discharge event if it is able to do so?
For both programs, will energy discharged from a battery serve on-site needs first, or will it be exported to the grid?
If these programs would have been available in the 2020-2024 calendar years, how frequently would systems have been discharged under each program? Please provide your answer in an Excel spreadsheet that provides the date, time, and expected duration of each would-be call.
response:
For the purposes of the Residential and Commercial Solar Plus Storage Pilot Program, small commercial is defined as customers with peak load less than or equal to 250 kW, as stated on page 102 of Georgia Power’s 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) Main Document.
For the Company-Directed pathway, the Company anticipates discharging customer battery energy storage systems (“BESS”) daily when conditions are appropriate to benefit the grid.
Under the Company-Directed pathway, the BESS dispatch would not be discrete-event driven. The Company will continually monitor and control the distributed BESS assets based on System need. The incentive was derived based on the Effective Load Carrying Capability (“ELCC”) of a 2-hour battery, which assumes those assets can contribute to reserves and/or other ancillary services.
For the Customer-Directed pathway, the Company would work with the implementor to determine the optimal dispatch strategy during an event call. This could include either a consistent discharge rate over the event duration or discharging at maximum until reaching a customer-established threshold.
Yes, under the Customer-Directed pathway, customers will have the ability to reserve a portion of their BESS for resiliency purposes. They will be compensated under the pay for performance model only for energy delivered during event calls.
No, under the Company-Directed pathway, customers will not be directly operating the BESS. The BESS operation will be managed by the Company based on System need, which should be correlated with TOU pricing signals.
Under the Customer-Directed pathway, the Company intends to give customers notice of an anticipated call/discharge event like the existing residential demand response (“DR”) program. In the Company-Directed pathway, the Company does not plan on notifying the customer each time the BESS is operated.
For both pathways, energy discharged from a BESS will be capable of export to the grid if discharge exceeds load but will serve on-site needs first.
The Company has not conducted a retrospective analysis to determine when systems would have been discharged if this pilot program had been in place in previous years.

question: Please refer to “STF-PIA-3-22 Attachment A TRADE SECRET.xlsx” regarding the Locational Transmission Value.  Refer to the “Project estimate” tab. Please explain why several projects do not include a cost estimate in column H. Are the impacts of any accelerations/delays included in the analysis?
response:
There are two categories of projects that do not include cost estimates in the ‘Project estimate’ tab of the referenced file. The first category is 500 kV Transmission Line Rebuilds. Four of these segments were identified in the study.
Each constraint identified in the locational value study was assigned a potential project to raise the MVA rating of the constraint. These projects were intentionally kept simple in scope for consistency with the 2022 iteration of the locational value study.
The 500 kV transmission line rebuilds were excluded from cost estimation because rebuilds of that scope are not economically strategic solutions. The inclusion of these 500 kV rebuild costs would create ambiguity and obscure the locational value results. The total cost of the four projects alone would more than double the total transmission capital of distributed solar in each region. The Company determined that including these significant costs for unrealistic projects was not appropriate for the locational value study.
The second category of projects excluded from cost estimation were Generator Step-Up transformers (“GSUs”). GSUs are the responsibility of the generator and are not a system cost. This category represents the remaining constraints excluded from cost estimation in the 'Project estimate' tab of the file.
The full project cost was included in the identified year of need. Projects that were accelerated or delayed by the presence of distributed energy resources were accounted for.

question: Please refer to Technical Appendix Vol. 2, the 2024 Renewable Integration Study, p. 12, stating: “To prepare this base case for the solar integration analysis, all solar and BESS resources were removed from the case.” Please explain why all existing and committed BESS resources were removed from the case.
response: One of the objectives of the Renewable Integration Study is to determine the flexibility benefit associated with battery energy storage system (“BESS”) resources at multiple solar penetrations. If BESS resources were embedded into the no-solar base case, it would not have been possible to determine the flexibility credit associated with the first tranche of BESS added to the System. As performed, the Renewable Integration Study accurately captures the integration costs of solar resources, excluding any impact from embedded flexible BESS resources. This also means that BESS resources are receiving the proper credit for helping to mitigate solar intermittence.

question:
Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-45, noting that “the model demonstrated a need for higher operating reserves targets during overnight hours to force commitment of resources to ensure availability during daytime hours.”
Does the advanced commitment of these resources incur a production cost in the model?
Please provide analysis quantifying the production cost impact of committing resources during the overnight hours.
response:
The commitment of all dispatchable resources incurs a production cost.
It is not possible to isolate these additional production costs . First, the commitment of a resource incurs a startup cost captured by the model, but that cost does not vary by time of day. The startup cost would have been realized if the resource was committed during daylight hours. Second, at steady-state load conditions, the commitment of a resource would require one or more online resources to ramp down to account for the minimum output of the newly committed resource. This scenario likely happened when advanced commitment occurred, but the per-unit intra-hour dispatch cost details from the study are not available to calculate a change in production cost. If the data were available, hourly system load rarely remains the same across two consecutive hours so it would be difficult to conclusively determine the cost of committing a unit during overnight hours instead of daylight hours when there was a change in load served as well.
