question: Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-42(a), stating that “If operating reserves drop below 1,250 MW during intra-hour, a flex violation is recorded.”  Does the use of operating reserves qualify as a violation of NERC Reliability Standard BAL-001-2?  If so, provide supporting documentation.  If not, please explain why this system condition is used to define a “flexibility violation.”
response:
The operation of the Southern Company System requires the use of operating reserves on a sub-minute basis in order to ensure appropriate balancing behavior is achieved. Therefore, the use of operating reserves is not a violation of any North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) standards. In the context of the Renewable Integration Study, the term "violation" indicates that the system's operating reserves fell below the required threshold of 1,250 MW at least once within a 5-minute interval during a single day. This does not imply that the Company would be out of compliance with NERC Reliability Standard BAL-001-2 if its real-time reserves were to drop below 1,250 MW.
The choice of the 1,250 MW threshold is simply a target used to determine if intra-hour violations are occurring and is consistent with the load shed point applied in the Reserve Margin Study. Another key consideration is that the 1,250 MW threshold plays a big part in establishing a 1-event-in-10-year loss of load expectation (“LOLE”) level of reliability, as described on page 10 of the study. For example, if the threshold was instead lowered to 0 MW, annual reliability would then be better than 1-in-10 years, so capacity would be removed from the model to return to the 1-in-10-year target. The baseline level of flexibility violations would again be established but with lower system capacity. The Study would still record a flexibility violation if reserves dropped below 0 MW, except the System would not have any additional reserves available to mitigate the system imbalance.

question: Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-31(b), stating that 3,800 MW of CT capacity was added to the Base Case to meet the LOLE standard of 0.1 days/year, and the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-34, stating that for the 7.5 GW case, 2,875 MW was removed from the case to meet the 1-in-10 standard.  Is it a correct interpretation that the Base Case with 3,800 MW of CT capacity and the solar case with 7,500 MW of solar plus 925 MW of CT capacity both met the LOLE standard of 0.1 days/year?
response: Yes, 3,800 MW of CT-Gas resources were added to establish an annual 0.1 days/year no-solar base case. When 7.5 GW of solar were also added, 2,875 MW of the same CT-Gas resources were removed to re-establish the annual loss of load expectation (“LOLE”) of 0.1 days/year due to the capacity value that solar provided. The CT-Gas resources were also removed for the entire year when the solar was added. Therefore, the seasonal LOLE likely showed lower reliability in the winter and greater reliability in the summer even though the annual LOLE remained at 0.1 days/year. This is due to solar resources historically having a lower capacity contribution during the winter months as compared to summer months.

question:
Please refer to the Company’s response to “STF-PIA-3-8 Attachment B TRADE SECRET.xlsx”:
Please explain why the 2-hr Battery receives 100% ELCC while the 4-hr Demand Response ELCC receives 85%. Provide any workpapers to support this if applicable.
Please explain why the Loss Factor is set at 5.24%. Please provide workpapers to support this calculation.
Provide all analysis and workpapers to support the Retail Capacity Price Forecast found in cells C11 through C44.
Did the Company consider energy benefits when calculating the incentive values? Explain why this was or was not included.
Please explain whether the Company considered any additional RCB components when calculating the incentive values. If so, which components were considered.
Explain how the MUSH/LMI incentive of $1,000/kW was calculated for the Company-Directed option.
Explain how the $15/kW incentive was calculated for the Customer-Directed option.
response:
The 2-hour battery resource used to determine incentive levels in the Company-Directed pathway is assumed to be capable of providing operating reserves in the form of spinning and regulating reserves. To enable the System to respond to unforeseen events such as forced generator outages and maintain grid stability, a minimum level of operating reserves is maintained at all times. Because of the flexibility that batteries provide, they are well suited to perform this task provided they can respond in near real time. The Company anticipates this will be possible in the Company-Directed pathway. At this point in time, the System has not reached this operating reserve saturation point with committed or in-service battery resources, so incremental 2-hour batteries are receiving a 100% effective load carrying capability (“ELCC”) as they displace other resources from commitments to reserves. Once there are enough batteries on the System to cover the minimum operating reserves requirement, the high ELCC value of 2-hour batteries degrades.
Battery resources in the Customer-Directed option will be dispatched in discrete events with advanced notice, similar to demand response programs and are not capable of providing operating reserves. Many of our modeled and historical reliability events are more than 4 hours in length, so a 4-hour demand response program is not capable of responding for the entire duration of those events. This duration restriction and the lead time for responses to materialize reduces the ELCC below 100%.
The Loss Factor is set at 5.24% based on the assumption that all participating customers are taking service at the secondary distribution level. This percentage reflects the average losses that occur in delivering energy from a bulk system generator to the customer load and is derived from historical System data.  Please see STF-PIA-12-17 Attachment A.
Please see STF-PIA-12-17 Attachment B TRADE SECRET.
No, the Company did not consider energy benefits when calculating the storage-based incentive values. The intent of the incentives is to promote the addition of storage, which is not an energy-generating resource. Participating customers will also benefit from reducing their own consumption and are able to participate in RNR which compensates customers for energy delivered to the grid.
When calculating the incentive values for storage, the Company considered several Renewable Cost Benefit (“RCB”) components. Specifically, deferred generation capacity costs, which account for the reduced need to invest in new generation facilities due to the storage capacity. The Company also included avoided transmission losses and avoided distribution losses, recognizing that customer-sited resources reduce energy losses associated with delivery of energy to the load.
The MUSH/LMI incentive of $1,000 per kW for the Company-Directed option was calculated based on the System value before applying the 75% shared savings factor. This approach reflects the full value of the avoided costs associated with the storage solutions in these segments.
The combination of upfront incentive and pay-for-performance incentive in the Customer-Directed pathway was set to achieve 75% of the total System value. Having most of the incentive allocated through pay-for-performance protects non-participants. The $15 per kW incentive for the Customer-Directed option yields a 1.50 $/kWh pay for performance incentive over 50 hours. These round numbers should make it easier for stakeholders to determine the benefits of participating in the program and calculate anticipated incentives.

question:
Please refer to the Company’s response to STF-PIA-3-8(b):
Please explain how the limits encourage “right-sizing the ratio of solar and storage”.
Please explain how the maximum system sizes will be calculated.
response:
The limits are intended to encourage an appropriate sizing of solar and battery capacity by achieving the following goals:
Encouraging solar system sizes that are consistent with existing behind the meter solar programs, which will enable more efficient and cost-effective program implementation and individual project management and processing.
Ensure that residential customers currently participating in existing solar programs can add an AC coupled battery, which could increase total export capacity, and still be eligible for participation.
Ensure that a participating battery can be adequately charged by the solar resource.
Limit potential distribution system upgrades and impacts, for which the costs are currently socialized across all retail customers and offset by the one-time Interconnection Fee.
The maximum system size will be calculated based on the expectation that behind-the-meter assets should not be capable of pushing back more than the stated limit onto the grid. Currently, system size as determined for the purposes of the solar program qualification is based on the maximum continuous output of the solar inverter. If a system is paired with a battery, the total of both the solar and the battery export capabilities will be used to determine the system’s overall size with respect to qualification. AC and DC coupled configurations will differ in how nameplate ratings of individual components may translate into system size determination for program qualification. Regardless of the configuration, the total maximum capacity that could be delivered to the grid at any point, should not exceed the program defined limitations.

question: Please confirm how the company’s methodology for the large load forecast external adjustment aligns with requirements set in the Official Code of Georgia Annotated § 46-3A-2 or GA PSC Rules and Regulations Subject 515-3-4 Integrated Resource Planning.
response:
O.C.G.A. § 46-3A-2 requires the Company to file an Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) every three years and provides for a public hearing before the Commission regarding the contents and adequacy of Georgia Power’s IRP. Following the hearing, the Commission is required to determine, in part, whether the Company’s forecast requirements are based on substantially accurate data and an adequate method of forecasting.
The 2025 IRP supports the reasonableness and accuracy of the data, assumptions, and methods underlying the Company’s 20-year load and energy forecast.
Commission Rule 515-3-4-.03 identifies detailed Energy and Demand Forecasting Requirements. The Commission Rules set forth a floor on the minimum requirements of the load and energy forecast in terms of the methodology, data, and determinants, as well as the appropriate sensitivity analysis for major assumptions. Consistent with prior IRPs, the Company’s forecast meets each of the requirements set forth in the Commission Rules.
The Company’s forecast accounts for organic growth associated with the residential, commercial, industrial, government, and MARTA classes, as well as for the impacts of demand-side management (“DSM”), behind the meter customer generation, electric vehicles, and large loads. Initially introduced in the Company’s 2023 IRP Update, in Docket No. 55378, the large load adjustment is an external adjustment applied to the organic forecast to account for the likelihood and volume of additional large customer load associated with Georgia’s extraordinary economic growth. This adjustment, which is developed using the probabilistic Load Realization Model, is necessary because it accounts for load that would not otherwise be captured in the extrapolation of historic, organic growth load.
The risk adjustment for large loads is appropriate and comparable to the other three external adjustments the Company has historically employed (DSM, behind the meter customer generation, and electric vehicles), which are consistent with the impact analysis required in Commission Rule 515-3-4-.03(c).

question:
Please describe how the demand response that Georgia Power calculates it will get from Real-Time Pricing customers is subdivided into regular price response, which is incorporated into the load forecast, and “Extreme Response” that is reflected in the Company’s resource ledger (i.e., DSO forecasts and the Territorial Base Case vs Existing Resources filed with the Mix Study) as megawatts of demand response capacity. The Beppler et al. panel discussed this breakdown during cross examination on March 27, 2025
If it based on a specific or relative RTP price level, please describe:
What is the price above which demand response is classified as Extreme Response?
For how many hours per year does the Company estimate RTP will exceed that hourly price in each of the years 2026 – 2035?
If it is based on a different metric, please describe that metric and how many hours per year the Company estimates RTP will enter Extreme Response conditions.
response:
The Real-Time Pricing (“RTP”) response study analyzes how customers’ demand responds to different pricing scenarios under RTP price levels. The study focuses on understanding and forecasting the megawatt (“MW”) response from customers when faced with normal RTP prices versus extreme RTP prices, calculated by averaging the top 10 highest hourly prices each month. Extreme RTP prices are defined as three times the forecasted RTP prices.
Below is a breakdown of the key components:
Segmented Responses
The study differentiates between Hour Ahead and Day Ahead RTP customers, allowing for a more tailored analysis of response behaviors.
Historical and Projected Response
Historical data is used to model the MW response to RTP prices. This model is then applied to predict future responses, taking into account normal and extreme pricing scenarios.
Normal versus Extreme Response
Normal Response: Captured in the forecast using average RTP prices observed in 2023. This reflects expected customer behavior under typical pricing conditions.
Extreme Response: Estimated using prices that are significantly higher (three times the hourly forecast RTP price for the year 2034). This scenario is designed to simulate customer behavior under unusually high price conditions, which are not expected to occur under normal circumstances.
Calculation of Extreme Response
The extreme response is calculated by subtracting the normal response from the total response at extreme price levels. For example, if the total response to extreme prices is 500 MW and the normal response is 250 MW, the extreme response would be 250 MW.
Use of Forecasted Prices
The study uses forecasted RTP prices for the years 2026-2035 to model responses. However, these forecasted prices under normal conditions do not reach the levels set for extreme response modeling, as extreme prices are unlikely in typical weather or operational scenarios.

question: What performance goals has Georgia Power adopted to ensure continuity of essential services while managing cybersecurity risk?
response:

These program requirements are designed to cover “all hazards,” which apply to cyber disruptions, especially as considered for Power Delivery and/or Customer Care Operations.
Business continuity plans identify the personnel, procedures, resources, and technical requirements needed to recover and restore business processes.
A business continuity plan is required for each business-critical process. All business units are encouraged to develop business continuity plans for other business processes to promote a culture of resilience.
All business continuity plans are documented and maintained in an application approved for use and supported by the Enterprise Resilience department.
All business continuity plans have an assigned primary and back-up plan owner. The plan owner(s) is responsible for ensuring plan development, maintenance, and testing. If updates are necessary, the plan owner(s) will communicate any changes to key stakeholders in the plan(s).
Business continuity plans are typically designed to contain the following components, as applicable:
The names and description of the business-critical process to be recovered.
Any strategies and/or specific tasks necessary to ensure the continuation of that process until normal business operations are restored.
Contact information for all stakeholders who should be notified in the event the plan is activated (this includes employees and third parties).
All Tier 0, 1, or 2 technology assets (applications and/or infrastructure) needed to support business critical processes and Technology Organization contacts for the related Asset Recovery Plans.
Alternate work locations and needs (e.g. supplies, equipment) identified.
Electronic copies of critical documents (e.g. procedures, guidelines, recovery tasks).
A pandemic plan.
Each Business Assurance Council (BAC) member (which includes the Incident Support Team (IST) leaders) will annually review their list of business-critical processes; and
Leadership of each business unit that has a business-critical process is required to ensure that a business continuity plan is in place, and that it is annually reviewed and exercised (e.g. tabletops, walkthroughs, workshops).

question: Please provide an update on current and potential impacts of artificial intelligence on Georgia Power’s operations. Are there any recent findings or case studies regarding malicious use of AI?
response:
Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) is affecting Georgia Power in two primary ways: (1) improving operations and (2) driving new demand. On operations, Georgia Power reports ongoing grid modernization using innovative technologies and a data driven reliability approach, with help from increased use of advanced analytics. Separately, AI is a major driver of load growth via data centers, with public reporting noting large capacity needs to serve that demand.
Georgia Power’s cybersecurity organization maintains continuous monitoring for threats that could affect utility infrastructure and business operations, recognizing that adversaries are increasingly using AI to scale social engineering and automate cyber activity against critical infrastructure operators. At the same time, we view AI as a dual use capability, it can strengthen defensive outcomes (e.g., faster detection and response), while also enabling attackers to increase speed, scale, and sophistication, requiring disciplined governance and ongoing control enhancements. Based on the Company’s current monitoring and controls, Georgia Power has not discovered or reported any material AI driven incidents impacting operations at this time, and Georgia Power will continue to adjust the Company’s detection and response posture as the threat environment evolves.

question: What does Georgia Power identify as the greatest challenges in improving cybersecurity and physical security practices across critical infrastructure?
response: Georgia Power identifies its greatest challenges in improving cybersecurity and physical security practices across critical infrastructure lie in keeping pace with rapidly evolving and increasingly sophisticated threat landscape. For example, the evolving threat of drones used against the electric sector remains a challenge to address due to the lack of state law that deems it illegal for drones to operate near or over critical infrastructure. Further, the pace at which threats are escalating has fundamentally changed due to the proliferation of AI and the speed at which attacks can be launched. In addition, supply chain risks present challenges for maintaining the cyber and physical security of critical infrastructure as many supply chain components are imported from overseas, which makes it difficult to track foreign entities that may exert control over or have another beneficial interest in a supplier or the supplier’s products. The Company must continuously assess and respond to emerging physical and cyber threats identified through the Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center (E-ISAC) and other industry information sharing programs. This dynamic environment requires ongoing adjustments to protective strategies as well as a multi-layered security approach to ensure continued resilience.

question:
How does Georgia Power determine the appropriate level of investment in cybersecurity and physical security measures?
a.	What benchmarks or industry standards are used to guide spending decisions?
b.	How does the Company evaluate cost-effectiveness of security controls?
response:
Georgia Power complies with all applicable NERC Critical Infrastructure Protection (“CIP”) Reliability Standard requirements and has strategically implemented a layered approach to both physical and cyber security that are based on industry standards for the electric sector. The Company continuously evaluates evolving physical and cyber threats, identified through the Electricity Information Sharing and Analysis Center (“E-ISAC”) and other industry information sharing programs, and has implemented corresponding resiliency measures to mitigate any potential vulnerabilities.
Georgia Power evaluates the cost-effectiveness of its security controls by ensuring that all implemented measures align with applicable NERC CIP Reliability Standards and support the Company’s layered security approach.
Security controls are designed to deter, detect, delay, and protect critical assets, ensuring that investments directly support risk reduction and operational resilience.
Georgia Power determines the appropriate level of security investment using a risk-based approach anchored to reliability standards, with oversight structures that drive prioritization and accountability. Georgia Power utilizes a “defense in depth” strategy led by a centralized Cybersecurity organization, intended to reduce risk through layered controls rather than reliance on any single measure.
Primary benchmarks include NERC CIP (including applicable physical security requirements for BES assets) and NIST CSF 2.0 as an enterprise risk framework to assess and prioritize cybersecurity outcomes; NIST also provides mapping guidance between CSF and NERC CIP to support maturity beyond minimum compliance.
Georgia Power evaluates the cost effectiveness of cybersecurity investments through a risk-based prioritization model and formal budget oversight. Investments are sized and sequenced based on the credible threat environment, asset criticality, and potential operational impact (including reliability and safety), ensuring the highest risk exposures are addressed first. This approach aligns with Georgia Power’s publicly described risk based, “defense in depth” strategy and enterprise accountability for protecting critical infrastructure. Budget discipline is enforced through portfolio level governance (e.g., a budget governance committee) that reviews and prioritizes security requests to confirm: (1) the investment is tied to a defined risk and business outcome and (2) it complements existing layered controls rather than duplicating capability.
For information on the Company’s Cybersecurity and Risk Management profile, see STF-PIA-18-17 Attachment.pdf

question: What processes are in place to prevent unnecessary duplication of cybersecurity tools or services?
response:
Georgia Power’s Cybersecurity Organization applies a structured governance framework to prevent unnecessary duplication of cybersecurity tools and services. Proposed security solutions are reviewed through an Architectural Review Board (“ARB”) prior to implementation to confirm architectural fit, alignment with existing capabilities, and a validated business use case. In addition, as a centralized Cybersecurity Architecture function, the ARB reviews all security products for appropriateness, overlap, and operational readiness.
Financial discipline is reinforced through a Budget Governance Committee, which reviews and prioritizes cybersecurity investments to ensure consolidation where possible and alignment with enterprise standards. Together, these controls provide layered oversight that limits tool proliferation, promotes efficient use of resources, and ensures cybersecurity investments are deliberate, coordinated, and risk driven.

question: How does the Company currently determine whether wildfires are identified as an ‘extreme weather risk’ in its service territory?
response:
The Company produces a five-day forecast of wildfire conditions over its service territory and maintains a corresponding Wildfire Operational Alert matrix to guide operational response in areas forecast to observe conditions favorable for wildfire ignition and spread. The forecast is evaluated using the Company's Fire Potential Index (FPI), which assigns one of five fire potential levels based on forecast conditions. The resulting fire potential level is used in conjunction with the Wildfire Operational Alert matrix to determine the appropriate level of preparedness and response.
Please see STF-PIA-22-2 Attachment for the matrix.
The Wildfire Operational Alert matrix provides a structured framework for evaluating identified wildfire risks and determining the appropriate level of operational response across the service territory. The FPI assesses fire risk over the next five days and provides a consistent basis for escalating preparedness and response activities as conditions warrant.
The FPI is calibrated using established thresholds in weather conditions and fire science, together with historical environment data in the vicinity of large fires that have occurred in the Southeast. By incorporating these factors, the FPI is designed to reflect conditions and wildfire characteristics relevant to the company's geographic region and operating environment. The index consists of five distinct levels representing increasing degrees of fire potential. Each level is associated with a corresponding set of actions and response measures, allowing the company to adjust its posture as fire conditions change.
Together, the Wildfire Operational Alert matrix and FPI provide a coordinated approach for identifying, evaluating, and responding to wildfire risk. The five FPI levels and the corresponding actions associated with each level are outlined in the attached matrix.

question: Does Georgia Power currently track grid utilization metrics at the transmission, substation, and distribution level? If so, please identify the metrics and provide a brief description of each. If not, what information would be needed to develop such metrics?
response:
In general, the Company interprets the broad industry definition of grid utilization as a measure of how much available capacity is being used by comparing facility loading to the applicable facility rating. The Company evaluates utilization based on usable capacity under defined operating and reliability conditions across the transmission, substation, and distribution systems as part of its planning processes to identify and understand loading trends, evaluate future system needs, and determine when facilities may approach planning or operational limitations.
Examples of grid utilization assessments performed include:
Transmission: Evaluation of loading on transmission facilities, such as transmission lines and bulk power transformers, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating and contingency scenarios across multiple seasons.
Substation: Evaluation of loading on substation facilities, such as load-serving power transformers, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating scenarios across multiple seasons.
Distribution: Evaluation of loading on distribution facilities, such as distribution feeders, relative to applicable ratings under normal operating scenarios across multiple seasons.
The Company’s transmission planning methodologies and guidelines are described in Sections A and B of Technical Appendix Volume 3 in the 2025 IRP in Docket No. 56002.  For load-serving substations and distribution feeders, the Company uses internal planning criteria to evaluate projected peak loads against facility ratings to maintain safe and reliable electric service to its customers.
While utilization assessments are considered as part of the Company’s planning process, utilization is viewed alongside other inputs including safety, reliability, resilience, operational flexibility, and affordability. The Company seeks to make efficient use of existing facilities and does not rely on a single, standalone grid utilization metric when identifying and evaluating system needs.

The Company does not calculate an aggregate system utilization figure for generation. Low utilization for these resources is expected and does not indicate inefficiency or ineffective operation.

question: Given that Georgia Power already maintains a target reserve margin above the industry standard of ~15%, can some of that existing transmission capacity headroom be used more efficiently to serve uncertain large-load growth before additional infrastructure is built, and if so, how much new large-load demand could that reserve margin accommodate before triggering new transmission investment?
response:
The reference to 15% as the industry-standard target reserve margin is inaccurate. In its reliability assessments, the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) compares each assessment area against the reference margin level set by that area’s state regulator, independent system operator/regional transmission organization, or other authority and applies 15% only as a default for predominantly thermal areas that do not provide one, which is the case for the Southeastern Subregion of SERC Reliability Corporation (SERC). The Company’s Commission-approved target reserve margins are set through a comprehensive reserve margin study specifically for the Southern Company System and are not comparable to NERC’s 15% reference margin  for reliability assessments.
Importantly, “transmission capacity headroom” and target reserve margin are two distinct and separate concepts. The target reserve margin is maintained to ensure generation resource-adequacy, while the transmission adequacy analysis, as described in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 3, addresses a different purpose. That analysis ensures reliable delivery of energy from generation resources to loads under various planning events and ensures compliance with mandatory NERC reliability standards.
The Company’s transmission planning process and methodologies are described in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix, Volume 3. This document includes information regarding transmission planning principles, transmission system evaluation, planning coordination, project development and evaluation, planning tools, planning guidelines, applicable NERC reliability standards, and other considerations used in developing the Ten-Year Plan. The ability to serve new large loads depends on a variety of factors, including the location, timing, and load profile of the customer under contract, as well as the generation, transmission, distribution, and interconnection facilities necessary to reliably serve all customers. Please refer to the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix, Volume 3, for a complete discussion of these topics.

question: Do any DSM/energy-efficiency programs get credited toward reducing system peak demand in a way that shows up in the reserve margin or IRP planning numbers?
response:
In IRP planning numbers, the Company considers cost-effective energy efficiency and demand response programs as priority resources. These programs are the first resources considered in serving customers’ future needs and are included in the planning process prior to identifying the need for any new supply-side resources.
Energy efficiency programs reduce the Company’s load forecast directly. Their projected energy and demand savings are embedded in the forecast used for planning. Demand response measures, by contrast, are treated as a capacity resource and are included in the resource ledger under Dispatchable Demand-Side Options (“DSOs”), as consistently demonstrated in all of the Company’s filed workpapers and models in IRPs and resource certification filings.
Both the load forecast (reflecting energy efficiency savings) and the capacity resource ledger (reflecting demand response capacity) feed into the reserve margin study. Energy efficiency reduces the peak demand the reserve margin is measured against, while demand response adds capacity that counts toward meeting it.

question: How does SAIDI/SAIFI performance get weighed against utilization goals — is there a risk that running assets harder to raise utilization could work against the reliability metrics Georgia Power is already held to?
response:
Adopting broad grid utilization metrics with goals to increase said metrics would create unnecessary risk to reliability performance and overall customer experience. Such risks include reduced equipment life, longer outage times, and diminished customer value taken from the Company’s longstanding smart grid investments.
For example, if every feeder operated at or near its full capacity all the time, the system would not have the capacity to manage reliability events. If an outage impacted a portion of one circuit, neighboring circuits could not take on the affected load because the system is already at full capacity. Customers would then face longer outages and lower reliability, impacting SAIDI/SAIFI, and safety may also be at risk. Operational flexibility is intentional because it allows the system to respond when problems occur.
Georgia Power has practices and work processes across multiple workgroups to mitigate risks related to asset loading and grid configuration. The Company does not operate equipment outside of rated capabilities or historical best practices to meet any particular metric. The Company works to improve SAIDI and SAIFI performance metrics by operating the system efficiently and pursuing system improvements that deliver greater value to customers.

question: Some recent studies show that flexible resources may be good options for large load by the use of existing headroom plus flexible resources plus phased investment and then build permanent infrastructure as load becomes more certain. In other words, build less first and keep options open. For example: use of battery, demand response, flexible interconnection, managed load, and use of grid enhancing technologies. Use these flexible resources until load becomes sufficiently certain to justify the permanent investment. However, they may also require major transmission upgrades because of fundamental thermal or stability constraints. For example, A 100 MW battery cannot simply replace 1000 MW transmission investment. Therefore, when large load project is uncertain or phased, has Georgia Power evaluated flexible interconnection, storage, demand response, managed load, and grid- enhancing technologies etc. as an interim solution to reduce the risk of building infrastructure that could later be underutilized? response:
As discussed in the 2025 IRP Technical Appendix Volume 3, transmission capacity is determined by transmission system evaluations using a measured approach that balances safety, reliability, affordability, and resiliency.
Consistent with that approach, the Company plans and builds for firm and future firm load commitments. The Company is not building infrastructure to accommodate non-committed large load growth, as doing so could result in unnecessary costs being borne by customers.
Under the Commission-approved rules and regulations for large load customers, the Commission and the Company protect existing customers from bearing any of the costs of adding large load customers. Contract provisions such as minimum term lengths, minimum bills, performance security, and termination schedules ensure large load customers cover all costs necessary to serve their load, including upstream transmission system enhancements and infrastructure investments. In addition, through existing cost recovery mechanisms such as upfront payments, large load customers are responsible for all the costs of the local infrastructure required to serve their load.
The Company’s measured approach also includes customer-specific flexibility options designed to support system safety, reliability, affordability, and resiliency while accommodating for economic development growth in a responsible manner. See the Company’s load flexibility Compliance Report filed with the Commission on June 30, 2026, in Docket Nos. 56298 & 56310.

question: Refer to the 2025 IRP Main Document, page 102, which states “The largest procurement of energy from customer-sited resources comes from residential solar installations, which are compensated at prices above the value these resources deliver.” Provide workpapers supporting this statement, including the details of how customers are being compensated and the details behind the valuation of those resources.
response:
Please reference the workpaper “Customer-sited Program Volume – Table 10.2” provided to Commission Staff on January 31, 2025, in the 2025 Integrated Resource Plan (“IRP”) Workpapers 1-31-25 TRADE SECRET, Main Document folder, which supports the statement that “the largest procurement of energy from customer-sited resources comes from residential solar installations” and is the source for the data provided in Table 10.2 on page 100 of the 2025 IRP Main Document.
The statement that such customer generators “are compensated at prices above the value these resources deliver” is based on a comparison of the compensation paid to these customer generators to the Company’s annual Solar Avoided Cost. The Solar Avoided Cost is calculated using the Commission-approved Renewable Cost Benefit (“RCB”) Framework, which establishes the value of energy that renewable resources deliver to the grid. It is Georgia Power’s position that any renewable generator compensated at a rate that exceeds the Solar Avoided Cost is compensated greater than the value of the energy that resource is delivering. This position is consistent with the Company’s testimony in the 2022 Rate Case in Docket No. 44280 and 2023 IRP Update in Docket No. 55378.
The Renewable and Nonrenewable Resources (“RNR”) tariff outlines the compensation mechanism and methodology for residential customer-sited generators up to ten kilowatts (“kW”) and Commercial or Industrial customer-sited generators up to 250 kW. Under the standard RNR compensation methodology, customers receive credit at the annual Solar Avoided Cost rate for any excess energy delivered to the grid by their resource. As ordered in the 2019 IRP, Georgia Power established a monthly netting compensation mechanism for the first 5,000 participants in the RNR tariff. Under this methodology, known as “RNR-Monthly Netting,” customer generators receive net retail energy credit for excess energy, thereby providing participating customers the full retail credit for the energy the Company procures from them. Further, as ordered in the 2022 IRP, any subsequent customer participants in the RNR tariff are to receive Solar Avoided Cost credit, plus an additional four-cents per kilowatt hour for excess energy delivered to the grid, known as RNR-Instantaneous Netting. Thus, all customer generators participating in these RNR programs are compensated at prices that exceed the Company’s Solar Avoided Cost and the corresponding value of the energy delivered to the grid, as determined by the RCB Framework.

Refer to the 2025 IRP Main Document, page 107, which describes the Large Customer Owned Resiliency Program.
It appears to PIA Staff that the Company’s DPEC-4 tariff/demand response credit program already provides “economic value for firm load reductions while accelerating the timeframe in which capacity can be recognized”. Given the Company’s DPEC-4 tariff/credit program, please explain why this proposed program is necessary.
Refer to the statement “Like all the Company’s DER programs, non- participating customers benefit through the shared savings model where capacity is being procured at a discount relative to generic capacity costs.” Provide the workpapers indicating (or estimating) i) the price at which capacity is likely to be procured under the program; ii) generic capacity costs and iii) a sample calculation using current capacity values.
response:
The Large Customer Owned Resiliency Program (“LCOR”) requires the installation and performance of non-emergency generators with a firm fuel supply. To allow for operational certainty of the demand response when called upon, customers will be isolated from the grid if no response is received from assets during events called under Energy Emergency Alert (“EEA”) conditions. This program design provides operational certainty not provided through the Demand Plus Energy Credit (“DPEC”) program. In addition, LCOR will also be a long-term contract rather than a one-year commitment, which will provide assurance of capacity availability over a longer term.
Please refer to STF-WG-1-11 Attachment TRADE SECRET.

question:
Refer to the 2025 IRP Main Document, page 108, which states “The Company is currently administering a residential pilot with both passive and active managed charging participation options for customers.” Please provide relevant internal documents regarding this pilot, including:
A description of the pilot and its design, including a list of all learning objectives and specific results to be measured.
A description of the pilot’s costs, presentations provided to Company management to secure spending approval, and Company management and/or Commission approval of the pilot.
Current status of the pilot, including passive participants, active participants, expected pilot completion, and anticipated pilot results reporting date.
response:
The following pilot information was shared with Commission Staff on August 16, 2023:
The Company is proactively preparing for continued growth in the rate of electric vehicle adoption and wishes to launch a multi-phase Electric Vehicle Managed Charging Pilot with our customers, which will help us:
Evaluate the effectiveness and potential of utilizing electric vehicle chargers as a low demand response resource from passive charging and active managed charging.
Study customer behavior and charging patterns within the existing structure of passive charging and monitor various metrics, including start and stop times of charging, energy per charging session, and average and peak demand per charging session.
Learnings from the analysis of passive managed charging will inform a baseline for active managed charging for demand response purposes.
Identify hotspots and grid assets that could be strained by increased load from electric vehicle charging and incorporate insights into distribution asset planning, O&M activities, or infrastructure upgrade efforts.
Utilize program participation from the electric vehicle charger measures in the existing Home Energy Improvement/Marketplace energy efficiency offerings.
Conduct at least 4 DR events, 2 in winter and 2 in summer.
Educate pilot participants on additional energy efficiency and demand response programs.
This pilot was developed and funded as part of the DSM pilot budget of $3 million dollars per year approved by the Commission in paragraph 59 of the 2022 Integrated Resource Plan and DSM Application Final Order. The pilot cost was $630,000 for implementation, participant incentives, and the third-party evaluation. Commission Staff approved the pilot via email on August 23, 2023.
Pilot enrollment closed on September 30, 2024. As of March 4, 2025, there are 360 passive participants and 431 active participants. The pilot ends on June 30, 2025, and the anticipated pilot results will be reported in Q3 2025.

question:
Refer to the 2025 IRP Main Document, page 109, regarding the descriptions of the Company’s efforts to deploy a DERMS. Refer also to the Company’s 2025 IRP Renewable Cost-Benefit Framework.
a. 	Provide a description of the capabilities and benefits of each of the systems referred to on page 109, including but not limited to DERMS, ADMS, EMS, PPC, and other “existing and upcoming systems”.
b. 	Provide the DER gateway requirements and the Company’s anticipated implementation timelines, including any applications anticipated by the Company to update its DER interconnection standards. Specifically, include a description of the circumstances in which the Company expects to control customer-owned DER by customer DER program/DER facility capacity.
c. 	Refer to the list of systems and descriptions provided in response to subpart (a) above. For each, provide the anticipated dollar amount of rate base additions required for deployment, along with the depreciation period the Company will use for each.
d. 	Refer generally to the list of systems and descriptions provided in response to subpart (a) above. Please explain how Georgia Power accounts for the benefits and costs of these systems in the Company’s 2025 IRP Renewable Cost Benefit framework.
response:
Please see below for a description of the capabilities and benefits requested.
Distributed Energy Resource Management System (“DERMS”)
The Company is in the process of implementing a new GE DERMS platform. This  DERMS acts as a centralized system-of-systems and is comprised of both hardware and software designed to provide visibility, forecasting, control, and optimization of distributed energy resource (“DER”) devices in coordination with existing grid real-time operations control systems. Enhanced control of DER devices through DERMS will enable the Company to ensure grid reliability, enable, and optimize DER grid support functions in a way that coordinates among both Company- and customer-owned DER devices. Specifically, having enhanced control of DERs will allow for these devices to be dispatched to ensure optimal grid operation across different resource types and within program parameters. This capability can expand potential DER use cases and value to the grid, including but not limited to the ability to recognize capacity value for aggregated assets.
Advanced Distribution Management System (“ADMS”)
The Company is in the process of transitioning from Oracle Network Management System (“NMS”) to GE ADMS. ADMS software platforms provide real-time monitoring and control capabilities, as well as a suite of tools and advanced applications that are needed to reliably manage the distribution grid in real-time. Grid operators use ADMS for many purposes, such as identifying grid disturbances, analyzing system power flows, and managing device switching and outages. The benefits of ADMS include continued reliable and efficient operation of the distribution network, enhanced situational awareness, faster response to grid issues, and enabling better integration of renewable energy sources and DERs.
Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA)
SCADA systems provide real-time data acquisition and control capabilities for the electric grid. They enable the monitoring and control of various power system assets from a centralized location. SCADA systems will integrate with other systems like DERMS and ADMS to enhance grid visibility and operational efficiency. The benefits of SCADA include improved real-time monitoring and control of grid operations, faster response to grid anomalies, enhanced data collection for better decision-making, and improved overall reliability and efficiency of the power system.
Energy Management System (“EMS”)
An EMS provides real-time monitoring and control capabilities, as well as a suite of tools and advanced applications, that are needed to manage the transmission grid. Grid operators can use EMS for outage management, optimization of power flows, reactive power control, managing system switching, and forecasting and planning potential impacts to real-time grid operations. The benefits of EMS include improved reliability and stability of the transmission network, enhanced operational efficiency and cost savings, and better integration of large-scale renewable energy sources and DERs.
Power Plant Controller (“PPC”)
A PPC is a control device installed in the field at a DER site and is responsible for the control and coordination of power generation assets downstream of the PPC at that site. A PPC can communicate with one or more DERs at a site, monitoring real-time data, and adjusting the operation of a connected DER in response to grid conditions or utility signals. A PPC managing a site with multiple DERs can simplify operations by serving as a centralized hub for communications and controls. IEEE 1547-2018 requires DER sites to have a single local communication interface for integration with the utility. A PPC meets that requirement for interconnection, enabling a single interface for utility monitoring and control of DER. The benefits of PPC include improved efficiency and reliability of power generation, enhanced ability to respond to grid demands and fluctuations, and better integration of DERs.
DER Gateway
A DER Gateway is a utility-owned device that facilitates secure communications between the utility and the local DER communications interface in the field (i.e., PPC), allowing for enhanced control of the DER via DERMS. With enhanced control capabilities, the Company’s DERMS will be able to issue control communications to the DER gateway in the field, which then communicates with the PPC at the DER site. The PPC then issues commands to the DER device(s) at that site to ensure a response to the signal from DERMS. A DER gateway provides additional security by protecting against cyber threats and data manipulation, and it can provide communication protocol translation, if needed. The DER gateway is a necessary field component that allows for cyber secure monitoring and enhanced control of DER via DERMS, which enables the Company to utilize DER grid support functions for grid support and optimization.
As required by IEEE 1547, the Company’s DER policy dictates that DERs shall be equipped with a local DER communication interface capable of providing nameplate information, monitoring information, reading or writing of configuration information, and reading or writing of management information. Communication protocols are also specified for the DER communications interface. The Company’s DER policy currently requires interval recording interchange metering equipment for DER capable of exporting 250 kW of real power. For DER capable of exporting 500 kW or more, interchange metering equipment and power quality monitoring must include current and voltage waveforms. The Company is currently developing DER gateway requirements to ensure reliable and cybersecure enhanced control of DER systems with an aggregate size of 250kVA or greater. The Company will require generators to install communications and control equipment, such as a PPC, that can communicate with a Company-owned DER gateway device and adhere to specific data telemetry requirements. These requirements would likely go into effect in the proposed 2026 DG RFP. Control of customer-owned DER will be limited to DER that customers choose to enroll in regulated retail programs offered by the Company and approved by the Commission. The controls executed will be limited to the contractual parameters of the program in which the DER is enrolled.

question:
Referring to the new DER Customer program, DCO-1, proposed in the 2025 IRP:
Please provide details for how the credit is calculated.
What would the credit per MW or per MWh have been if calculated for the period January 1, 2024, to December 31, 2024, per the credit calculation detail?
response:
The DER Customer Owned Program (“DCO-1”) was approved in the 2023 IRP Update, not proposed in the 2025 IRP.
In general, to calculate the credit for DCO-1:
Identify the DER’s capacity rating (MW).
Calculate the levelized capacity value ($/MW).
Calculate the capacity value by taking the Retail Capacity Price Forecast (“RCPF”) [$/kW-yr] from the in-service year through the term of the requested agreement.
Levelize these annual values with an appropriate discount rate.
Multiply by 75%.
Calculate the levelized energy value (if applicable) ($/MW).
Calculate the energy value [$/kW-yr] based on the forecasted margin between the DER and a generic peaking resource.
Levelize these annual values with an appropriate discount rate.
Multiply by 75%.
Sum the capacity and energy values from Steps 2 and 3 ($/MW).
Multiply the capacity rating (Step 1) by the levelized DER system value (Step 4) and divide by 12 to determine the fixed monthly credit for the term of the agreement ($).
In order to accurately calculate the credit value during this time period, certain variables, as outlined under the response to subpart (a), would need to be identified, including:
Resource type
Resource capacity
Resource in-service date
Contract duration
Fuel type and costs

question:
Referring to the new DER Customer program, LCO-1, proposed in the 2025 IRP:
Please provide details for how the credit is calculated with an example.
How does this compare for demand response credits for DPEC-4?
response:
In general, to calculate the credit for the Large Customer Owned Resiliency (“LCOR”) Program:
Establish the amount of demand response the customer can provide by using on-site eligible generation.
Calculate the levelized DER capacity value, similar to the DER Customer Owned Program (“DCO-1”) calculation in response to STF-WG-3-2(a).
Calculate the capacity value by taking the Retail Capacity Price Forecast (“RCPF”) [$/kW-yr] from the in-service year through the term of the requested agreement.
Levelize these annual values with an appropriate discount rate.
Multiply by 75%.
Multiply the demand response capacity (Step 1) by the levelized DER capacity value (Step 2) and divide by 12 to determine the fixed monthly credit for the term of the agreement.
Theoretically, if the customer has a firm base load of 100 MW and commits to reduce to 50 MW during a demand response event, the capacity credit would be derived from the difference between the firm load and the demand response commitment (i.e., 100 MW -50 MW = 50 MW). With an assumed $100/kW-yr levelized capacity value, the resulting monthly credit value would be (50,000 kW x $100/kW-yr x 0.75 ÷ 12 months/yr) = $312,500/mo. That said, specific parameters regarding customer load and demand reductions can affect credit value and will be identified in the customer specific agreement.
Demand response credits for the Demand Plus Energy Credit (“DPEC”) program have been reviewed and established during rate case proceedings and outlined in the current DPEC-5 tariff.
